abstract: This paper describes a CMOS artificial neuron. The circuit is directly derived from the voltage-gated channel model of neural membrane, has low power dissipation, and small layout geometry. The principal motivations behind this work include a desire for high performance, more accurate neuron emulation, and the need for higher density in practical neural network implementations.

paragraphs: This paper describes an artificial neuron implemented as a CMOS electronic circuit. The design targets the electrical behavior of neurons over time. Its starting point is a model of voltage-gated channels in the neural membrane, making the biological mechanism the basis for the circuit’s construction.

The connection to a membrane model matters because the intended object of emulation is a neuron’s changing electrical response. Voltage-dependent channel behavior provides the organizing model for that response. The contribution is therefore both a circuit implementation and an approach to translating a biological description into an artificial neuron.

The abstract identifies low power dissipation and a small physical layout as properties of the circuit. These address the authors’ motivation to place more neurons into practical network implementations while pursuing high performance and more accurate emulation. The work brings those concerns together at the level of a single circuit element: the neuron must represent temporal behavior while remaining economical enough in power and space to support denser networks.
summary.tldr: A compact, low-power CMOS neuron derives its design from voltage-gated membrane channels to emulate neuronal electrical behavior over time.

title: A Low-Power CMOS Circuit Which Emulates Temporal Electrical Properties of Neurons

paragraphs: The paper studies the computational power of threshold circuits through geometry. It represents each Boolean function of n variables as a vector with one coordinate for each possible input. This turns questions about which functions a circuit can implement into problems that can be approached using linear algebra and linear programming.

The framework yields several kinds of bounds. These concern spurious memories in Hopfield networks, the number of functions available to circuits of a given depth, and the input functions needed to construct a threshold function. It also gives a lower bound on the error of approximating Boolean functions with sparse polynomials, connecting circuit representation with approximation quality.

A further result limits a correlation-based method for proving circuit-depth lower bounds. The authors construct representations in which polynomially many input functions jointly implement a target even though none is significantly correlated with it individually. This exposes a weakness of judging representational power through individual correlations. The geometric approach also generalizes earlier results and supplies simpler proofs based on elementary linear algebra.
summary.tldr: A geometric view of Boolean functions yields threshold-circuit bounds and exposes limits of correlation-based complexity arguments.

title: On the Circuit Complexity of Neural Networks

abstract: Signal processing capabilities of biological neurons are investigated. Temporally coded signals in neurons can be multiplexed to increase the transmission capacity. Multiplexing of signal is suggested in bi-threshold neurons with high-threshold and low-thre shold for switching firing II II II II modes. To extract the signal embedded in the interspikeintervals of firing, the encoded signal are de multiplexed and multiplexed by a network of neurons with delayed-line circuitry for signal processing. The temporally coded input signal is transformed spatially by mapping the firing intervals topographically to the output of the network, thus decoding the specific firing inters pike-intervals. The network also provides a band-pass filtering capability where the variability of the timing of the original signal can be decoded.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how neurons might process signals carried by the timing of their spikes. It proposes multiplexing temporally coded signals to increase transmission capacity. The suggested mechanism uses neurons with a high threshold and a low threshold for switching between firing modes, providing a basis for handling the encoded information.

The information of interest lies in interspike intervals, the times separating successive firing events. A network with delay-line circuitry multiplexes and demultiplexes these signals. Its decoding operation converts timing differences into a spatial pattern: particular firing intervals map to particular locations in the network's output.

This temporal-to-spatial transformation makes specific intervals identifiable through where activity appears. The network also provides a band-pass filtering capability and can decode variability in the timing of the original signal. The contribution is a proposed neural signal-processing mechanism connecting firing-mode changes, delays, and spatial organization. It shows how a circuit could both separate information carried in spike timing and selectively respond to aspects of that temporal structure.
summary.tldr: A proposed neural circuit uses firing thresholds and delays to multiplex spike-timing signals and decode intervals into spatial activity.

title: Signal Processing by Multiplexing and Demultiplexing in Neurons

abstract: The goal of perception is to extract invariant properties of the underly(cid:173) ing world. By computing contrast at edges, the retina reduces incident light intensities spanning twelve decades to a twentyfold variation. In one stroke, it solves the dynamic range problem and extracts relative reflec(cid:173) tivity, bringing us a step closer to the goal. We have built a contrast(cid:173) sensitive silicon retina that models all major synaptic interactions in the outer-plexiform layer of the vertebrate retina using current-mode CMOS circuits: namely, reciprocal synapses between cones and horizontal cells, which produce the antagonistic center/surround receptive field, and cone and horizontal cell gap junctions, which determine its size. The chip has 90 x 92 pixels on a 6.8 x 6.9mm die in 2/lm n-well technology and is fully functional.

paragraphs: This paper presents a functioning silicon retina designed to respond to contrast. The motivation is that raw light intensity varies enormously, while differences between neighboring regions can reveal more stable properties of a scene. The biological retina's contrast processing compresses this intensity range and helps extract relative reflectivity.

The device models the major synaptic interactions in the vertebrate retina's outer plexiform layer using current-mode CMOS circuits. Reciprocal connections between cone and horizontal-cell circuits produce opposing responses to stimulation at the center and surrounding region. Connections corresponding to gap junctions between cones and between horizontal cells determine the spatial size of that response pattern.

The resulting chip contains a 90 by 92 pixel array and is reported to be fully functional. Its significance is the physical implementation of interconnected retinal mechanisms that jointly determine contrast sensitivity and spatial processing. The abstract's biological discussion explains the motivation for this design; the concrete engineering result is a working circuit that reproduces the specified interactions.
summary.tldr: A working silicon retina uses reciprocal connections and gap-junction circuits to implement retinal contrast processing.

title: A Contrast Sensitive Silicon Retina with Reciprocal Synapses
Neurobiology, Psychophysics, and Computational Models of Visual Attention

abstract: This paper describes the application of reinforcement learning (RL) to the difficult real world problem of elevator dispatching. The el(cid:173) evator domain poses a combination of challenges not seen in most RL research to date. Elevator systems operate in continuous state spaces and in continuous time as discrete event dynamic systems. Their states are not fully observable and they are nonstationary due to changing passenger arrival rates. In addition, we use a team of RL agents, each of which is responsible for controlling one ele(cid:173) vator car. The team receives a global reinforcement signal which appears noisy to each agent due to the effects of the actions of the other agents, the random nature of the arrivals and the incomplete observation of the state. In spite of these complications, we show results that in simulation surpass the best of the heuristic elevator control algorithms of which we are aware. These results demon(cid:173) strate the power of RL on a very large scale stochastic dynamic optimization problem of practical utility.

paragraphs: This paper applies reinforcement learning to elevator dispatching, a control problem with changing demand and incomplete information. Elevator operation unfolds in continuous time with discrete events and a continuous state space. Passenger arrival rates also change, so the learning system must act in a setting whose behavior is not stationary.

The system uses a team of agents, each controlling one elevator car. All agents receive a shared reinforcement signal describing the team's performance. For any individual agent, that feedback appears noisy because it also reflects other cars' actions, random passenger arrivals, and aspects of the state the agent cannot observe. Learning must therefore connect local decisions with a shared outcome.

Despite these complications, the reported simulation results exceed those of the best heuristic elevator controllers known to the authors. The result supports reinforcement learning for a large stochastic control problem with interacting decision makers. Its stated scope is simulation, where the approach succeeds despite combining partial observability, changing demand, and team-level feedback.
summary.tldr: A team of reinforcement learning agents controls elevator cars and outperforms the authors' strongest known heuristic controllers in simulation.

title: Improving Elevator Performance Using Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The Facial Action Coding System, (FACS), devised by Ekman and Friesen (1978), provides an objective meanS for measuring the facial muscle contractions involved in a facial expression. In this paper, we approach automated facial expression analysis by detecting and classifying facial actions. We generated a database of over 1100 image sequences of 24 subjects performing over 150 distinct facial actions or action combinations. We compare three different ap(cid:173) proaches to classifying the facial actions in these images: Holistic spatial analysis based on principal components of graylevel images; explicit measurement of local image features such as wrinkles; and template matching with motion flow fields. On a dataset contain(cid:173) ing six individual actions and 20 subjects, these methods had 89%, 57%, and 85% performances respectively for generalization to novel subjects. When combined, performance improved to 92%.

paragraphs: This paper approaches facial-expression analysis through the muscle actions that produce visible facial changes. It uses the Facial Action Coding System as the basis for detecting and classifying these actions. The authors assembled more than 1,100 image sequences from 24 people performing over 150 individual actions or combinations, providing material for studying this task.

Three approaches extract different kinds of evidence. One analyzes overall graylevel appearance using principal components. Another explicitly measures local details, such as wrinkles. The third matches templates using motion flow fields, drawing on how the face changes across images. Together, they compare broad appearance, localized features, and movement as sources of classification information.

On a dataset covering six individual actions and 20 subjects, performance on new subjects was 89%, 57%, and 85%, respectively. Combining the approaches increased performance to 92%. This improvement indicates that their information was complementary in that evaluation. The reported comparison applies to the six-action subset, while the larger collection includes many more actions and combinations.
summary.tldr: Combining overall appearance, local features, and facial motion improved classification of six facial actions on new subjects to 92%.

title: Classifying Facial Action

Here the local fields are no longer described by Gaussian distributions. We use dynamical replica theory to predict the evolution of macroscopic observables, including the relevant error measures, incorporating the old formalism in the limit piN --t 00.

paragraphs: The paper studies how supervised learning evolves in layered neural networks when the training set remains restricted relative to the network's input size. Specifically, the number of training examples is proportional to the number of inputs. This makes the ratio between data size and input size a central feature of the analysis.

In this regime, the local fields involved in the learning dynamics no longer have Gaussian distributions. The authors use dynamical replica theory to predict the evolution of macroscopic observables, including relevant error measures. The emphasis is on describing aggregate learning behavior over time while accounting for the distributional structure of the restricted-data setting.

The resulting theory also incorporates the earlier formalism when the ratio of training examples to inputs grows without bound. This connects the restricted-training-set analysis with the large-data limit. The contribution is a theoretical description that handles the stated proportional-size regime while recovering the previous account in the limiting case where training data becomes comparatively abundant.
summary.tldr: Dynamical replica theory describes supervised-learning dynamics when training-set size is proportional to input size and local fields are non-Gaussian.

title: Dynamics of Supervised Learning with Restricted Training Sets

abstract: Despite the popularity of connectionist models in cognitive science, their performance can often be diﬃcult to evaluate. Inspired by the geometric approach to statistical model selection, we introduce a conceptually similar method to examine the global behavior of a connectionist model, by counting the number and types of response patterns it can simulate. The Markov Chain Monte Carlo-based algorithm that we constructed (cid:222)nds these patterns eﬃciently. We demonstrate the approach using two localist network models of speech perception.

The Markov Chain Monte Carlo-based algorithm that we constructed (cid:222)nds these patterns eﬃciently. We demonstrate the approach using two localist network models of speech perception.

paragraphs: Connectionist models are widely used to explain cognition, but evaluating what their behavior tells us can be difficult. This paper approaches evaluation by examining the range of response patterns a model can generate. The object of comparison is therefore the model’s global behavioral repertoire, including both how many patterns it supports and what kinds they are.

Inspired by a geometric approach to statistical model selection, the authors develop a conceptually related counting method. They construct a Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm to find response patterns efficiently. The computational method supports a broader examination of model behavior by searching for patterns that the network is capable of simulating.

The approach is demonstrated on two localist network models of speech perception. This application shows how the proposed analysis can be used to compare cognitive models through their possible responses. Its contribution is a practical method for investigating behavioral flexibility, giving model evaluation an explicit account of the diversity of patterns each network can produce.
summary.tldr: An MCMC method compares connectionist models by efficiently finding and counting the kinds of response patterns they can produce.

title: An MCMC-Based Method of Comparing Connectionist Models in Cognitive Science

abstract: Empirical risk minimization offers well-known learning guarantees when training and test data come from the same domain. In the real world, though, we often wish to adapt a classifier from a source domain with a large amount of training data to different target domain with very little training data. In this work we give uniform convergence bounds for algorithms that minimize a convex combination of source and target empirical risk. The bounds explicitly model the inherent trade-off between training on a large but inaccurate source data set and a small but accurate target training set. Our theory also gives results when we have multiple source domains, each of which may have a different number of instances, and we exhibit cases in which minimizing a non-uniform combination of source risks can achieve much lower target error than standard empirical risk minimization.
originalAbstract: Empirical risk minimization offers well-known learning guarantees when training and test data come from the same domain. In the real world, though, we often wish to adapt a classifier from a source domain with a large amount of training data to different target domain with very little training data. In this work we give uniform convergence bounds for algorithms that minimize a convex combination of source and target empirical risk. The bounds explicitly model the inherent trade-off between training on a large but inaccurate source data set and a small but accurate target training set. Our theory also gives results when we have multiple source domains, each of which may have a different number of instances, and we exhibit cases in which minimizing a non-uniform combination of source risks can achieve much lower target error than standard empirical risk minimization.

paragraphs: A classifier may have abundant training data from one domain but little data from the domain where it will be used. The larger source sample offers more evidence, yet may describe the target poorly. This paper analyzes that tension for learning methods that minimize a weighted combination of source and target training errors.

The authors derive uniform convergence bounds for convex combinations of these empirical risks. Such combinations use nonnegative weights that sum to one. The bounds explicitly account for the trade-off between the amount of source data and its mismatch with the target, alongside the smaller but more directly relevant target sample.

The theory also covers multiple source domains with different sample counts. The authors exhibit cases where unequal weighting of source risks can produce much lower target error than standard empirical risk minimization. This establishes that treating all available training evidence uniformly can be substantially worse in some settings. The result provides a theoretical basis for considering both domain relevance and sample size when combining data.
summary.tldr: Domain-adaptation bounds explain how to balance abundant source data against scarce target data and show cases where unequal source weighting helps.

title: Learning Bounds for Domain Adaptation

abstract: Machine learning contains many computational bottlenecks in the form of nested summations over datasets. Kernel estimators and other methods are burdened by these expensive computations. Exact evaluation is typically O(n2 ) or higher, which severely limits application to large datasets. We present a multi-stage stratified Monte Carlo method for approximating such summations with probabilistic relative error control. The essential idea is fast approximation by sampling in trees. This method differs from many previous scalability techniques (such as standard multi-tree methods) in that its error is stochastic, but we derive conditions for error control and demonstrate that they work. Further, we give a theoretical sample complexity for the method that is independent of dataset size, and show that this appears to hold in experiments, where speedups reach as high as 1014 , many orders of magnitude beyond the previous state of the art.

paragraphs: Many machine-learning calculations contain nested sums over datasets, making exact evaluation quadratic in dataset size or even more expensive. This paper targets that bottleneck in kernel estimators and related methods. It proposes approximating the sums through a multi-stage, stratified Monte Carlo method whose central operation is sampling within trees.

The approximation comes with probabilistic relative-error control. Because sampling makes the error stochastic, the authors derive conditions under which that control applies and demonstrate their effectiveness. This makes the accuracy statement a probabilistic one: the method connects computational savings to conditions governing the approximation error rather than requiring exact evaluation of every contribution.

The paper also gives a theoretical sample-complexity result independent of dataset size and reports experimental behavior consistent with it. Reported speedups reach as high as 10^14, an extreme observed result rather than a uniform guarantee. The contribution combines tree-based sampling, explicit stochastic error control, and a sample-complexity analysis to make expensive statistical summations accessible at substantially reduced computational cost.
summary.tldr: Tree-based stratified Monte Carlo approximates expensive statistical sums with probabilistic error control and dataset-size-independent theoretical sample complexity.

title: Ultrafast Monte Carlo for Statistical Summations

abstract: Learning graphical models with hidden variables can offer semantic insights to complex data and lead to salient structured predictors without relying on expensive, sometime unattainable fully annotated training data. While likelihood-based methods have been extensively explored, to our knowledge, learning structured prediction models with latent variables based on the max-margin principle remains largely an open problem. In this paper, we present a partially observed Maximum Entropy Discrimination Markov Network (PoMEN) model that attempts to combine the advantages of Bayesian and margin based paradigms for learning Markov networks from partially labeled data. PoMEN leads to an averaging prediction rule that resembles a Bayes predictor that is more robust to overfitting, but is also built on the desirable discriminative laws resemble those of the M$^3$N. We develop an EM-style algorithm utilizing existing convex optimization algorithms for M$^3$N as a subroutine. We demonstrate competent performance of PoMEN over existing methods on a real-world web data extraction task.

paragraphs: Structured prediction often involves relationships among several output variables, but fully labeling those outputs can be expensive or infeasible. Hidden variables offer a way to learn from partially annotated data while representing meaningful underlying structure. This paper tackles the comparatively less explored problem of combining such latent structure with margin-based learning.

The proposed partially observed Maximum Entropy Discrimination Markov Network, or PoMEN, brings Bayesian and margin-based ideas together. It uses an averaging prediction rule resembling a Bayes predictor, described as more robust to overfitting, while retaining discriminative principles similar to maximum-margin Markov networks. These features connect uncertainty-aware prediction with learning that emphasizes separation between competing outputs.

The authors develop an expectation-maximization-style training algorithm that uses existing convex maximum-margin Markov network optimization as a subroutine. A real-world web-data extraction task demonstrates competent performance relative to existing methods. The contribution is a combined modeling and training approach for structured prediction from partial labels, with the application providing evidence of its practical usefulness.
summary.tldr: PoMEN combines Bayesian averaging and margin-based learning for structured prediction from partially labeled data.

title: Partially Observed Maximum Entropy Discrimination Markov Networks

abstract: For many computer vision applications, the ideal image feature would be invariant to multiple confounding image properties, such as illumination and viewing angle. Recently, deep architectures trained in an unsupervised manner have been proposed as an automatic method for extracting useful features. However, outside of using these learning algorithms in a classiﬁer, they can be sometimes difﬁcult to evaluate. In this paper, we propose a number of empirical tests that directly measure the degree to which these learned features are invariant to different image transforms. We ﬁnd that deep autoencoders become invariant to increasingly complex image transformations with depth. This further justiﬁes the use of “deep” vs. “shallower” representations. Our performance metrics agree with existing measures of invariance. Our evaluation metrics can also be used to evaluate future work in unsupervised deep learning, and thus help the development of future algorithms.

paragraphs: Useful image features often need to remain stable when properties such as illumination or viewing angle change. Evaluating an unsupervised representation only through a classifier can make that stability difficult to assess directly. This paper proposes empirical tests that measure how invariant learned features are to different image transformations.

The tests examine a property of the representation itself: how much it changes under transformations that can confound vision tasks. This provides a way to study learned features without relying solely on their role in a classification system. The authors report that their performance metrics agree with existing measures of invariance.

In the deep autoencoders studied, deeper representations become invariant to increasingly complex transformations. This empirical finding supports the use of depth for learning such invariances in those models. The contribution includes both evidence about the representations and evaluation tools that can be applied to future unsupervised learning methods, making transformation stability a directly assessable part of their behavior.
summary.tldr: Direct empirical invariance tests show that deeper autoencoder representations tolerate increasingly complex image transformations.

title: Measuring Invariances in Deep Networks

abstract: The goal of perception is to infer the hidden states in the hierarchical process by which sensory data are generated. Human behavior is consistent with the optimal statistical solution to this problem in many tasks, including cue combination and orientation detection. Understanding the neural mechanisms underlying this behavior is of particular importance, since probabilistic computations are notoriously challenging. Here we propose a simple mechanism for Bayesian inference which involves averaging over a few feature detection neurons which fire at a rate determined by their similarity to a sensory stimulus. This mechanism is based on a Monte Carlo method known as importance sampling, commonly used in computer science and statistics. Moreover, a simple extension to recursive importance sampling can be used to perform hierarchical Bayesian inference. We identify a scheme for implementing importance sampling with spiking neurons, and show that this scheme can account for human behavior in cue combination and oblique effect.

paragraphs: Perception requires inferring hidden causes from sensory observations, often across several levels of a generative hierarchy. Human behavior resembles optimal statistical inference in tasks such as cue combination and orientation detection. This paper asks how neurons might perform the probabilistic computations needed to produce such behavior.

The proposed mechanism averages over a small number of feature-detection neurons whose firing rates depend on how closely they match the sensory stimulus. The authors connect this mechanism to importance sampling, a Monte Carlo method for approximate inference. A recursive extension allows the same basic computational idea to support inference through a hierarchy rather than at only one level.

The paper identifies a way to implement importance sampling with spiking neurons and shows that it can account for human cue-combination behavior and the oblique effect. Its significance is the explicit connection between a statistical approximation and a proposed neural operation. Explaining these behavioral patterns makes the mechanism a candidate account of neural inference; it does not establish that the brain necessarily uses this implementation.
summary.tldr: A proposed spiking-neuron importance-sampling mechanism supports hierarchical Bayesian inference and accounts for two human perceptual phenomena.

title: Neural Implementation of Hierarchical Bayesian Inference by Importance Sampling

abstract: We introduce a novel multivariate Laplace (MVL) distribution as a sparsity promoting prior for Bayesian source localization that allows the specification of constraints between and within sources. We represent the MVL distribution as a scale mixture that induces a coupling between source variances instead of their means. Approximation of the posterior marginals using expectation propagation is shown to be very efficient due to properties of the scale mixture representation. The computational bottleneck amounts to computing the diagonal elements of a sparse matrix inverse. Our approach is illustrated using a mismatch negativity paradigm for which MEG data and a structural MRI have been acquired. We show that spatial coupling leads to sources which are active over larger cortical areas as compared with an uncoupled prior.

We represent the MVL distribution as a scale mixture that induces a coupling between source variances instead of their means. Approximation of the posterior marginals using expectation propagation is shown to be very efficient due to properties of the scale mixture representation. The computational bottleneck amounts to computing the diagonal elements of a sparse matrix inverse. Our approach is illustrated using a mismatch negativity paradigm for which MEG data and a structural MRI have been acquired. We show that spatial coupling leads to sources which are active over larger cortical areas as compared with an uncoupled prior.

The prior encourages sparse explanations while allowing constraints both within individual sources and between sources. This combination matters when a localization model needs to favor limited activity while still representing relationships among possible sources.

The distribution is expressed as a scale mixture that couples source variances rather than their means. In this representation, the connections act through the sources’ variability. The authors show that properties of the scale mixture make expectation propagation efficient for approximating posterior marginals. The remaining computational bottleneck is obtaining diagonal entries of the inverse of a sparse matrix.

The approach is illustrated with a mismatch negativity paradigm using MEG measurements and structural MRI. In that application, spatial coupling produces sources active over larger cortical areas than an uncoupled prior does. The example shows how the prior’s dependency structure changes the spatial extent of inferred activity, alongside the paper’s contribution of an efficient approximate inference method.
summary.tldr: A multivariate Laplace prior combines sparse Bayesian source localization with dependencies that can produce more spatially extended activity.

title: Bayesian Source Localization with the Multivariate Laplace Prior

abstract: Artists, advertisers, and photographers are routinely presented with the task of creating an image that a viewer will remember. While it may seem like image memorability is purely subjective, recent work shows that it is not an inexplicable phenomenon: variation in memorability of images is consistent across subjects, suggesting that some images are intrinsically more memorable than others, independent of a subjects' contexts and biases. In this paper, we used the publicly available memorability dataset of Isola et al., and augmented the object and scene annotations with interpretable spatial, content, and aesthetic image properties. We used a feature-selection scheme with desirable explaining-away properties to determine a compact set of attributes that characterizes the memorability of any individual image. We find that images of enclosed spaces containing people with visible faces are memorable, while images of vistas and peaceful scenes are not. Contrary to popular belief, unusual or aesthetically pleasing scenes do not tend to be highly memorable. This work represents one of the first attempts at understanding intrinsic image memorability, and opens a new domain of investigation at the interface between human cognition and computer vision.

This paper investigates which interpretable image attributes help characterize that variation. The goal is to move from observing differences in memorability to understanding the visual content associated with them.

The researchers extend an existing public memorability dataset with spatial, content, and aesthetic attributes, supplementing its object and scene annotations. They then use feature selection with explaining-away properties to identify a compact set of relevant attributes. This approach seeks an economical explanation of an individual image's memorability from its annotated properties.

summary.tldr: Interpretable image attributes connect memorability with scene content, while unusualness and aesthetic appeal do not reliably imply high memorability.

title: Understanding the Intrinsic Memorability of Images

abstract: This paper describes gradient methods based on a scaled metric on the Grassmann manifold for low-rank matrix completion. The proposed methods significantly improve canonical gradient methods especially on ill-conditioned matrices, while maintaining established global convegence and exact recovery guarantees. A connection between a form of subspace iteration for matrix completion and the scaled gradient descent procedure is also established. The proposed conjugate gradient method based on the scaled gradient outperforms several existing algorithms for matrix completion and is competitive with recently proposed methods.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix completion aims to reconstruct a matrix from incomplete observations using its low-rank structure. This paper develops gradient methods on a Grassmann manifold, a space used to represent subspaces. Its central change is a scaled metric, which changes the geometry used to determine gradient updates during the search for a suitable low-rank completion.

The proposed scaling significantly improves canonical gradient methods, with especially strong benefits reported for ill-conditioned matrices. The authors state that the methods maintain established global convergence and exact recovery guarantees. Thus, the contribution improves the optimization procedure while preserving the theoretical guarantees available in the relevant setting, rather than asserting recovery for arbitrary incomplete matrices.

The paper also establishes a connection between scaled gradient descent and a form of subspace iteration for matrix completion. Building on the scaled gradient, the authors propose a conjugate gradient method that outperforms several existing algorithms and is competitive with recently proposed alternatives. These results connect a geometric change in the optimization method with improved practical performance and a relationship to another subspace-based procedure.
summary.tldr: Scaled Grassmann-manifold gradients improve low-rank matrix completion, especially for ill-conditioned matrices, while retaining established guarantees.

title: Scaled Gradients on Grassmann Manifolds for Matrix Completion

abstract: Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) are extremely useful for modeling and solving sequential decision making problems. Graph-based MDPs provide a compact representation for MDPs with large numbers of random variables. However, the complexity of exactly solving a graph-based MDP usually grows exponentially in the number of variables, which limits their application. We present a new variational framework to describe and solve the planning problem of MDPs, and derive both exact and approximate planning algorithms. In particular, by exploiting the graph structure of graph-based MDPs, we propose a factored variational value iteration algorithm in which the value function is first approximated by the multiplication of local-scope value functions, then solved by minimizing a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. The KL divergence is optimized using the belief propagation algorithm, with complexity exponential in only the cluster size of the graph. Experimental comparison on different models shows that our algorithm outperforms existing approximation algorithms at finding good policies.

paragraphs: Graph-based Markov decision processes compactly represent sequential decision problems involving many random variables. However, solving them exactly usually requires computation that grows exponentially with the number of variables. This paper introduces a variational framework for planning and derives both exact and approximate algorithms within it.

Its main approximate method is factored variational value iteration. The value function is represented approximately as a product of functions involving local groups of variables. The algorithm then minimizes a Kullback-Leibler divergence using belief propagation. This uses the graph's structure to organize the planning calculation around smaller interacting groups.

The resulting computational complexity is exponential only in graph cluster size, rather than in the full number of variables. Consequently, cluster size remains an important determinant of tractability. Experiments across different models show that the algorithm finds better policies than existing approximation algorithms in those comparisons. The contribution combines a general planning formulation with a specific structural approximation that improves the practical reach of graph-based MDP planning.
summary.tldr: Factored variational value iteration uses graph structure to make approximate MDP planning exponential in cluster size rather than total variable count.

title: Variational Planning for Graph-based MDPs

abstract: Variational inference algorithms have proven successful for Bayesian analysis in large data settings, with recent advances using stochastic variational inference (SVI). However, such methods have largely been studied in independent or exchangeable data settings. We develop an SVI algorithm to learn the parameters of hidden Markov models (HMMs) in a time-dependent data setting. The challenge in applying stochastic optimization in this setting arises from dependencies in the chain, which must be broken to consider minibatches of observations. We propose an algorithm that harnesses the memory decay of the chain to adaptively bound errors arising from edge effects. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm on synthetic experiments and a large genomics dataset where a batch algorithm is computationally infeasible.

paragraphs: Stochastic variational inference makes Bayesian analysis practical for large datasets, but its usual setting treats observations as independent or exchangeable. Hidden Markov models describe sequences with dependencies across time. This paper develops an SVI algorithm for learning their parameters while addressing the complications created by splitting a dependent sequence into minibatches.

Breaking the chain creates boundary effects because observations near a minibatch edge are separated from part of their surrounding sequence. The proposed algorithm uses the chain's memory decay to adaptively bound the errors introduced by those edges. This directly connects the stochastic approximation to the sequence's dependence structure, rather than simply treating sampled observations as independent.

The authors demonstrate the method on synthetic experiments and a large genomics dataset for which a batch algorithm is computationally infeasible. These results support its usefulness for large sequential datasets. The contribution is a way to extend minibatch-based Bayesian learning to HMMs while explicitly controlling errors caused by cutting the chain.
summary.tldr: An SVI algorithm learns hidden Markov models from minibatches by using memory decay to bound errors at sequence boundaries.

title: Stochastic variational inference for hidden Markov models

abstract: Local differential privacy has recently surfaced as a strong measure of privacy in contexts where personal information remains private even from data analysts. Working in a setting where the data providers and data analysts want to maximize the utility of statistical inferences performed on the released data, we study the fundamental tradeoff between local differential privacy and information theoretic utility functions. We introduce a family of extremal privatization mechanisms, which we call staircase mechanisms, and prove that it contains the optimal privatization mechanism that maximizes utility. We further show that for all information theoretic utility functions studied in this paper, maximizing utility is equivalent to solving a linear program, the outcome of which is the optimal staircase mechanism. However, solving this linear program can be computationally expensive since it has a number of variables that is exponential in the data size. To account for this, we show that two simple staircase mechanisms, the binary and randomized response mechanisms, are universally optimal in the high and low privacy regimes, respectively, and well approximate the intermediate regime.

paragraphs: Local differential privacy protects personal information even from the analyst receiving released data. The paper studies how much statistical usefulness can be retained under this protection when both providers and analysts want useful inferences. It frames the tradeoff using information-theoretic utility functions and asks which privatization mechanisms maximize those utilities.

The authors introduce staircase mechanisms and prove that this family contains an optimal mechanism. For every information-theoretic utility function studied in the paper, utility maximization can be expressed as a linear program whose solution selects an optimal staircase mechanism. This gives a concrete optimization formulation, although the number of variables grows exponentially with data size and can make computation expensive.

The paper also identifies simpler choices. Within the studied setting, the binary mechanism is universally optimal in the high-privacy regime, while randomized response is universally optimal in the low-privacy regime. Both approximate the intermediate regime well. These results make the abstract privacy-utility tradeoff more actionable by connecting exact optimality to a structured family and practical choices to privacy strength.
summary.tldr: Staircase mechanisms characterize optimal local privacy-utility tradeoffs, with simple optimal choices in the high- and low-privacy regimes studied.

title: Extremal Mechanisms for Local Differential Privacy

abstract: We demonstrate that a generative model for object shapes can achieve state of the art results on challenging scene text recognition tasks, and with orders of magnitude fewer training images than required for competing discriminative methods. In addition to transcribing text from challenging images, our method performs fine-grained instance segmentation of characters. We show that our model is more robust to both affine transformations and non-affine deformations compared to previous approaches.
originalAbstract: We demonstrate that a generative model for object shapes can achieve state of the art results on challenging scene text recognition tasks, and with orders of magnitude fewer training images than required for competing discriminative methods. In addition to transcribing text from challenging images, our method performs fine-grained instance segmentation of characters. We show that our model is more robust to both affine transformations and non-affine deformations compared to previous approaches.

paragraphs: Recognizing text in scene images involves interpreting character shapes despite changes in their appearance. This paper approaches the task with a generative model of object shapes. The model supports both reading the text and identifying the individual characters within the image, connecting recognition with a detailed account of character shape.

The reported method achieves state-of-the-art results on challenging scene-text recognition tasks while using orders of magnitude fewer training images than competing discriminative methods. This makes training-data efficiency a central finding: strong recognition performance is demonstrated with substantially less image supervision than those alternatives require.

The method also produces fine-grained instance segmentation, distinguishing individual character instances rather than returning only a transcription. The authors further report greater robustness to affine transformations and non-affine deformations than previous approaches. Together, these findings show that the tested shape model combines accurate reading, detailed character segmentation, and resilience to shape changes. The evidence concerns the challenging recognition tasks and comparisons reported in the paper.
summary.tldr: A generative shape model achieves strong scene-text recognition and character segmentation with far fewer training images and improved deformation robustness.

title: Generative Shape Models: Joint Text Recognition and Segmentation with Very Little Training Data

abstract: Proteins are the "building blocks of life", the most abundant organic molecules, and the central focus of most areas of biomedicine. Protein structure is strongly related to protein function, thus structure prediction is a crucial task on the way to solve many biological questions. A contact map is a compact representation of the three-dimensional structure of a protein via the pairwise contacts between the amino acid constituting the protein. We use a convolutional network to calculate protein contact maps from inferred statistical coupling between positions in the protein sequence. The input to the network has an image-like structure amenable to convolutions, but every "pixel" instead of color channels contains a bipartite undirected edge-weighted graph. We propose several methods for treating such "graph-valued images" in a convolutional network. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a large margin. It also allows for a great flexibility with regard to the input data, which makes it useful for studying a wide range of problems.

paragraphs: A protein contact map records which pairs of amino acids are close in its three-dimensional structure. Because structure is closely related to function, predicting these contacts can help address biological questions. This paper uses a convolutional network to infer contact maps from statistical couplings between positions in a protein sequence.

The input resembles an image because information is arranged across pairs of sequence positions. However, each location contains a bipartite, undirected, weighted graph rather than ordinary color channels. The authors propose several ways for convolutional networks to process these graph-valued images, preserving a richer kind of information at each position in the input.

The proposed method is reported to outperform state-of-the-art contact prediction methods by a large margin. Its input representation also permits substantial flexibility in the data supplied to the network. The broader contribution is therefore a way to connect convolutional processing with image-like arrays whose entries have graph structure, alongside the demonstrated application to predicting protein contacts from inferred sequence couplings.
summary.tldr: Convolutional networks process graph-valued sequence-coupling inputs to predict protein contacts with a large reported improvement over existing methods.

title: Protein contact prediction from amino acid co-evolution using convolutional networks for graph-valued images

abstract: High demand for computation resources severely hinders deployment of large-scale Deep Neural Networks (DNN) in resource constrained devices. In this work, we propose a Structured Sparsity Learning (SSL) method to regularize the structures (i.e., filters, channels, filter shapes, and layer depth) of DNNs. SSL can: (1) learn a compact structure from a bigger DNN to reduce computation cost; (2) obtain a hardware-friendly structured sparsity of DNN to efficiently accelerate the DNN’s evaluation. Experimental results show that SSL achieves on average 5.1X and 3.1X speedups of convolutional layer computation of AlexNet against CPU and GPU, respectively, with off-the-shelf libraries. These speedups are about twice speedups of non-structured sparsity; (3) regularize the DNN structure to improve classification accuracy. The results show that for CIFAR-10, regularization on layer depth reduces a 20-layer Deep Residual Network (ResNet) to 18 layers while improves the accuracy from 91.25% to 92.60%, which is still higher than that of original ResNet with 32 layers. For AlexNet, SSL reduces the error by ~1%.

paragraphs: Large neural networks can demand too much computation for devices with limited resources. Structured Sparsity Learning addresses this by regularizing network structures, including filters, channels, filter shapes, and layer depth. The method learns a compact structure from a larger network while encouraging sparsity that hardware and existing software libraries can exploit efficiently.

The experiments report average AlexNet convolutional-layer speedups of 5.1 times on CPU and 3.1 times on GPU using off-the-shelf libraries. These improvements are about twice the speedups obtained with unstructured sparsity. The distinction matters because the arrangement of the remaining computation affects whether a smaller network actually runs faster.

The method also serves as structural regularization that can improve classification accuracy. On CIFAR-10, depth regularization reduces a 20-layer residual network to 18 layers while increasing accuracy from 91.25% to 92.60%, exceeding the original 32-layer network as well. For AlexNet, the reported error reduction is approximately 1%. These findings demonstrate computational and accuracy benefits in the evaluated models, without making either outcome universal.
summary.tldr: Structured Sparsity Learning produces compact, hardware-friendly neural networks with demonstrated speedups and classification improvements.

title: Learning Structured Sparsity in Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have achieved state-of-the-art performances in many natural language processing tasks, such as language modeling and machine translation. However, when the vocabulary is large, the RNN model will become very big (e.g., possibly beyond the memory capacity of a GPU device) and its training will become very inefficient. In this work, we propose a novel technique to tackle this challenge. The key idea is to use 2-Component (2C) shared embedding for word representations. We allocate every word in the vocabulary into a table, each row of which is associated with a vector, and each column associated with another vector. Depending on its position in the table, a word is jointly represented by two components: a row vector and a column vector. Since the words in the same row share the row vector and the words in the same column share the column vector, we only need $2 \sqrt{|V|}$ vectors to represent a vocabulary of $|V|$ unique words, which are far less than the $|V|$ vectors required by existing approaches. Based on the 2-Component shared embedding, we design a new RNN algorithm and evaluate it using the language modeling task on several benchmark datasets. The results show that our algorithm significantly reduces the model size and speeds up the training process, without sacrifice of accuracy (it achieves similar, if not better, perplexity as compared to state-of-the-art language models). Remarkably, on the One-Billion-Word benchmark Dataset, our algorithm achieves comparable perplexity to previous language models, whilst reducing the model size by a factor of 40-100, and speeding up the training process by a factor of 2. We name our proposed algorithm \emph{LightRNN} to reflect its very small model size and very high training speed.

paragraphs: LightRNN addresses the memory and training costs of recurrent language models with large vocabularies. A conventional representation assigns a separate vector to every word, so vocabulary growth expands the model. The paper replaces those individual vectors with a shared representation built from two components.

Words are placed in a table. Each row has a vector and each column has another vector; a word is represented by the pair associated with its position. Words therefore share one component with others in their row and another with those in their column. This scheme requires only twice the square root of the vocabulary size in vectors, rather than one vector per word.

The authors build an RNN algorithm around this representation and evaluate language modeling on several benchmarks. They report smaller models and faster training with similar or better perplexity. On the One-Billion-Word benchmark, model size falls by a factor of 40 to 100 and training is twice as fast, while perplexity remains comparable to previous models. These results demonstrate the practical value of sharing word-representation components.
summary.tldr: LightRNN shares row and column vectors across words to substantially shrink language models and accelerate training while maintaining comparable perplexity.

title: LightRNN: Memory and Computation-Efficient Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: A problem that has been of recent interest in statistical inference, machine learning and signal processing is that of understanding the asymptotic behavior of regularized least squares solutions under random measurement matrices (or dictionaries). The Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO or least-squares with $\ell_1$ regularization) is perhaps one of the most interesting examples. Precise expressions for the asymptotic performance of LASSO have been obtained for a number of different cases, in particular when the elements of the dictionary matrix are sampled independently from a Gaussian distribution. It has also been empirically observed that the resulting expressions remain valid when the entries of the dictionary matrix are independently sampled from certain non-Gaussian distributions. In this paper, we confirm these observations theoretically when the distribution is sub-Gaussian. We further generalize the previous expressions for a broader family of regularization functions and under milder conditions on the underlying random, possibly non-Gaussian, dictionary matrix. In particular, we establish the universality of the asymptotic statistics (e.g., the average quadratic risk) of LASSO with non-Gaussian dictionaries.

paragraphs: Regularized least squares fits observations while penalizing undesirable properties of the solution. LASSO, which uses an absolute-value penalty, is a prominent example. This paper studies how such solutions behave as problems become large, when the measurement matrix is random. The central question is whether precise performance predictions depend on the particular distribution used to generate that matrix.

Previous expressions described LASSO performance in several settings, especially matrices with independent Gaussian entries. Experiments had suggested that some non-Gaussian matrices follow the same expressions. The paper supplies a theoretical justification for this observation when the relevant distribution is sub-Gaussian, establishing a qualified form of universality across matrix distributions.

The analysis also extends earlier expressions to a wider family of regularization functions and relaxes conditions on the random matrix. Its contribution is therefore a broader basis for predicting asymptotic statistics, including average quadratic risk. These are large-problem results under specified distributional conditions; universality here does not mean that every matrix distribution or every finite problem has identical performance.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes when large-scale LASSO and other regularized least-squares solutions share asymptotic behavior across different random measurement distributions.

title: A Universal Analysis of Large-Scale Regularized Least Squares Solutions

abstract: We provide novel theoretical insights on structured prediction in the context of efficient convex surrogate loss minimization with consistency guarantees. For any task loss, we construct a convex surrogate that can be optimized via stochastic gradient descent and we prove tight bounds on the so-called "calibration function" relating the excess surrogate risk to the actual risk. In contrast to prior related work, we carefully monitor the effect of the exponential number of classes in the learning guarantees as well as on the optimization complexity. As an interesting consequence, we formalize the intuition that some task losses make learning harder than others, and that the classical 0-1 loss is ill-suited for structured prediction.

For any task loss, we construct a convex surrogate that can be optimized via stochastic gradient descent and we prove tight bounds on the so-called "calibration function" relating the excess surrogate risk to the actual risk. In contrast to prior related work, we carefully monitor the effect of the exponential number of classes in the learning guarantees as well as on the optimization complexity. As an interesting consequence, we formalize the intuition that some task losses make learning harder than others, and that the classical 0-1 loss is ill-suited for structured prediction.

paragraphs: Structured prediction involves output spaces that can contain exponentially many classes. Learning often optimizes a convex surrogate loss in place of the actual task loss. This paper studies how reliably improvements in that surrogate translate into better task performance, while accounting for the size of the output space.

For any task loss, the authors construct a convex surrogate that can be optimized with stochastic gradient descent. They prove tight bounds on its calibration function, which relates excess surrogate risk to actual risk. This connection supplies consistency guarantees and quantifies how accurately the surrogate objective must be optimized to obtain useful performance on the task.

The analysis tracks the effect of exponentially many classes on both learning guarantees and optimization complexity. As a consequence, it formalizes why different task losses can make structured learning more or less difficult. In particular, the results identify the classical zero-one loss as ill-suited to structured prediction. The contribution therefore connects the choice of evaluation loss with both statistical requirements and computational demands.
summary.tldr: The paper connects convex surrogate optimization to structured task risk through tight calibration bounds that account for exponentially large output spaces.

title: On Structured Prediction Theory with Calibrated Convex Surrogate Losses

abstract: The count-min sketch is a time- and memory-efficient randomized data structure that provides a point estimate of the number of times an item has appeared in a data stream. The count-min sketch and related hash-based data structures are ubiquitous in systems that must track frequencies of data such as URLs, IP addresses, and language n-grams. We present a Bayesian view on the count-min sketch, using the same data structure, but providing a posterior distribution over the frequencies that characterizes the uncertainty arising from the hash-based approximation. In particular, we take a nonparametric approach and consider tokens generated from a Dirichlet process (DP) random measure, which allows for an unbounded number of unique tokens. Using properties of the DP, we show that it is possible to straightforwardly compute posterior marginals of the unknown true counts and that the modes of these marginals recover the count-min sketch estimator, inheriting the associated probabilistic guarantees. Using simulated data with known ground truth, we investigate the properties of these estimators. Lastly, we also study a modified problem in which the observation stream consists of collections of tokens (i.e., documents) arising from a random measure drawn from a stable beta process, which allows for power law scaling behavior in the number of unique tokens.

abstract: We address the problem of Bayesian structure learning for domains with hundreds of variables by employing non-parametric bootstrap, recursively. We propose a method that covers both model averaging and model selection in the same framework. The proposed method deals with the main weakness of constraint-based learning---sensitivity to errors in the independence tests---by a novel way of combining bootstrap with constraint-based learning. Essentially, we provide an algorithm for learning a tree, in which each node represents a scored CPDAG for a subset of variables and the level of the node corresponds to the maximal order of conditional independencies that are encoded in the graph. As higher order independencies are tested in deeper recursive calls, they benefit from more bootstrap samples, and therefore are more resistant to the curse-of-dimensionality. Moreover, the re-use of stable low order independencies allows greater computational efficiency. We also provide an algorithm for sampling CPDAGs efficiently from their posterior given the learned tree. That is, not from the full posterior, but from a reduced space of CPDAGs encoded in the learned tree. We empirically demonstrate that the proposed algorithm scales well to hundreds of variables, and learns better MAP models and more reliable causal relationships between variables, than other state-of-the-art-methods.

This paper addresses that sensitivity by recursively applying the nonparametric bootstrap, using resampled data to support structure learning within a framework that handles both selecting a model and averaging over models.

The method builds a tree whose nodes contain scored CPDAGs, graph representations of classes of compatible structures, for subsets of variables. Deeper levels encode independence statements involving more conditioning variables. That distribution covers the reduced space encoded in the tree, rather than the full space of possible structures. Experiments show scaling to hundreds of variables, better maximum-posterior models, and more reliable causal relationships than the compared methods.
summary.tldr: Recursive bootstrapping makes Bayesian graph structure learning more reliable and computationally practical for hundreds of variables.

title: Bayesian Structure Learning by Recursive Bootstrap

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning methods traditionally struggle with tasks where environment rewards are particularly sparse. One successful method of guiding exploration in these domains is to imitate trajectories provided by a human demonstrator. However, these demonstrations are typically collected under artificial conditions, i.e. with access to the agent’s exact environment setup and the demonstrator’s action and reward trajectories. Here we propose a method that overcomes these limitations in two stages. First, we learn to map unaligned videos from multiple sources to a common representation using self-supervised objectives constructed over both time and modality (i.e. vision and sound). Second, we embed a single YouTube video in this representation to learn a reward function that encourages an agent to imitate human gameplay. This method of one-shot imitation allows our agent to convincingly exceed human-level performance on the infamously hard exploration games Montezuma’s Revenge, Pitfall! and Private Eye for the first time, even if the agent is not presented with any environment rewards.

paragraphs: Sparse rewards make exploration difficult because an agent may receive little feedback about useful behavior. Human demonstrations can guide it, but conventional demonstrations often require matching environment setups and recorded actions and rewards. This paper instead develops a method that learns from gameplay videos without those specially collected demonstration records.

The method has two stages. First, self-supervised objectives across time, vision, and sound map unaligned videos from multiple sources into a shared representation. Second, a single YouTube video is embedded in that representation and used to learn a reward function encouraging imitation. The single-video imitation stage therefore builds on representation learning from multiple videos.

The authors report performance exceeding human level on Montezuma’s Revenge, Pitfall!, and Private Eye, including when the agent receives no environment rewards. In that setting, the learned imitation reward still supplies guidance. The findings show that video-derived progress signals can support exploration in these difficult games, extending the usefulness of demonstrations beyond recordings captured specifically for the agent’s training setup.
summary.tldr: A shared audiovisual representation turns a single gameplay video into an imitation reward that supports strong performance on sparse-reward games.

title: Playing hard exploration games by watching YouTube

abstract: Real-time automatic speech recognition (ASR) on mobile and embedded devices has been of great interests for many years. We present real-time speech recognition on smartphones or embedded systems by employing recurrent neural network (RNN) based acoustic models, RNN based language models, and beam-search decoding. The acoustic model is end-to-end trained with connectionist temporal classification (CTC) loss. The RNN implementation on embedded devices can suffer from excessive DRAM accesses because the parameter size of a neural network usually exceeds that of the cache memory and the parameters are used only once for each time step. To remedy this problem, we employ a multi-time step parallelization approach that computes multiple output samples at a time with the parameters fetched from the DRAM. Since the number of DRAM accesses can be reduced in proportion to the number of parallelization steps, we can achieve a high processing speed. However, conventional RNNs, such as long short-term memory (LSTM) or gated recurrent unit (GRU), do not permit multi-time step parallelization. We construct an acoustic model by combining simple recurrent units (SRUs) and depth-wise 1-dimensional convolution layers for multi-time step parallelization. Both the character and word piece models are developed for acoustic modeling, and the corresponding RNN based language models are used for beam search decoding. We achieve a competitive WER for WSJ corpus using the entire model size of around 15MB and achieve real-time speed using only a single core ARM without GPU or special hardware.

It also runs in real time on a single ARM core without a GPU or special hardware, demonstrating the practical value of designing around memory access.
summary.tldr: A speech recognizer designed to reuse parameters across time steps achieves competitive WSJ recognition and real-time operation on one ARM core.

title: Fully Neural Network Based Speech Recognition on Mobile and Embedded Devices

abstract: We address the problem of algorithmic fairness: ensuring that sensitive information does not unfairly influence the outcome of a classifier. We present an approach based on empirical risk minimization, which incorporates a fairness constraint into the learning problem. It encourages the conditional risk of the learned classifier to be approximately constant with respect to the sensitive variable. We derive both risk and fairness bounds that support the statistical consistency of our methodology. We specify our approach to kernel methods and observe that the fairness requirement implies an orthogonality constraint which can be easily added to these methods. We further observe that for linear models the constraint translates into a simple data preprocessing step. Experiments indicate that the method is empirically effective and performs favorably against state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: The paper incorporates fairness directly into the problem used to train a classifier. Its chosen requirement encourages conditional risk to remain approximately constant as a sensitive variable changes. This makes fairness a constraint on the classifier's error behavior across sensitive-variable values, alongside the usual objective of reducing prediction loss.

The authors derive bounds for both prediction risk and fairness that support statistical consistency of the method. Addressing both quantities matters because a useful constrained learner must account for predictive performance as well as the fairness condition it was designed to satisfy. The theoretical results connect learning from finite data to these two objectives.

For kernel methods, the fairness requirement produces an orthogonality constraint that can be incorporated into training. For linear models, it becomes a simple preprocessing operation on the data. These specializations make the general formulation concrete for established learning methods. Experiments indicate favorable performance against existing approaches. The findings concern the paper's specific conditional-risk fairness criterion, providing a statistically supported and empirically evaluated way to impose it.
summary.tldr: A fairness-constrained learning approach encourages similar conditional risk across sensitive-variable values, with theoretical bounds and practical kernel and linear formulations.

title: Empirical Risk Minimization Under Fairness Constraints

abstract: Detecting test samples drawn sufficiently far away from the training distribution statistically or adversarially is a fundamental requirement for deploying a good classifier in many real-world machine learning applications. However, deep neural networks with the softmax classifier are known to produce highly overconfident posterior distributions even for such abnormal samples. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective method for detecting any abnormal samples, which is applicable to any pre-trained softmax neural classifier. We obtain the class conditional Gaussian distributions with respect to (low- and upper-level) features of the deep models under Gaussian discriminant analysis, which result in a confidence score based on the Mahalanobis distance. While most prior methods have been evaluated for detecting either out-of-distribution or adversarial samples, but not both, the proposed method achieves the state-of-the-art performances for both cases in our experiments. Moreover, we found that our proposed method is more robust in harsh cases, e.g., when the training dataset has noisy labels or small number of samples. Finally, we show that the proposed method enjoys broader usage by applying it to class-incremental learning: whenever out-of-distribution samples are detected, our classification rule can incorporate new classes well without further training deep models.

paragraphs: A neural classifier can assign high confidence to inputs that differ substantially from its training data, including adversarial inputs. This paper proposes a detection method applicable to any pretrained neural classifier with a softmax output. It uses the network's internal features to assess whether an input resembles the examples associated with a known class.

The method models class-conditional feature distributions as Gaussian distributions, using features from both lower and upper levels of the network. It then derives a confidence score from Mahalanobis distance. This gives the detection rule a statistical reference based on class-specific feature distributions, rather than relying only on the classifier's output confidence.

In the reported experiments, the method achieves state-of-the-art performance for detecting both out-of-distribution and adversarial examples. The authors also observe greater robustness when training labels are noisy or examples are scarce. A further application concerns class-incremental learning: the classification rule can incorporate new classes associated with detected unfamiliar samples without additional training of the deep model.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian model of pretrained network features supplies a Mahalanobis confidence score that detects unfamiliar and adversarial inputs effectively in experiments.

title: A Simple Unified Framework for Detecting Out-of-Distribution Samples and Adversarial Attacks

abstract: Deep neural networks have been very successful in compressive-sensing and image restoration applications, as a means to estimate images from partial, blurry, or otherwise degraded measurements. These networks are trained on a large number of corresponding pairs of measurements and ground-truth images, and thus implicitly learn to exploit domain-specific image statistics. But unlike measurement data, it is often expensive or impractical to collect a large training set of ground-truth images in many application settings. In this paper, we introduce an unsupervised framework for training image estimation networks, from a training set that contains only measurements---with two varied measurements per image---but no ground-truth for the full images desired as output. We demonstrate that our framework can be applied for both regular and blind image estimation tasks, where in the latter case parameters of the measurement model (e.g., the blur kernel) are unknown: during inference, and potentially, also during training. We evaluate our framework for training networks for compressive-sensing and blind deconvolution, considering both non-blind and blind training for the latter. Our framework yields models that are nearly as accurate as those from fully supervised training, despite not having access to any ground-truth images.

paragraphs: Image estimation networks reconstruct images from incomplete, blurred, or otherwise degraded measurements. Conventional supervised training uses corresponding ground-truth images, which can be expensive or impractical to obtain. This paper introduces a training framework that uses measurements alone, with the specific requirement of two varied measurements for each underlying image.

The framework applies to ordinary estimation tasks and to blind tasks, where parameters of the measurement process are unknown. A blur kernel is one such parameter. The authors consider settings where these parameters are unknown during inference and potentially during training as well, extending the approach beyond reconstruction with a fully specified measurement process.

Experiments evaluate compressive sensing and blind deconvolution, including both blind and non-blind training for deconvolution. The resulting models are reported to be nearly as accurate as models trained with full supervision despite using no ground-truth images. The findings support paired varied measurements as a useful training resource when complete target images are unavailable, while preserving the distinction between known and unknown measurement parameters.
summary.tldr: Image estimation networks trained from two varied measurements per image approach supervised accuracy without ground-truth images.

title: Training Image Estimators without Image Ground Truth

abstract: Trajectory optimization using a learned model of the environment is one of the core elements of model-based reinforcement learning. This procedure often suffers from exploiting inaccuracies of the learned model. We propose to regularize trajectory optimization by means of a denoising autoencoder that is trained on the same trajectories as the model of the environment. We show that the proposed regularization leads to improved planning with both gradient-based and gradient-free optimizers. We also demonstrate that using regularized trajectory optimization leads to rapid initial learning in a set of popular motor control tasks, which suggests that the proposed approach can be a useful tool for improving sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning can plan actions by optimizing trajectories through a learned model of the environment. A central difficulty is that an optimizer may exploit inaccuracies in that model. A trajectory can consequently appear attractive because of the model's errors, making the quality of planning depend on more than optimizing the predicted outcome.

The paper proposes regularizing trajectory optimization with a denoising autoencoder trained on the same trajectories as the environment model. This adds a learned source of regularization to planning using the data already used to model the environment. The authors show improved planning with both gradient-based and gradient-free optimizers, indicating that the reported benefit is compatible with different optimization approaches.

They also evaluate regularized trajectory optimization as part of learning on several popular motor-control tasks. The method produces rapid initial learning in those experiments. This suggests that the regularizer could help improve sample efficiency by making early model-based planning more useful, while the sample-efficiency implication remains a suggestion supported by the reported learning behavior.
summary.tldr: A denoising autoencoder regularizes planning through learned dynamics, improving trajectory optimization and producing rapid initial learning in tested motor-control tasks.

title: Regularizing Trajectory Optimization with Denoising Autoencoders

abstract: Modelling the dynamics of multi-agent learning has long been an important research topic, but all of the previous works focus on 2-agent settings and mostly use evolutionary game theoretic approaches. In this paper, we study an n-agent setting with n tends to infinity, such that agents learn their policies concurrently over repeated symmetric bimatrix games with some other agents. Using mean field theory, we approximate the effects of other agents on a single agent by an averaged effect. A Fokker-Planck equation that describes the evolution of the probability distribution of Q-values in the agent population is derived. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time to show the Q-learning dynamics under an n-agent setting can be described by a system of only three equations. We validate our model through comparisons with agent-based simulations on typical symmetric bimatrix games and different initial settings of Q-values.
