paragraphs: When many agents learn at once, each agent’s changing behavior affects the learning environment experienced by others. This paper studies those dynamics for agents playing repeated symmetric bimatrix games while updating their policies concurrently. Its analysis considers a population whose size tends to infinity, extending the focus beyond the two-agent settings described in prior work.

The authors use mean field theory to replace the detailed influence of other agents on an individual with an averaged effect. They derive a Fokker–Planck equation describing how the population’s distribution of Q-values evolves. The resulting description uses a system of only three equations, providing a compact representation of learning dynamics across a large population.

The model is checked against agent-based simulations on typical symmetric bimatrix games with different initial Q-values. These comparisons validate its account of the population behavior in the tested settings. The contribution is an analytical approximation of collective learning dynamics under the large-population setup, making the evolving distribution of learned values the central object of study.
summary.tldr: A mean field model describes large-population Q-learning dynamics in repeated symmetric games using a compact system of three equations.

title: Modelling the Dynamics of Multiagent Q-Learning in Repeated Symmetric Games: a Mean Field Theoretic Approach

abstract: We propose to learn a hierarchical prior in the context of variational autoencoders to avoid the over-regularisation resulting from a standard normal prior distribution. To incentivise an informative latent representation of the data, we formulate the learning problem as a constrained optimisation problem by extending the Taming VAEs framework to two-level hierarchical models. We introduce a graph-based interpolation method, which shows that the topology of the learned latent representation corresponds to the topology of the data manifold---and present several examples, where desired properties of latent representation such as smoothness and simple explanatory factors are learned by the prior.

paragraphs: This paper studies how the prior distribution in a variational autoencoder shapes its learned latent representation. The authors target over-regularization associated with a standard normal prior. They propose learning a hierarchical prior so that the representation is not governed solely by that fixed distribution, with the aim of retaining informative structure about the data.

The learning objective is formulated as a constrained optimization problem. Specifically, the work extends the Taming VAEs framework to a two-level hierarchical model. The constraints are intended to encourage informative latent representations, while the learned prior participates in shaping how the data are organized within that representation.

The authors also introduce a graph-based method for interpolation. Using it, they show correspondence between the topology of the learned latent representation and that of the data manifold. Several examples illustrate the prior learning desirable properties, including smoothness and simple explanatory factors. These examples connect the proposed training formulation to the organization of the resulting latent space, beyond simply specifying a more elaborate prior.
summary.tldr: Learning a hierarchical VAE prior helps address over-regularization and produces latent representations with useful structure in the presented examples.

title: Learning Hierarchical Priors in VAEs

abstract: We study the problem of learning the transition matrices of a set of Markov chains from a single stream of observations on each chain. We assume that the Markov chains are ergodic but otherwise unknown. The learner can sample Markov chains sequentially to observe their states. The goal of the learner is to sequentially select various chains to learn transition matrices uniformly well with respect to some loss function. We introduce a notion of loss that naturally extends the squared loss for learning distributions to the case of Markov chains, and further characterize the notion of being \emph{uniformly good} in all problem instances. We present a novel learning algorithm that efficiently balances \emph{exploration} and \emph{exploitation} intrinsic to this problem, without any prior knowledge of the chains. We provide finite-sample PAC-type guarantees on the performance of the algorithm. Further, we show that our algorithm asymptotically attains an optimal loss.

We introduce a notion of loss that naturally extends the squared loss for learning distributions to the case of Markov chains, and further characterize the notion of being \emph{uniformly good} in all problem instances. We present a novel learning algorithm that efficiently balances \emph{exploration} and \emph{exploitation} intrinsic to this problem, without any prior knowledge of the chains. We provide finite-sample PAC-type guarantees on the performance of the algorithm. Further, we show that our algorithm asymptotically attains an optimal loss.

paragraphs: A Markov chain describes a process whose next state depends on its current state through transition probabilities. This paper considers learning several such transition matrices from one observation stream per chain. The chains are assumed to be ergodic but are otherwise unknown, and the learner sequentially chooses which chain to sample.

The objective is to learn all transition matrices uniformly well according to a specified loss. The authors introduce a loss that extends squared error for distribution learning to Markov chains, then characterize what uniformly good performance means across problem instances. Their algorithm adaptively balances exploration and exploitation without requiring prior knowledge of the chains.

The analysis provides finite-sample, probably approximately correct guarantees, giving a probabilistic account of performance with a limited observation budget. It also proves that the algorithm approaches an optimal loss asymptotically. Together, these results connect the practical allocation question—which chain to observe next—with guarantees for both finite data and the long-run learning limit.
summary.tldr: An adaptive sampling algorithm learns multiple unknown ergodic Markov chains with finite-sample guarantees and asymptotically optimal loss.

title: Learning Multiple Markov Chains via Adaptive Allocation

abstract: Understanding why and how certain neural networks outperform others is key to guiding future development of network architectures and optimization methods. To this end, we introduce a novel visualization algorithm that reveals the internal geometry of such networks: Multislice PHATE (M-PHATE), the first method designed explicitly to visualize how a neural network's hidden representations of data evolve throughout the course of training. We demonstrate that our visualization provides intuitive, detailed summaries of the learning dynamics beyond simple global measures (i.e., validation loss and accuracy), without the need to access validation data. Furthermore, M-PHATE better captures both the dynamics and community structure of the hidden units as compared to visualization based on standard dimensionality reduction methods (e.g., ISOMAP, t-SNE). We demonstrate M-PHATE with two vignettes: continual learning and generalization. In the former, the M-PHATE visualizations display the mechanism of "catastrophic forgetting" which is a major challenge for learning in task-switching contexts. In the latter, our visualizations reveal how increased heterogeneity among hidden units correlates with improved generalization performance. An implementation of M-PHATE, along with scripts to reproduce the figures in this paper, is available at https://github.com/scottgigante/M-PHATE.

To this end, we introduce a novel visualization algorithm that reveals the internal geometry of such networks: Multislice PHATE (M-PHATE), the first method designed explicitly to visualize how a neural network's hidden representations of data evolve throughout the course of training. We demonstrate that our visualization provides intuitive, detailed summaries of the learning dynamics beyond simple global measures (i.e., validation loss and accuracy), without the need to access validation data. Furthermore, M-PHATE better captures both the dynamics and community structure of the hidden units as compared to visualization based on standard dimensionality reduction methods (e.g., ISOMAP, t-SNE). We demonstrate M-PHATE with two vignettes: continual learning and generalization. In the former, the M-PHATE visualizations display the mechanism of "catastrophic forgetting" which is a major challenge for learning in task-switching contexts. In the latter, our visualizations reveal how increased heterogeneity among hidden units correlates with improved generalization performance. An implementation of M-PHATE, along with scripts to reproduce the figures in this paper, is available at https://github.com/scottgigante/M-PHATE.

paragraphs: Loss and accuracy summarize network performance, but they offer limited insight into how internal representations develop during training. This paper introduces Multislice PHATE, or M-PHATE, to visualize that development. The method is designed specifically to reveal the changing geometry of hidden representations across training, providing a more detailed picture of learning dynamics without needing validation data.

The authors report that M-PHATE captures both changes over time and community structure among hidden units better than visualizations based on standard dimensionality-reduction methods such as ISOMAP and t-SNE. Its purpose is to make relationships among internal units and their evolution visible, expanding what can be examined beyond a single global performance curve.

Two demonstrations concern continual learning and generalization. In continual learning, the visualizations display the mechanism of catastrophic forgetting when tasks change. In the generalization example, greater heterogeneity among hidden units correlates with better generalization performance. That finding identifies an association visible through the representation geometry; it does not establish that increasing heterogeneity would itself cause better generalization.
summary.tldr: M-PHATE visualizes evolving neural representations, revealing forgetting dynamics and an association between hidden-unit heterogeneity and generalization.

title: Visualizing the PHATE of Neural Networks

abstract: For several problems of interest, there are natural constraints which exist over the output label space. For example, for the joint task of NER and POS labeling, these constraints might specify that the NER label ‘organization’ is consistent only with the POS labels ‘noun’ and ‘preposition’. These constraints can be a great way of injecting prior knowledge into a deep learning model, thereby improving overall performance. In this paper, we present a constrained optimization formulation for training a deep network with a given set of hard constraints on output labels. Our novel approach first converts the label constraints into soft logic constraints over probability distributions outputted by the network. It then converts the constrained optimization problem into an alternating min-max optimization with Lagrangian variables defined for each constraint. Since the constraints are independent of the target labels, our framework easily generalizes to semi-supervised setting. We experiment on the tasks of Semantic Role Labeling (SRL), Named Entity Recognition (NER) tagging, and fine-grained entity typing and show that our constraints not only significantly reduce the number of constraint violations, but can also result in state-of-the-art performance

Such rules offer information beyond individual training examples: a network can produce plausible labels separately while producing an inconsistent combination. This paper develops a training formulation that incorporates a supplied set of hard rules about output labels.

The method first translates those rules into soft logical constraints on the probability distributions produced by the network. It then expresses training as an alternating minimization and maximization problem, with a Lagrangian variable associated with each constraint. This connects learning the network parameters with accounting for violations of the supplied rules.

Because the constraints do not depend on knowing an example’s target labels, the formulation also extends to semi-supervised learning. Experiments cover semantic role labeling, named entity recognition, and fine-grained entity typing. The authors report substantially fewer constraint violations and show that the approach can also achieve state-of-the-art predictive performance. The findings support using output relationships as useful training information, alongside labeled examples.
summary.tldr: A constrained training formulation incorporates output-label rules into neural networks, reducing violations and sometimes achieving state-of-the-art performance.

title: A Primal Dual Formulation For Deep Learning With Constraints

abstract: The log-likelihood of a generative model often involves both positive and negative terms. For a temporal multivariate point process, the negative term sums over all the possible event types at each time and also integrates over all the possible times. As a result, maximum likelihood estimation is expensive. We show how to instead apply a version of noise-contrastive estimation---a general parameter estimation method with a less expensive stochastic objective. Our specific instantiation of this general idea works out in an interestingly non-trivial way and has provable guarantees for its optimality, consistency and efficiency. On several synthetic and real-world datasets, our method shows benefits: for the model to achieve the same level of log-likelihood on held-out data, our method needs considerably fewer function evaluations and less wall-clock time.

paragraphs: A temporal multivariate point process models events that can occur at different times and have different types. Training such a model by maximum likelihood can be expensive because the objective must account for all possible event types across time. Its negative term requires both a sum over types and an integral over possible times.

The paper develops a version of noise-contrastive estimation for this setting. This replaces the expensive likelihood-based training calculation with a less costly stochastic objective. The authors explain that adapting the general estimation idea to temporal point processes is nontrivial, and provide guarantees addressing optimality, consistency, and efficiency for their specific construction.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets compare the work required to reach the same held-out log-likelihood. The proposed method needs considerably fewer function evaluations and less elapsed time to reach that level. This comparison matters because it connects computational savings to a common measure of model fit, showing that the observed efficiency gains do not merely come from accepting a lower evaluated likelihood.
summary.tldr: A noise-contrastive estimator trains multivariate point processes more efficiently while offering theoretical guarantees and matching held-out likelihood with less computation.

title: Noise-Contrastive Estimation for Multivariate Point Processes

abstract: Sortition is a political system in which decisions are made by panels of randomly selected citizens. The process for selecting a sortition panel is traditionally thought of as uniform sampling without replacement, which has strong fairness properties. In practice, however, sampling without replacement is not possible since only a fraction of agents is willing to participate in a panel when invited, and different demographic groups participate at different rates. In order to still produce panels whose composition resembles that of the population, we develop a sampling algorithm that restores close-to-equal representation probabilities for all agents while satisfying meaningful demographic quotas. As part of its input, our algorithm requires probabilities indicating how likely each volunteer in the pool was to participate. Since these participation probabilities are not directly observable, we show how to learn them, and demonstrate our approach using data on a real sortition panel combined with information on the general population in the form of publicly available survey data.

paragraphs: Sortition selects citizens at random to serve on decision-making panels. Equal random invitations do not automatically produce equal representation, because people differ in their willingness to participate. When demographic groups accept invitations at different rates, the available volunteer pool can depart from the composition of the wider population.

This paper develops a sampling algorithm that aims to restore close-to-equal representation probabilities for individuals while meeting demographic quotas. These are related but distinct objectives: a panel should have an appropriate demographic composition, and individuals should have similar chances of representation. The algorithm explicitly addresses both within the selection process.

The method needs estimates of how likely each volunteer was to participate when invited. Because those probabilities are not directly observable, the authors also show how to learn them. They demonstrate the approach using data from a real sortition panel combined with publicly available population survey information. The resulting contribution joins participation modeling with panel sampling to counter the bias introduced by voluntary participation.
summary.tldr: A panel-selection algorithm uses learned participation probabilities to approach equal individual representation while satisfying demographic quotas.

title: Neutralizing Self-Selection Bias in Sampling for Sortition

abstract: Unsupervised and self-supervised learning approaches have become a crucial tool to learn representations for downstream prediction tasks. While these approaches are widely used in practice and achieve impressive empirical gains, their theoretical understanding largely lags behind. Towards bridging this gap, we present a unifying perspective where several such approaches can be viewed as imposing a regularization on the representation via a learnable function using unlabeled data. We propose a discriminative theoretical framework for analyzing the sample complexity of these approaches, which generalizes the framework of (Balcan and Blum, 2010) to allow learnable regularization functions. Our sample complexity bounds show that, with carefully chosen hypothesis classes to exploit the structure in the data, these learnable regularization functions can prune the hypothesis space, and help reduce the amount of labeled data needed. We then provide two concrete examples of functional regularization, one using auto-encoders and the other using masked self-supervision, and apply our framework to quantify the reduction in the sample complexity bound of labeled data. We also provide complementary empirical results to support our analysis.

paragraphs: Unsupervised and self-supervised learning often improve representations used for later prediction tasks, but explaining their benefits theoretically remains difficult. This paper presents a common perspective: several such methods use unlabeled data and a learnable function to regularize the representation. That function restricts which representations are considered suitable before or alongside learning the downstream prediction task.

The authors build a discriminative framework for analyzing sample complexity, meaning how much labeled data learning requires. Their bounds show that learnable regularization can prune the hypothesis space when the chosen classes of functions exploit the data's structure. The benefit is conditional on those choices; the theory does not say that any auxiliary objective automatically reduces label requirements.

Two examples make the framework concrete: auto-encoder-based regularization and masked self-supervision. For each, the authors quantify a reduction in the labeled-data sample complexity bound. Complementary experiments support the analysis. The contribution is a shared theoretical language for understanding how useful constraints learned from unlabeled examples can narrow the downstream learning problem.
summary.tldr: A unified theory shows how suitably chosen learnable regularization from unlabeled data can reduce downstream labeled-data requirements.

title: Functional Regularization for Representation Learning: A Unified Theoretical Perspective

abstract: Existing neural network based one-class learning methods mainly use various forms of auto-encoders or GAN style adversarial training to learn a latent representation of the given one class of data. This paper proposes an entirely different approach based on a novel regularization, called holistic regularization (or H-regularization), which enables the system to consider the data holistically, not to produce a model that biases towards some features. Combined with a proposed 2-norm instance-level data normalization, we obtain an effective one-class learning method, called HRN. To our knowledge, the proposed regularization and the normalization method have not been reported before. Experimental evaluation using both benchmark image classification and traditional anomaly detection datasets show that HRN markedly outperforms the state-of-the-art existing deep/non-deep learning models.

paragraphs: One-class learning builds a model from data belonging to a single class. The paper observes that neural approaches commonly use autoencoders or adversarial training to learn a hidden representation of that class. HRN instead centers its design on how the learning objective treats the available features, aiming to avoid a model that favors only some of them.

Its main component is holistic regularization, called H-regularization. This is designed to make the system consider the data as a whole rather than develop feature-specific bias. The authors combine it with a proposed instance-level normalization based on the 2-norm. Together, these two components form the HRN method, making regularization and normalization central to its approach.

The evaluation covers both benchmark image-classification datasets and traditional anomaly-detection datasets. The authors report that HRN substantially outperforms the deep and non-deep state-of-the-art methods compared in these experiments. The findings support this combination as an effective approach to one-class learning across the evaluated data settings.
summary.tldr: HRN combines holistic regularization with instance-level normalization to improve one-class learning on image and anomaly-detection benchmarks.

title: HRN: A Holistic Approach to One Class Learning

abstract: We propose self-adaptive training---a new training algorithm that dynamically calibrates training process by model predictions without incurring extra computational cost---to improve generalization of deep learning for potentially corrupted training data. This problem is important to robustly learning from data that are corrupted by, e.g., random noises and adversarial examples. The standard empirical risk minimization (ERM) for such data, however, may easily overfit noises and thus suffers from sub-optimal performance. In this paper, we observe that model predictions can substantially benefit the training process: self-adaptive training significantly mitigates the overfitting issue and improves generalization over ERM under both random and adversarial noises. Besides, in sharp contrast to the recently-discovered double-descent phenomenon in ERM, self-adaptive training exhibits a single-descent error-capacity curve, indicating that such a phenomenon might be a result of overfitting of noises. Experiments on the CIFAR and ImageNet datasets verify the effectiveness of our approach in two applications: classification with label noise and selective classification. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/LayneH/self-adaptive-training}.

paragraphs: Training data can contain random corruption or adversarial noise, and ordinary empirical risk minimization may overfit that corruption. This paper proposes self-adaptive training, which uses the model’s own predictions to adjust the training process dynamically. The authors state that this adjustment adds no extra computational cost.

The approach treats predictions as information that can improve learning from potentially corrupted data. The reported results show substantially reduced overfitting and better generalization than empirical risk minimization under both random and adversarial noise. The key idea is that training need not follow the supplied data rigidly throughout learning when the evolving model can help calibrate the process.

The paper also reports a single-descent error-versus-capacity curve, contrasting with the double-descent behavior observed for empirical risk minimization. This suggests that fitting noise might contribute to double descent; it does not establish that explanation universally. Experiments on CIFAR and ImageNet demonstrate effectiveness for classification with noisy labels and selective classification. Together, the findings connect a practical training change with an observation about how model capacity and noise interact.
summary.tldr: Self-adaptive training uses model predictions to adjust learning, reducing noise overfitting and improving generalization without reported extra computational cost.

title: Self-Adaptive Training: beyond Empirical Risk Minimization

abstract: Modern large scale datasets are often plagued with missing entries. For tabular data with missing values, a flurry of imputation algorithms solve for a complete matrix which minimizes some penalized reconstruction error. However, almost none of them can estimate the uncertainty of its imputations. This paper pro- poses a probabilistic and scalable framework for missing value imputation with quantified uncertainty. Our model, the Low Rank Gaussian Copula, augments a standard probabilistic model, Probabilistic Principal Component Analysis, with marginal transformations for each column that allow the model to better match the distribution of the data. It naturally handles Boolean, ordinal, and real-valued observations and quantifies the uncertainty in each imputation. The time required to fit the model scales linearly with the number of rows and the number of columns in the dataset. Empirical results show the method yields state-of-the-art imputation accuracy across a wide range of data types, including those with high rank. Our uncertainty measure predicts imputation error well: entries with lower uncertainty do have lower imputation error (on average). Moreover, for real-valued data, the resulting confidence intervals are well-calibrated.

paragraphs: Filling missing entries in a table produces estimates, but those estimates can differ substantially in reliability. This paper introduces a probabilistic matrix-completion framework that provides both imputed values and uncertainty for each one. It addresses the gap between reconstructing a complete dataset and knowing how much confidence to place in its reconstructed entries.

The Low Rank Gaussian Copula model extends probabilistic principal component analysis with a separate marginal transformation for each column. Those transformations let the model better match the distributions of different variables. The framework handles Boolean, ordinal, and real-valued observations, while model-fitting time scales linearly with the number of rows and the number of columns.

Experiments report state-of-the-art imputation accuracy across varied data types, including high-rank data. The uncertainty estimates also carry useful information: entries assigned lower uncertainty have lower error on average. For real-valued data, the reported confidence intervals are well calibrated. These results support uncertainty as an informative companion to the completed table, while preserving the distinction between average reliability and correctness of every individual estimate.
summary.tldr: A Low Rank Gaussian Copula model fills mixed-type missing data and supplies uncertainty estimates that track imputation error.

title: Matrix Completion with Quantified Uncertainty through Low Rank Gaussian Copula

abstract: We study properties of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) by analyzing their behavior on standard models of random graphs, where nodes are represented by random latent variables and edges are drawn according to a similarity kernel. This allows us to overcome the difficulties of dealing with discrete notions such as isomorphisms on very large graphs, by considering instead more natural geometric aspects. We first study the convergence of GCNs to their continuous counterpart as the number of nodes grows. Our results are fully non-asymptotic and are valid for relatively sparse graphs with an average degree that grows logarithmically with the number of nodes. We then analyze the stability of GCNs to small deformations of the random graph model. In contrast to previous studies of stability in discrete settings, our continuous setup allows us to provide more intuitive deformation-based metrics for understanding stability, which have proven useful for explaining the success of convolutional representations on Euclidean domains.

paragraphs: Understanding graph convolutional networks becomes difficult when graphs are large and comparisons depend on discrete structures such as node correspondences. This paper studies them through random graph models in which each node has a latent variable and edges are sampled according to a similarity kernel. That setup provides an underlying geometric description of the graph.

The authors first analyze how a graph convolutional network approaches a continuous counterpart as the number of nodes increases. Their results are non-asymptotic, so they concern finite graph sizes rather than only an infinite-size limit. They also cover relatively sparse graphs whose average degree increases logarithmically with the number of nodes.

The second contribution examines stability when the underlying random graph model undergoes small deformations. Working in the continuous description allows changes to be measured geometrically, offering a more intuitive account than purely discrete comparisons. Together, the results connect finite graph computations to continuous representations and provide a framework for understanding how sensitive those computations are to changes in the graph-generating model.
summary.tldr: The paper connects GCNs on large random graphs to continuous models and analyzes their convergence and stability under geometric deformations.

title: Convergence and Stability of Graph Convolutional Networks on Large Random Graphs

abstract: We introduce TransformerFusion, a transformer-based 3D scene reconstruction approach. From an input monocular RGB video, the video frames are processed by a transformer network that fuses the observations into a volumetric feature grid representing the scene; this feature grid is then decoded into an implicit 3D scene representation. Key to our approach is the transformer architecture that enables the network to learn to attend to the most relevant image frames for each 3D location in the scene, supervised only by the scene reconstruction task. Features are fused in a coarse-to-fine fashion, storing fine-level features only where needed, requiring lower memory storage and enabling fusion at interactive rates. The feature grid is then decoded to a higher-resolution scene reconstruction, using an MLP-based surface occupancy prediction from interpolated coarse-to-fine 3D features. Our approach results in an accurate surface reconstruction, outperforming state-of-the-art multi-view stereo depth estimation methods, fully-convolutional 3D reconstruction approaches, and approaches using LSTM- or GRU-based recurrent networks for video sequence fusion.

paragraphs: TransformerFusion reconstructs a three-dimensional scene from a monocular color video. A Transformer combines information from the video frames into a volumetric feature grid, which is then decoded into an implicit scene representation. The central task is to select useful visual evidence for each location in three-dimensional space.

The attention mechanism learns which frames are most relevant to each scene location using supervision from reconstruction alone. Features are combined from coarse to fine, and detailed features are stored only where needed. This reduces memory requirements and enables fusion at interactive rates. A multilayer perceptron then predicts surface occupancy from interpolated features across these levels to produce a higher-resolution reconstruction.

The reported results show accurate surfaces and improvements over state-of-the-art multi-view stereo depth estimation methods, fully convolutional reconstruction approaches, and recurrent video-fusion approaches using LSTMs or GRUs. These findings support attention as an effective mechanism for combining observations across frames. The coarse-to-fine representation also connects reconstruction detail to selective memory use, making efficiency part of the scene representation itself.
summary.tldr: TransformerFusion attends to relevant video frames at each 3D location to reconstruct detailed scenes with selective fine-scale storage.

title: TransformerFusion: Monocular RGB Scene Reconstruction using Transformers

abstract: We study online change point detection problems under the constraint of local differential privacy (LDP) where, in particular, the statistician does not have access to the raw data. As a concrete problem, we study a multivariate nonparametric regression problem. At each time point $t$, the raw data are assumed to be of the form $(X_t, Y_t)$, where $X_t$ is a $d$-dimensional feature vector and $Y_t$ is a response variable. Our primary aim is to detect changes in the regression function $m_t(x)=\mathbb{E}(Y_t |X_t=x)$ as soon as the change occurs. We provide algorithms which respect the LDP constraint, which control the false alarm probability, and which detect changes with a minimal (minimax rate-optimal) delay. To quantify the cost of privacy, we also present the optimal rate in the benchmark, non-private setting. These non-private results are also new to the literature and thus are interesting \emph{per se}. In addition, we study the univariate mean online change point detection problem, under privacy constraints. This serves as the blueprint of studying more complicated private change point detection problems.

paragraphs: Online change detection aims to recognise a shift soon after it happens while avoiding false alarms. This paper studies that problem when local differential privacy prevents the statistician from seeing raw observations. The challenge is to detect changes from privacy-protected information without losing control over either detection speed or mistaken alerts.

The main setting is multivariate nonparametric regression. Each observation contains a feature vector and a response, and the quantity that may change is the expected response given those features. The authors develop algorithms that satisfy the privacy constraint, control false alarm probability, and achieve minimax rate-optimal detection delay in the studied problem.

They also derive the optimal rate without privacy constraints, providing a benchmark for quantifying the cost of privacy. Those non-private results are themselves new contributions. A simpler problem involving changes in a univariate mean serves as a blueprint for the more complex analysis. Together, the results characterise how quickly changes can be detected while respecting local privacy.
summary.tldr: The paper gives locally private change detectors with controlled false alarms and minimax rate-optimal detection delays.

title: Locally private online change point detection

abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning has attracted wide attention due to its superior sample efficiency. Despite its impressive success so far, it is still unclear how to appropriately schedule the important hyperparameters to achieve adequate performance, such as the real data ratio for policy optimization in Dyna-style model-based algorithms. In this paper, we first theoretically analyze the role of real data in policy training, which suggests that gradually increasing the ratio of real data yields better performance. Inspired by the analysis, we propose a framework named AutoMBPO to automatically schedule the real data ratio as well as other hyperparameters in training model-based policy optimization (MBPO) algorithm, a representative running case of model-based methods. On several continuous control tasks, the MBPO instance trained with hyperparameters scheduled by AutoMBPO can significantly surpass the original one, and the real data ratio schedule found by AutoMBPO shows consistency with our theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning can learn efficiently from limited real experience, but its performance depends on training choices that may need to change over time. This paper focuses on scheduling those choices, especially the proportion of real data used for policy optimization in Dyna-style methods. The question is how that proportion should evolve during training.

The authors first analyze the role of real data theoretically. Their analysis suggests that gradually increasing its share can improve performance. They then introduce AutoMBPO, a framework that automatically schedules this ratio and other training hyperparameters for model-based policy optimization, using MBPO as the representative algorithm.

On several continuous-control tasks, MBPO trained with AutoMBPO’s schedules significantly outperforms the original version. The learned real-data schedule also agrees with the direction suggested by the theoretical analysis. These results connect an explanation of why real data matters with an automated way to adjust its use. The findings support dynamic scheduling in the studied setting rather than establishing one universal schedule for every model-based reinforcement learning method.
summary.tldr: AutoMBPO improves MBPO on continuous-control tasks by automatically scheduling training hyperparameters, including a real-data ratio consistent with theoretical analysis.

title: On Effective Scheduling of Model-based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Learning good feature representations is important for deep reinforcement learning (RL). However, with limited experience, RL often suffers from data inefficiency for training. For un-experienced or less-experienced trajectories (i.e., state-action sequences), the lack of data limits the use of them for better feature learning. In this work, we propose a novel method, dubbed PlayVirtual, which augments cycle-consistent virtual trajectories to enhance the data efficiency for RL feature representation learning. Specifically, PlayVirtual predicts future states in a latent space based on the current state and action by a dynamics model and then predicts the previous states by a backward dynamics model, which forms a trajectory cycle. Based on this, we augment the actions to generate a large amount of virtual state-action trajectories. Being free of groudtruth state supervision, we enforce a trajectory to meet the cycle consistency constraint, which can significantly enhance the data efficiency. We validate the effectiveness of our designs on the Atari and DeepMind Control Suite benchmarks. Our method achieves the state-of-the-art performance on both benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/Playvirtual.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning needs useful feature representations, but learning them is difficult when an agent has little experience. Rarely visited or entirely unvisited state-action sequences offer little direct training data. PlayVirtual addresses this problem by generating virtual trajectories that provide additional structure for learning features from limited interaction.

The method operates in a latent space. A forward dynamics model predicts future states from a current state and actions, while a backward model predicts the preceding states. Together they form a cycle. By varying the actions, PlayVirtual creates many virtual trajectories and constrains the forward and backward predictions to be consistent with one another, without requiring ground-truth states for those trajectories.

This consistency requirement supplies a learning signal for the generated sequences, linking imagined transitions to the representation being trained. The authors validate the design on Atari and the DeepMind Control Suite and report state-of-the-art performance on both benchmarks. The findings support virtual trajectory augmentation as a way to improve data efficiency in reinforcement learning feature learning.
summary.tldr: PlayVirtual improves reinforcement learning data efficiency by training representations with virtual trajectories constrained to agree forward and backward.

title: PlayVirtual: Augmenting Cycle-Consistent Virtual Trajectories for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In recent years, personalized federated learning (pFL) has attracted increasing attention for its potential in dealing with statistical heterogeneity among clients. However, the state-of-the-art pFL methods rely on model parameters aggregation at the server side, which require all models to have the same structure and size, and thus limits the application for more heterogeneous scenarios. To deal with such model constraints, we exploit the potentials of heterogeneous model settings and propose a novel training framework to employ personalized models for different clients. Specifically, we formulate the aggregation procedure in original pFL into a personalized group knowledge transfer training algorithm, namely, KT-pFL, which enables each client to maintain a personalized soft prediction at the server side to guide the others' local training. KT-pFL updates the personalized soft prediction of each client by a linear combination of all local soft predictions using a knowledge coefficient matrix, which can adaptively reinforce the collaboration among clients who own similar data distribution. Furthermore, to quantify the contributions of each client to others' personalized training, the knowledge coefficient matrix is parameterized so that it can be trained simultaneously with the models. The knowledge coefficient matrix and the model parameters are alternatively updated in each round following the gradient descent way. Extensive experiments on various datasets (EMNIST, Fashion\_MNIST, CIFAR-10) are conducted under different settings (heterogeneous models and data distributions). It is demonstrated that the proposed framework is the first federated learning paradigm that realizes personalized model training via parameterized group knowledge transfer while achieving significant performance gain comparing with state-of-the-art algorithms.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning lets clients adapt to differences in their local data. However, aggregating model parameters at a server can require every client to use the same model structure and size. This paper introduces KT-pFL to support clients with heterogeneous models through personalized knowledge transfer based on their soft predictions.

Each client has a personalized soft prediction maintained at the server to guide local training. That prediction is formed as a linear combination of all clients' local soft predictions. A learned knowledge coefficient matrix determines the contributions, allowing the framework to strengthen collaboration among clients with similar data distributions. The matrix and model parameters are updated alternately through gradient descent in each round.

This design makes the strength of knowledge sharing trainable alongside the models themselves. Experiments on EMNIST, Fashion_MNIST, and CIFAR-10 cover differing model architectures and data distributions. The authors report significant gains over state-of-the-art algorithms in those settings. The contribution is a parameterized mechanism for personalized collaboration that accommodates both model differences and differences in client data.
summary.tldr: KT-pFL learns how clients with different models should share soft predictions to improve personalized federated training.

title: Parameterized Knowledge Transfer for Personalized Federated Learning

abstract: Extracting the interaction rules of biological agents from movement sequences pose challenges in various domains. Granger causality is a practical framework for analyzing the interactions from observed time-series data; however, this framework ignores the structures and assumptions of the generative process in animal behaviors, which may lead to interpretational problems and sometimes erroneous assessments of causality. In this paper, we propose a new framework for learning Granger causality from multi-animal trajectories via augmented theory-based behavioral models with interpretable data-driven models. We adopt an approach for augmenting incomplete multi-agent behavioral models described by time-varying dynamical systems with neural networks. For efficient and interpretable learning, our model leverages theory-based architectures separating navigation and motion processes, and the theory-guided regularization for reliable behavioral modeling. This can provide interpretable signs of Granger-causal effects over time, i.e., when specific others cause the approach or separation. In experiments using synthetic datasets, our method achieved better performance than various baselines. We then analyzed multi-animal datasets of mice, flies, birds, and bats, which verified our method and obtained novel biological insights.

paragraphs: Animal movement sequences contain information about how individuals influence one another. Granger causality provides a framework for studying such interactions from time series, but it can overlook assumptions about how animal behavior generates the observations. This paper argues that ignoring those structures can make causal interpretations misleading and proposes incorporating behavioral theory directly into the analysis.

The method augments incomplete, time-varying behavioral models with interpretable neural components. Its architecture separates navigation from motion, while theory-guided regularization supports reliable behavioral modeling. This combination is designed to learn interactions efficiently and express the signs of Granger-causal effects over time, indicating when another animal's influence is associated with approach or separation.

On synthetic datasets, the method performs better than the compared baselines. The authors also analyze trajectories from mice, flies, birds, and bats, reporting biological insights from those applications. The contribution is a way to connect learned interaction patterns with an explicit model of behavior. Its causal interpretation remains framed in terms of Granger causality, the framework used by the paper.
summary.tldr: Combining behavioral models with neural components yields interpretable, time-varying Granger-causal interactions from animal trajectories.

title: Learning interaction rules from multi-animal trajectories via augmented behavioral models

abstract: We seek an entropy estimator for discrete distributions with fully empirical accuracy bounds. As stated, this goal is infeasible without some prior assumptions on the distribution. We discover that a certain information moment assumption renders the problem feasible. We argue that the moment assumption is natural and, in some sense, {\em minimalistic} --- weaker than finite support or tail decay conditions. Under the moment assumption, we provide the first finite-sample entropy estimates for infinite alphabets, nearly recovering the known minimax rates. Moreover, we demonstrate that our empirical bounds are significantly sharper than the state-of-the-art bounds, for various natural distributions and non-trivial sample regimes. Along the way, we give a dimension-free analogue of the Cover-Thomas result on entropy continuity (with respect to total variation distance) for finite alphabets, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether entropy, a measure of uncertainty in a distribution, can be estimated with accuracy bounds determined empirically from observations. For arbitrary discrete distributions, that goal is impossible without additional assumptions. The authors identify an information-moment assumption that makes it feasible, including when the set of possible outcomes is infinite.

The assumption is central to the result. The authors describe it as natural and, in a qualified sense, minimal: it is weaker than requiring finite support or imposing tail-decay conditions. Under this assumption, they provide finite-sample entropy estimates for infinite alphabets that nearly attain known minimax rates. This connects practical estimation from a limited sample with theoretical benchmarks for achievable accuracy.

The empirical accuracy bounds are also reported to be substantially sharper than existing bounds for several natural distributions and meaningful sample regimes. A further theoretical contribution concerns continuity: how much entropy can change when distributions are close in total variation distance. Their dimension-free result extends a finite-alphabet continuity result, making the number of possible outcomes less restrictive in this analysis.
summary.tldr: An information-moment assumption enables empirical entropy accuracy bounds and near-minimax finite-sample estimation even for infinite alphabets.

title: Dimension-free empirical entropy estimation

abstract: Recently, Vision Transformer and its variants have shown great promise on various computer vision tasks. The ability to capture local and global visual dependencies through self-attention is the key to its success. But it also brings challenges due to quadratic computational overhead, especially for the high-resolution vision tasks(e.g., object detection). Many recent works have attempted to reduce the cost and improve model performance by applying either coarse-grained global attention or fine-grained local attention. However, both approaches cripple the modeling power of the original self-attention mechanism of multi-layer Transformers, leading to sub-optimal solutions. In this paper, we present focal attention, a new attention mechanism that incorporates both fine-grained local and coarse-grained global interactions. In this new mechanism, each token attends its closest surrounding tokens at the fine granularity and the tokens far away at a coarse granularity and thus can capture both short- and long-range visual dependencies efficiently and effectively. With focal attention, we propose a new variant of Vision Transformer models, called Focal Transformers, which achieve superior performance over the state-of-the-art (SoTA) Vision Transformers on a range of public image classification and object detection benchmarks. In particular, our Focal Transformer models with a moderate size of 51.1M and a large size of 89.8M achieve 83.6% and 84.0%Top-1 accuracy, respectively, on ImageNet classification at 224×224. When employed as the backbones, Focal Transformers achieve consistent and substantial improvements over the current SoTA Swin Transformers [44] across 6 different object detection methods. Our largest Focal Transformer yields58.7/59.0boxmAPs and50.9/51.3mask mAPs on COCO mini-val/test-dev, and55.4mIoU onADE20K for semantic segmentation, creating new SoTA on three of the most challenging computer vision tasks.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers use attention to relate information across an image, but full attention has a computational cost that grows quadratically. This becomes particularly demanding for high-resolution tasks. The paper argues that relying only on detailed local attention or only on coarse global attention restricts the visual relationships a model can capture.

Focal attention combines both resolutions in one mechanism. Each token attends to nearby tokens in fine detail and to distant tokens at a coarser level. This gives the model access to local structure and broad image context without treating every distant location at the same fine resolution. The authors build a family of Focal Transformers around this attention pattern.

The models outperform the compared Vision Transformers on the reported classification and detection benchmarks. On ImageNet at 224×224 resolution, models with 51.1 million and 89.8 million parameters achieve 83.6% and 84.0% top-1 accuracy. As backbones, they improve on Swin Transformers across six detection methods. The reported detection and segmentation results further support the usefulness of combining nearby detail with distant context.
summary.tldr: Focal attention combines detailed local interactions with coarse distant interactions to improve Vision Transformer efficiency and benchmark performance.

title: Focal Attention for Long-Range Interactions in Vision Transformers

abstract: Various graph contrastive learning models have been proposed to improve the performance of tasks on graph datasets in recent years. While effective and prevalent, these models are usually carefully customized. In particular, despite all recent work create two contrastive views, they differ in a variety of view augmentations, architectures, and objectives. It remains an open question how to build your graph contrastive learning model from scratch for particular graph tasks and datasets. In this work, we aim to fill this gap by studying how graph information is transformed and transferred during the contrastive learning process, and proposing an information-aware graph contrastive learning framework called InfoGCL. The key to the success of the proposed framework is to follow the Information Bottleneck principle to reduce the mutual information between contrastive parts while keeping task-relevant information intact at both the levels of the individual module and the entire framework so that the information loss during graph representation learning can be minimized. We show for the first time that all recent graph contrastive learning methods can be unified by our framework. Based on theoretical and empirical analysis on benchmark graph datasets, we show that InfoGCL achieves state-of-the-art performance in the settings of both graph classification and node classification tasks.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning methods typically construct two views of graph data, but differ in their transformations, architectures, and objectives. Those choices are often carefully customized, leaving limited guidance for designing a method for a new task. InfoGCL addresses this problem by examining how information moves through the learning process.

The framework follows the Information Bottleneck principle. It aims to reduce mutual information between the contrasted parts while preserving information relevant to the target task. The authors apply this reasoning both to individual modules and to the complete framework, using task-relevant information preservation as a guide for design.

The paper reports that its framework unifies the recent graph contrastive methods considered in the work. Theoretical and empirical analyses support the approach, and benchmark experiments achieve state-of-the-art performance on graph classification and node classification. The contribution combines a shared explanation of existing designs with a framework for constructing graph representations that retain the information needed for downstream prediction.
summary.tldr: InfoGCL uses information-bottleneck reasoning to unify graph contrastive learning designs and achieves leading benchmark results for graph and node classification.

title: InfoGCL: Information-Aware Graph Contrastive Learning

abstract: We consider experiments in dynamical systems where interventions on some experimental units impact other units through a limiting constraint (such as a limited supply of products). Despite outsize practical importance, the best estimators for this `Markovian' interference problem are largely heuristic in nature, and their bias is not well understood. We formalize the problem of inference in such experiments as one of policy evaluation. Off-policy estimators, while unbiased, apparently incur a large penalty in variance relative to state-of-the-art heuristics. We introduce an on-policy estimator: the Differences-In-Q's (DQ) estimator. We show that the DQ estimator can in general have exponentially smaller variance than off-policy evaluation. At the same time, its bias is second order in the impact of the intervention. This yields a striking bias-variance tradeoff so that the DQ estimator effectively dominates state-of-the-art alternatives. From a theoretical perspective, we introduce three separate novel techniques that are of independent interest in the theory of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Our empirical evaluation includes a set of experiments on a city-scale ride-hailing simulator.

paragraphs: In a dynamic system, treating one experimental unit can affect others through a shared constraint, such as limited product supply. This interference complicates the estimation of intervention effects. The paper formulates this Markovian interference problem as policy evaluation, bringing reinforcement-learning tools to the analysis of experiments.

The authors introduce the Differences-In-Q's estimator, an on-policy alternative to off-policy evaluation. Off-policy estimators are unbiased but can carry a large variance cost relative to existing heuristics. The new estimator can have exponentially smaller variance, while its bias is second order in the size of the intervention's impact.

That combination gives a specific bias–variance tradeoff: it accepts a controlled form of bias in exchange for potentially substantial reductions in variability. The authors report that this tradeoff lets the estimator effectively dominate state-of-the-art alternatives. Their empirical evaluation includes experiments in a city-scale ride-hailing simulator. The theoretical development also introduces three techniques of independent interest to reinforcement learning, connecting practical interference estimation to broader policy-evaluation questions.
summary.tldr: The Differences-In-Q's estimator addresses dynamic experimental interference with second-order bias and potentially exponentially lower variance than off-policy evaluation.

title: Markovian Interference in Experiments

abstract: Diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs) are emerging powerful generative models. Despite their high-quality generation performance, DPMs still suffer from their slow sampling as they generally need hundreds or thousands of sequential function evaluations (steps) of large neural networks to draw a sample. Sampling from DPMs can be viewed alternatively as solving the corresponding diffusion ordinary differential equations (ODEs). In this work, we propose an exact formulation of the solution of diffusion ODEs. The formulation analytically computes the linear part of the solution, rather than leaving all terms to black-box ODE solvers as adopted in previous works. By applying change-of-variable, the solution can be equivalently simplified to an exponentially weighted integral of the neural network. Based on our formulation, we propose DPM-Solver, a fast dedicated high-order solver for diffusion ODEs with the convergence order guarantee. DPM-Solver is suitable for both discrete-time and continuous-time DPMs without any further training. Experimental results show that DPM-Solver can generate high-quality samples in only 10 to 20 function evaluations on various datasets. We achieve 4.70 FID in 10 function evaluations and 2.87 FID in 20 function evaluations on the CIFAR10 dataset, and a 4~16x speedup compared with previous state-of-the-art training-free samplers on various datasets.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate high-quality samples, but sampling often requires hundreds or thousands of sequential neural-network evaluations. DPM-Solver addresses this cost by treating generation as solving a diffusion ordinary differential equation and designing a numerical method specifically for that equation’s structure.

The authors derive an exact solution formulation that handles the linear component analytically. A change of variables then expresses the remaining computation as an exponentially weighted integral of the neural network. This formulation supports a high-order numerical solver with a convergence-order guarantee. The exact formulation underlies the solver; it does not mean that a finite-step numerical sample is exact.

The method works with both discrete-time and continuous-time diffusion models without further training. Experiments report high-quality samples using 10 to 20 network evaluations and speedups of four to sixteen times over previous state-of-the-art training-free samplers. The contribution is a sampling improvement for existing models, demonstrating how exploiting the equation’s structure can substantially reduce generation cost.
summary.tldr: DPM-Solver exploits diffusion equations’ structure to generate high-quality samples in 10–20 network evaluations without additional training.

title: DPM-Solver: A Fast ODE Solver for Diffusion Probabilistic Model Sampling in Around 10 Steps

abstract: The ability of continual learning systems to transfer knowledge from previously seen tasks in order to maximize performance on new tasks is a significant challenge for the field, limiting the applicability of continual learning solutions to realistic scenarios. Consequently, this study aims to broaden our understanding of transfer and its driving forces in the specific case of continual reinforcement learning. We adopt SAC as the underlying RL algorithm and Continual World as a suite of continuous control tasks. We systematically study how different components of SAC (the actor and the critic, exploration, and data) affect transfer efficacy, and we provide recommendations regarding various modeling options. The best set of choices, dubbed ClonEx-SAC, is evaluated on the recent Continual World benchmark. ClonEx-SAC achieves 87% final success rate compared to 80% of PackNet, the best method in the benchmark. Moreover, the transfer grows from 0.18 to 0.54 according to the metric provided by Continual World.

paragraphs: Continual reinforcement learning asks an agent to learn across a sequence of tasks. A central challenge is making experience on earlier tasks improve performance on later ones. This paper investigates which parts of a learning system drive that transfer, using Soft Actor-Critic, or SAC, and the continuous-control tasks in Continual World.

The study systematically examines the actor, the critic, exploration, and data. These components cover the agent's action choices, its assessment of actions, how it seeks experience, and the experience available for learning. By examining their contributions to transfer, the authors develop recommendations for modeling choices. They combine their best choices into a method called ClonEx-SAC.

On the Continual World benchmark, ClonEx-SAC reaches an 87% final success rate, compared with 80% for PackNet, described as the benchmark's best existing method. Transfer also rises from 0.18 to 0.54 under the benchmark's metric. These results support the selected combination of design choices in this setting and show improvement in both final task success and measured transfer.
summary.tldr: A systematic study of SAC's components produces ClonEx-SAC, improving both final success and measured transfer on Continual World.

title: Disentangling Transfer in Continual Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Although deep neural networks (DNN) have achieved great success, their applications in safety-critical areas are hindered due to their vulnerability to adversarial attacks. Some recent works have accordingly proposed to enhance the robustness of DNN from a dynamic system perspective. Following this line of inquiry, and inspired by the asymptotic stability of the general nonautonomous dynamical system, we propose to make each clean instance be the asymptotically stable equilibrium points of a slowly time-varying system in order to defend against adversarial attacks. We present a theoretical guarantee that if a clean instance is an asymptotically stable equilibrium point and the adversarial instance is in the neighborhood of this point, the asymptotic stability will reduce the adversarial noise to bring the adversarial instance close to the clean instance. Motivated by our theoretical results, we go on to propose a nonautonomous neural ordinary differential equation (ASODE) and place constraints on its corresponding linear time-variant system to make all clean instances act as its asymptotically stable equilibrium points. Our analysis suggests that the constraints can be converted to regularizers in implementation. The experimental results show that ASODE improves robustness against adversarial attacks and outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

Some recent works have accordingly proposed to enhance the robustness of DNN from a dynamic system perspective. Following this line of inquiry, and inspired by the asymptotic stability of the general nonautonomous dynamical system, we propose to make each clean instance be the asymptotically stable equilibrium points of a slowly time-varying system in order to defend against adversarial attacks. We present a theoretical guarantee that if a clean instance is an asymptotically stable equilibrium point and the adversarial instance is in the neighborhood of this point, the asymptotic stability will reduce the adversarial noise to bring the adversarial instance close to the clean instance. Motivated by our theoretical results, we go on to propose a nonautonomous neural ordinary differential equation (ASODE) and place constraints on its corresponding linear time-variant system to make all clean instances act as its asymptotically stable equilibrium points. Our analysis suggests that the constraints can be converted to regularizers in implementation. The experimental results show that ASODE improves robustness against adversarial attacks and outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: The paper approaches adversarial defense through the behavior of a dynamical system. Its idea is to make a clean input an asymptotically stable equilibrium: a point toward which nearby disturbed inputs move as the system evolves. If a malicious perturbation starts sufficiently close to that point, the dynamics could reduce the disturbance.

The authors provide a theoretical guarantee with precisely that local condition. When the clean instance is an asymptotically stable equilibrium and the adversarial instance lies in its neighborhood, stability brings the adversarial instance closer to the clean one. They use this result to motivate ASODE, a neural ordinary differential equation whose dynamics change with time.

ASODE places constraints on an associated linear time-varying system to make clean instances act as stable equilibria. The analysis suggests implementing those constraints as regularization terms. Experiments report improved adversarial robustness and performance above state-of-the-art methods. The theoretical protection remains tied to the equilibrium and neighborhood assumptions, while the experiments provide evidence for the resulting implementation.
summary.tldr: ASODE uses stability-inspired neural dynamics to reduce nearby adversarial perturbations and reports improved robustness in experiments.

title: Defending Against Adversarial Attacks via Neural Dynamic System

abstract: In this paper, we investigate Nash-regret minimization in congestion games, a class of games with benign theoretical structure and broad real-world applications. We first propose a centralized algorithm based on the optimism in the face of uncertainty principle for congestion games with (semi-)bandit feedback, and obtain finite-sample guarantees. Then we propose a decentralized algorithm via a novel combination of the Frank-Wolfe method and G-optimal design. By exploiting the structure of the congestion game, we show the sample complexity of both algorithms depends only polynomially on the number of players and the number of facilities, but not the size of the action set, which can be exponentially large in terms of the number of facilities. We further define a new problem class, Markov congestion games, which allows us to model the non-stationarity in congestion games. We propose a centralized algorithm for Markov congestion games, whose sample complexity again has only polynomial dependence on all relevant problem parameters, but not the size of the action set.

paragraphs: Congestion games describe interactions in which multiple players use shared facilities and their choices affect one another. This paper studies learning in these games with limited feedback, focusing on Nash regret. A central difficulty is that the available actions can form an exponentially large set even when the number of facilities is relatively modest.

The authors develop two algorithms that exploit the game's structure. A centralized algorithm follows the principle of optimism under uncertainty and supports bandit or semi-bandit feedback, with finite-sample guarantees. A decentralized algorithm combines the Frank-Wolfe optimization method with G-optimal design. For both, sample complexity depends polynomially on player and facility counts rather than on the action-set size.

The paper also introduces Markov congestion games to represent non-stationarity in congestion settings. Its centralized algorithm for this extension again has polynomial sample complexity in the relevant problem parameters without depending on action-set size. The shared contribution is a way to obtain learning guarantees that avoid scaling with the potentially enormous collection of actions.
summary.tldr: Structure-aware algorithms learn in congestion games with sample guarantees that avoid dependence on exponentially large action sets.

title: Learning in Congestion Games with Bandit Feedback

abstract: The key to Black-Box Optimization is to efficiently search through input regions with potentially widely-varying numerical properties, to achieve low-regret descent and fast progress toward the optima. Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) methods have recently been introduced to improve Bayesian optimization by computing better partitioning of the search space that balances exploration and exploitation. Extending this promising framework, we study how to further integrate sample-based descent for faster optimization. We design novel ways of expanding Monte Carlo search trees, with new descent methods at vertices that incorporate stochastic search and Gaussian Processes. We propose the corresponding rules for balancing progress and uncertainty, branch selection, tree expansion, and backpropagation. The designed search process puts more emphasis on sampling for faster descent and uses localized Gaussian Processes as auxiliary metrics for both exploitation and exploration. We show empirically that the proposed algorithms can outperform state-of-the-art methods on many challenging benchmark problems.

paragraphs: Black-box optimization must find promising inputs through evaluations, even when different regions of the search space behave very differently. Tree-based approaches can organize that space and balance exploring uncertain regions against exploiting promising ones. This paper extends that approach by integrating sample-based descent more deeply into Monte Carlo tree search.

The authors develop new tree-expansion mechanisms and descent methods at tree vertices, combining stochastic search with Gaussian processes. They also design rules for branch selection, uncertainty versus progress, and propagating information back through the tree. Localized Gaussian processes provide auxiliary guidance for exploration and exploitation, while the search puts greater emphasis on sampling that can produce faster descent.

Experiments show that the proposed algorithms can outperform state-of-the-art methods on many challenging benchmark problems. This is an empirical finding rather than a universal claim about every black-box objective. The main contribution is a coordinated search procedure in which regional organization and local improvement work together to accelerate progress toward good solutions.
summary.tldr: Monte Carlo Tree Descent combines tree search, stochastic descent, and localized Gaussian processes to improve black-box optimization on many benchmarks.

title: Monte Carlo Tree Descent for Black-Box Optimization

abstract: Despite achieving superior performance in human-level control problems, unlike humans, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) lacks high-order intelligence (e.g., logic deduction and reuse), thus it behaves ineffectively than humans regarding learning and generalization in complex problems. Previous works attempt to directly synthesize a white-box logic program as the DRL policy, manifesting logic-driven behaviors. However, most synthesis methods are built on imperative or declarative programming, and each has a distinct limitation, respectively. The former ignores the cause-effect logic during synthesis, resulting in low generalizability across tasks. The latter is strictly proof-based, thus failing to synthesize programs with complex hierarchical logic. In this paper, we combine the above two paradigms together and propose a novel Generalizable Logic Synthesis (GALOIS) framework to synthesize hierarchical and strict cause-effect logic programs. GALOIS leverages the program sketch and defines a new sketch-based hybrid program language for guiding the synthesis. Based on that, GALOIS proposes a sketch-based program synthesis method to automatically generate white-box programs with generalizable and interpretable cause-effect logic. Extensive evaluations on various decision-making tasks with complex logic demonstrate the superiority of GALOIS over mainstream baselines regarding the asymptotic performance, generalizability, and great knowledge reusability across different environments.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can struggle to reuse logical knowledge across complex decision-making tasks. One approach is to synthesize an explicit program that serves as a policy. The paper identifies complementary weaknesses in existing synthesis approaches: imperative methods neglect cause-and-effect logic during synthesis, while strictly proof-based declarative methods struggle with complex hierarchical logic.

GALOIS combines these programming paradigms to synthesize policies with both hierarchical organization and explicit cause-and-effect logic. It uses a program sketch to guide the search and introduces a hybrid programming language built around that sketch. A corresponding synthesis method automatically generates programs whose decision logic is interpretable and intended to transfer across tasks.

Evaluations on decision-making tasks involving complex logic show stronger eventual performance, generalization, and knowledge reuse across environments than the mainstream baselines tested. These findings support combining logical constraints with program structure when learning reusable policies. The contribution encompasses both a representation for such policies and a method for constructing them, connecting interpretable program generation to improvements in the evaluated reinforcement learning settings.
summary.tldr: GALOIS combines imperative and declarative program synthesis to learn interpretable hierarchical policies with improved generalization and knowledge reuse in evaluated tasks.

title: GALOIS: Boosting Deep Reinforcement Learning via Generalizable Logic Synthesis

abstract: Reliable predictive uncertainty estimation plays an important role in enabling the deployment of neural networks to safety-critical settings. A popular approach for estimating the predictive uncertainty of neural networks is to define a prior distribution over the network parameters, infer an approximate posterior distribution, and use it to make stochastic predictions. However, explicit inference over neural network parameters makes it difficult to incorporate meaningful prior information about the data-generating process into the model. In this paper, we pursue an alternative approach. Recognizing that the primary object of interest in most settings is the distribution over functions induced by the posterior distribution over neural network parameters, we frame Bayesian inference in neural networks explicitly as inferring a posterior distribution over functions and propose a scalable function-space variational inference method that allows incorporating prior information and results in reliable predictive uncertainty estimates. We show that the proposed method leads to state-of-the-art uncertainty estimation and predictive performance on a range of prediction tasks and demonstrate that it performs well on a challenging safety-critical medical diagnosis task in which reliable uncertainty estimation is essential.
