paragraphs: Numeric planning extends symbolic planning by allowing states to include numerical variables. Graphs are a natural fit for the symbolic part because they represent relationships among objects and can accommodate planning instances with different numbers of objects. This paper develops learning methods that also handle the numerical information.

The authors introduce a graph kernel for graphs containing both continuous and categorical attributes. This gives the model a way to compare planning instances while retaining both kinds of information. They also develop optimization methods for learning heuristic functions, which guide the process of solving numeric planning tasks. The intended models are data-efficient and interpretable.

In the reported experiments, the graph kernels are substantially more efficient and generalize better than graph neural networks for numeric planning. They also achieve competitive coverage relative to domain-independent numeric planners. These findings support graph kernels as a useful approach to this planning setting: a representation designed around mixed attributes can provide strong learning behavior while remaining competitive in its ability to solve tasks.
summary.tldr: New graph kernels and heuristic-learning methods deliver efficient, generalizable numeric planning in the reported experiments.

title: Graph Learning for Numeric Planning

abstract: We study the problem of learning a Nash equilibrium (NE) in Markov games which is a cornerstone in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). In particular, we focus on infinite-horizon adversarial team Markov games (ATMGs) in which agents that share a common reward function compete against a single opponent, *the adversary*. These games unify two-player zero-sum Markov games and Markov potential games, resulting in a setting that encompasses both collaboration and competition. Kalogiannis et al. (2023) provided an efficient equilibrium computation algorithm for ATMGs which presumes knowledge of the reward and transition functions and has no sample complexity guarantees. We contribute a learning algorithm that utilizes MARL policy gradient methods with iteration and sample complexity that is polynomial in the approximation error $\epsilon$ and the natural parameters of the ATMG, resolving the main caveats of the solution by (Kalogiannis et al., 2023). It is worth noting that previously, the existence of learning algorithms for NE was known for Markov two-player zero-sum and potential games but not for ATMGs. Seen through the lens of min-max optimization, computing a NE in these games consists a nonconvex--nonconcave saddle-point problem. Min-max optimization has received an extensive study. Nevertheless, the case of nonconvex--nonconcave landscapes remains elusive: in full generality, finding saddle-points is computationally intractable (Daskalakis et al., 2021). We circumvent the aforementioned intractability by developing techniques that exploit the hidden structure of the objective function via a nonconvex--concave reformulation. However, this introduces a challenge of a feasibility set with coupled constraints. We tackle these challenges by establishing novel techniques for optimizing weakly-smooth nonconvex functions, extending the framework of (Devolder et al., 2014).

The goal is to learn a Nash equilibrium, extending learning guarantees beyond the previously established two-player zero-sum and potential-game settings.

The authors develop an algorithm using multi-agent policy gradients and provide polynomial iteration and sample-complexity guarantees in the relevant approximation and game parameters. Learning from interactions is therefore central to the contribution.

That reformulation creates coupled feasibility constraints, which they handle through new techniques for weakly smooth nonconvex optimization. The result depends on the structure of these team games rather than solving arbitrary nonconvex-nonconcave games.
summary.tldr: A policy-gradient algorithm learns approximate equilibria in adversarial team Markov games by exploiting hidden optimization structure.

title: Learning Equilibria in Adversarial Team Markov Games: A Nonconvex-Hidden-Concave Min-Max Optimization Problem

abstract: We consider distributed learning scenarios where $M$ machines interact with a parameter server along several communication rounds in order to minimize a joint objective function. Focusing on the heterogeneous case, where different machines may draw samples from different data-distributions, we design the first local update method that provably benefits over the two most prominent distributed baselines: namely Minibatch-SGD and Local-SGD. Key to our approach is a slow querying technique that we customize to the distributed setting, which in turn enables a better mitigation of the bias caused by local updates.

paragraphs: Distributed learning can divide training across several machines that communicate with a parameter server over multiple rounds. This paper considers minimizing a shared objective when the machines may sample from different data distributions. That heterogeneity matters because local updates can introduce bias, complicating the task of making progress on the joint objective.

SLowcalSGD uses a slow-querying technique adapted to this distributed setting. The central idea is to change how query points evolve so that the method can better mitigate bias caused by local updates. The contribution focuses on the update procedure itself within stochastic convex optimization, with heterogeneous machine data explicitly included in the setting.

The authors present it as the first local-update method with a provable benefit over both Minibatch-SGD and Local-SGD, the two prominent baselines considered. This is a theoretical improvement tied to the stated optimization setting. Its significance is that changing the query-point behavior provides a way to improve distributed local learning even when different machines draw on different underlying distributions.
summary.tldr: SLowcalSGD uses slow query points to reduce local-update bias and provably improve on two distributed SGD baselines in heterogeneous convex optimization.

title: SLowcalSGD : Slow Query Points Improve Local-SGD for Stochastic Convex Optimization

abstract: Per-example gradient norms are a vital ingredient for estimating gradient noise scale (GNS) with minimal variance. Observing the tensor contractions required to compute them, we propose a method with minimal FLOPs in 3D or greater tensor regimes by simultaneously computing the norms while computing the parameter gradients. Using this method we are able to observe the GNS of different layers at higher accuracy than previously possible. We find that the total GNS of contemporary transformer models is predicted well by the GNS of only the normalization layers. As a result, focusing only on the normalization layer, we develop a custom kernel to compute the per-example gradient norms while performing the LayerNorm backward pass with zero throughput overhead. Tracking GNS on only those layers, we are able to guide a practical batch size schedule that reduces training time by 18% on a Chinchilla-optimal language model.

paragraphs: Gradient noise scale helps characterize variability in training gradients, and per-example gradient norms are important for estimating it accurately. The paper introduces a way to compute these norms alongside parameter gradients with minimal floating-point work in tensor regimes of three or more dimensions. This enables more accurate observation of noise scale across individual layers.

The finding connects an empirical predictor drawn from a small subset of layers to a practical training decision, allowing noise-scale tracking to inform batch sizing without the reported throughput penalty.
summary.tldr: Normalization-layer gradients predict transformer gradient noise scale well enough to guide a batch-size schedule that reduced training time by 18%.

title: Normalization Layer Per-Example Gradients are Sufficient to Predict Gradient Noise Scale in Transformers

abstract: Certified defenses against adversarial attacks offer formal guarantees on the robustness of a model, making them more reliable than empirical methods such as adversarial training, whose effectiveness is often later reduced by unseen attacks. Still, the limited certified robustness that is currently achievable has been a bottleneck for their practical adoption. Gowal et al. and Wang et al. have shown that generating additional training data using state-of-the-art diffusion models can considerably improve the robustness of adversarial training. In this work, we demonstrate that a similar approach can substantially improve deterministic certified defenses but also reveal notable differences in the scaling behavior between certified and empirical methods. In addition, we provide a list of recommendations to scale the robustness of certified training approaches. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art deterministic robustness certificates on CIFAR-10 for the $\ell_2$ ($\epsilon = 36/255$) and $\ell_{\infty}$ ($\epsilon = 8/255$) threat models, outperforming the previous results by $+3.95$ and $+1.39$ percentage points, respectively. Furthermore, we report similar improvements for CIFAR-100.

paragraphs: Certified defenses provide formal robustness guarantees within specified attack conditions. Their practical usefulness has been constrained by the level of certified robustness attainable. This paper asks whether additional training data generated by diffusion models can improve deterministic certified defenses, extending an approach previously shown to help empirical adversarial training.

The authors find that generated data can substantially improve certified defenses, but the scaling behavior differs notably from that of empirical methods. They also provide recommendations for scaling certified training. This distinction matters because gains observed in adversarial training do not by themselves establish how methods with formal certificates will respond to additional generated data.

The approach achieves state-of-the-art deterministic certificates on CIFAR-10 for an ℓ2 threat model with ε = 36/255 and an ℓ∞ threat model with ε = 8/255. Improvements over previous results are 3.95 and 1.39 percentage points, respectively, with similar gains reported on CIFAR-100. These findings demonstrate stronger certified robustness under the specified threat models.
summary.tldr: Diffusion-generated training data improves deterministic certified robustness, with scaling behavior that differs from empirical adversarial training.

title: On the Scalability of Certified Adversarial Robustness with Generated Data

abstract: Student cognitive modeling (SCM) is a fundamental task in intelligent education, with applications ranging from personalized learning to educational resource allocation. By exploiting students' response logs, SCM aims to predict their exercise performance as well as estimate knowledge proficiency in a subject. Data mining approaches such as matrix factorization can obtain high accuracy in predicting student performance on exercises, but the knowledge proficiency is unknown or poorly estimated. The situation is further exacerbated if only sparse interactions exist between exercises and students (or knowledge concepts). To solve this dilemma, we root monotonicity (a fundamental psychometric theory on educational assessments) in a co-factorization framework and present an autoencoder-like nonnegative matrix co-factorization (AE-NMCF), which improves the accuracy of estimating the student's knowledge proficiency via an encoder-decoder learning pipeline. The resulting estimation problem is nonconvex with nonnegative constraints. We introduce a projected gradient method based on block coordinate descent with Lipschitz constants and guarantee the method's theoretical convergence. Experiments on several real-world data sets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in terms of both performance prediction accuracy and knowledge estimation ability, when compared with existing student cognitive models.

These goals do not automatically coincide: a model can predict answers accurately while providing weak estimates of knowledge proficiency. The problem becomes more difficult when observations linking students, exercises, and knowledge concepts are sparse.

The paper introduces AE-NMCF, an autoencoder-like method based on nonnegative matrix co-factorization. Its encoder-decoder learning process incorporates monotonicity, a principle from educational assessment that connects greater proficiency with better performance. Bringing this principle into the factorization framework is intended to make the estimated proficiency more meaningful, while retaining the ability to predict exercise outcomes.

The contribution therefore addresses the quality of the inferred student profile alongside predictive accuracy.
summary.tldr: AE-NMCF incorporates an educational monotonicity principle into matrix co-factorization to improve student-performance predictions and knowledge estimates.

title: An Autoencoder-Like Nonnegative Matrix Co-Factorization for Improved Student Cognitive Modeling

abstract: A pivotal brain computation relies on the ability to sustain perception-action loops. Stochastic optimal control theory offers a mathematical framework to explain these processes at the algorithmic level through optimality principles. However, incorporating a realistic noise model of the sensorimotor system — accounting for multiplicative noise in feedback and motor output, as well as internal noise in estimation — makes the problem challenging. Currently, the algorithm that is commonly used is the one proposed in the seminal study in (Todorov, 2005). After discovering some pitfalls in the original derivation, i.e., unbiased estimation does not hold, we improve the algorithm by proposing an efficient gradient descent-based optimization that minimizes the cost-to-go while only imposing linearity of the control law. The optimal solution is obtained by iteratively propagating in closed form the sufficient statistics to compute the expected cost and then minimizing this cost with respect to the filter and control gains. We demonstrate that this approach results in a significantly lower overall cost than current state-of-the-art solutions, particularly in the presence of internal noise, though the improvement is present in other circumstances as well, with theoretical explanations for this enhanced performance. Providing the optimal control law is key for inverse control inference, especially in explaining behavioral data under rationality assumptions.

The optimal solution is obtained by iteratively propagating in closed form the sufficient statistics to compute the expected cost and then minimizing this cost with respect to the filter and control gains. Providing the optimal control law is key for inverse control inference, especially in explaining behavioral data under rationality assumptions.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimal control offers a mathematical account of how perception and action can work together under uncertainty. Realistic sensorimotor modeling includes multiplicative noise in feedback and motor output, together with internal noise in estimation. These noise sources make optimization difficult. The authors identify a problem in a commonly used derivation: its unbiased-estimation property does not hold.

They propose an efficient gradient-descent approach that minimizes future expected cost while imposing only linearity of the control law. The procedure repeatedly propagates sufficient statistics in closed form to calculate expected cost, then optimizes the filter and control gains. This directly connects the treatment of estimation with the choice of actions.

The method achieves significantly lower overall cost than the state-of-the-art solutions evaluated, with especially strong improvements under internal noise and gains in other circumstances as well. The paper also supplies theoretical explanations. Better control solutions matter for inverse control inference, where researchers use observed behavior to infer underlying objectives under assumptions of rational action.
summary.tldr: The paper corrects an estimation issue and jointly optimizes filtering and linear control to lower costs under sensorimotor noise.

title: Stochastic Optimal Control and Estimation with Multiplicative and Internal Noise

abstract: Accurately estimating depth in 360-degree imagery is crucial for virtual reality, autonomous navigation, and immersive media applications. Existing depth estimation methods designed for perspective-view imagery fail when applied to 360-degree images due to different camera projections and distortions. We propose a new depth estimation framework that uses unlabeled 360-degree data effectively. Our approach uses state-of-the-art perspective depth estimation models as teacher models to generate pseudo labels through a six-face cube projection technique, enabling efficient labeling of depth in 360-degree images. This method leverages the increasing availability of large datasets. It includes two main stages: offline mask generation for invalid regions and an online semi-supervised joint training regime. We tested our approach on benchmark datasets such as Matterport3D and Stanford2D3D, showing significant improvements in depth estimation accuracy, particularly in zero-shot scenarios. Our proposed training pipeline can enhance any 360 monocular depth estimator and demonstrate effective knowledge transfer across different camera projections and data types.

Models trained for perspective views therefore do not transfer directly. Depth Anywhere addresses this mismatch by using strong perspective-depth models to help train panoramic depth estimators with unlabeled 360-degree data.

The framework projects a panorama onto six cube faces, giving the teacher models perspective views from which to generate depth pseudo-labels. These generated labels provide training information for otherwise unlabeled panoramas. The pipeline includes offline masking of invalid regions and an online semi-supervised training stage, combining these components into a way to transfer depth knowledge across camera projections.

The authors present the pipeline as applicable to any monocular 360-degree depth estimator. The results support using existing perspective models and growing unlabeled panoramic collections together, making cross-projection knowledge transfer a central part of improving panoramic depth estimation.
summary.tldr: Depth Anywhere transfers perspective-depth knowledge to 360-degree estimators through cube-face pseudo-labels and semi-supervised training on unlabeled panoramas.

title: Depth Anywhere: Enhancing 360 Monocular Depth Estimation via Perspective Distillation and Unlabeled Data Augmentation

abstract: Fine urban change segmentation using multi-temporal remote sensing images is essential for understanding human-environment interactions in urban areas. Although there have been advances in high-quality land cover datasets that reveal the physical features of urban landscapes, the lack of fine-grained land use datasets hinders a deeper understanding of how human activities are distributed across landscapes and the impact of these activities on the environment, thus constraining proper technique development. To address this, we introduce FUSU, the first fine-grained land use change segmentation dataset for Fine-grained Urban Semantic Understanding. FUSU features the most detailed land use classification system to date, with 17 classes and 30 billion pixels of annotations. It includes bi-temporal high-resolution satellite images with 0.2-0.5 m ground sample distance and monthly optical and radar satellite time series, covering 847 km^2 across five urban areas in the southern and northern of China with different geographical features. The fine-grained land use pixel-wise annotations and high spatial-temporal resolution data provide a robust foundation for developing proper deep learning models to provide contextual insights on human activities and urbanization. To fully leverage FUSU, we propose a unified time-series architecture for both change detection and segmentation. We benchmark FUSU on various methods for several tasks. Dataset and code are available at: https://github.com/yuanshuai0914/FUSU.

The dataset provides a basis for developing models that connect urban image changes with categories of human activity. Its contribution is both the annotated resource and an initial framework for evaluating methods that use its spatial and temporal information.
summary.tldr: FUSU combines detailed land use annotations with high-resolution and monthly satellite imagery to study urban land use changes.

title: FUSU: A Multi-temporal-source Land Use Change Segmentation Dataset for Fine-grained Urban Semantic Understanding

abstract: Despite the success of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) in aligning language models with human values, reward hacking, also termed reward overoptimization, remains a critical challenge. This issue primarily arises from reward misgeneralization, where reward models (RMs) compute reward using spurious features that are irrelevant to human preferences. In this work, we tackle this problem from an information-theoretic perspective and propose a framework for reward modeling, namely InfoRM, by introducing a variational information bottleneck objective to filter out irrelevant information.Notably, we further identify a correlation between overoptimization and outliers in the IB latent space of InfoRM, establishing it as a promising tool for detecting reward overoptimization.Inspired by this finding, we propose the Cluster Separation Index (CSI), which quantifies deviations in the IB latent space, as an indicator of reward overoptimization to facilitate the development of online mitigation strategies. Extensive experiments on a wide range of settings and RM scales (70M, 440M, 1.4B, and 7B) demonstrate the effectiveness of InfoRM. Further analyses reveal that InfoRM's overoptimization detection mechanism is not only effective but also robust across a broad range of datasets, signifying a notable advancement in the field of RLHF. The code will be released upon acceptance.

paragraphs: A language model trained against a learned reward can exploit signals that raise its score without matching human preferences. This paper focuses on reward misgeneralization, where the reward model depends on irrelevant features. InfoRM addresses that problem by changing reward-model training so that its internal representation filters out information unrelated to the preference task.

The method introduces a variational information bottleneck objective. The authors also identify a correlation between reward overoptimization and outliers in the bottleneck’s latent representation. Building on that observation, they define the Cluster Separation Index, which measures deviations in this space and serves as an indicator of overoptimization. Such an indicator could support mitigation during training.

Experiments across multiple settings and reward-model sizes of 70 million, 440 million, 1.4 billion, and 7 billion parameters support InfoRM’s effectiveness. Further analysis finds the detection mechanism effective across a broad range of datasets. The work combines a way to reduce reliance on spurious reward features with an empirical warning signal for overoptimization, while the observed correlation supplies the basis for that signal.
summary.tldr: InfoRM uses an information bottleneck to reduce reward hacking and latent-space deviations to flag reward overoptimization.

title: InfoRM: Mitigating Reward Hacking in RLHF via Information-Theoretic Reward Modeling

abstract: The advancement of diffusion models has enhanced the realism of AI-generated content but also raised concerns about misuse, necessitating robust copyright protection and tampering localization. Although recent methods have made progress toward unified solutions, their reliance on post hoc processing introduces considerable application inconvenience and compromises forensic reliability. We propose StableGuard, a novel framework that seamlessly integrates a binary watermark into the diffusion generation process, ensuring copyright protection and tampering localization in Latent Diffusion Models through an end-to-end design. We develop a Multiplexing Watermark VAE (MPW-VAE) by equipping a pretrained Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a lightweight latent residual-based adapter, enabling the generation of paired watermarked and watermark-free images. These pairs, fused via random masks, create a diverse dataset for training a tampering-agnostic forensic network. To further enhance forensic synergy, we introduce a Mixture-of-Experts Guided Forensic Network (MoE-GFN) that dynamically integrates holistic watermark patterns, local tampering traces, and frequency-domain cues for precise watermark verification and tampered region detection. The MPW-VAE and MoE-GFN are jointly optimized in a self-supervised, end-to-end manner, fostering a reciprocal training between watermark embedding and forensic accuracy. Extensive experiments demonstrate that StableGuard consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in image fidelity, watermark verification, and tampering localization.

It is optimized jointly with the watermarking component through self-supervised training, linking watermark embedding to forensic performance. Experiments report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods in image fidelity, watermark verification, and tamper localization. The contribution is an integrated generation-and-analysis system whose components are trained to support one another.
summary.tldr: StableGuard jointly trains watermark embedding and forensic analysis within latent diffusion generation, improving image fidelity, watermark verification, and tamper localization.

title: StableGuard: Towards Unified Copyright Protection and Tamper Localization in Latent Diffusion Models

abstract: Synthetic video generation is progressing very rapidly. The latest models can produce very realistic high-resolution videos that are virtually indistinguishable from real ones. Although several video forensic detectors have been recently proposed, they often exhibit poor generalization, which limits their applicability in a real-world scenario. Our key insight to overcome this issue is to guide the detector towards _seeing_ _what_ _really_ _matters_. In fact, a well-designed forensic classifier should focus on identifying intrinsic low-level artifacts introduced by a generative architecture rather than relying on high-level semantic flaws that characterize a specific model. In this work, first, we study different generative architectures, searching and identifying discriminative features that are unbiased, robust to impairments, and shared across models. Then, we introduce a novel forensic-oriented data augmentation strategy based on the wavelet decomposition and replace specific frequency-related bands to drive the model to exploit more relevant forensic cues. Our novel training paradigm improves the generalizability of AI-generated video detectors, without the need for complex algorithms and large datasets that include multiple synthetic generators. To evaluate our approach, we train the detector using data from a single generative model and test it against videos produced by a wide range of other models. Despite its simplicity, our method achieves a significant accuracy improvement over state-of-the-art detectors and obtains excellent results even on very recent generative models, such as NOVA and FLUX.

title: Seeing What Matters: Generalizable AI-generated Video Detection with Forensic-Oriented Augmentation

abstract: Multimodal recommendation aims to integrate collaborative signals with heterogeneous content such as visual and textual information, but remains challenged by modality-specific noise, semantic inconsistency, and unstable propagation over user–item graphs. These issues are often exacerbated by naive fusion or shallow modeling strategies, leading to degraded generalization and poor robustness. While recent work has explored the frequency domain as a lens to separate stable from noisy signals, most methods rely on static filtering or reweighting, lacking the ability to reason over spectral structure or adapt to modality-specific reliability. To address these challenges, we propose a Structured Spectral Reasoning (SSR) framework for frequency-aware multimodal recommendation. Our method follows a four-stage pipeline: (i) Decompose graph-based multimodal signals into spectral bands via graph-guided transformations to isolate semantic granularity; (ii) Modulate band-level reliability with spectral band masking, a training-time masking with prediction-consistency objective that suppresses brittle frequency components; (iii) Fuse complementary frequency cues using hyperspectral reasoning with low-rank cross-band interaction; and (iv) Align modality-specific spectral features via contrastive regularization to promote semantic and structural consistency. Experiments on three real-world benchmarks show consistent gains over strong baselines, particularly under sparse and cold-start settings. Additional analyses indicate that structured spectral modeling improves robustness and provides clearer diagnostics of how different bands contribute to performance.

paragraphs: Multimodal recommendation combines user-item interactions with content such as images and text. These signals can disagree, contain different kinds of noise, or propagate unstably through the interaction graph. Structured Spectral Reasoning addresses these problems by separating graph-based multimodal signals into frequency bands and modeling how those bands contribute to reliable recommendations.

The framework has four stages. Graph-guided transformations first separate signals into bands reflecting different semantic granularity. During training, spectral band masking and a prediction-consistency objective reduce reliance on brittle components. Low-rank interactions then combine complementary information across bands. Finally, contrastive regularization aligns modality-specific spectral features to encourage consistent meaning and structure across the different information sources.

Experiments on three real-world benchmarks show consistent gains over strong baselines, especially when interactions are sparse or recommendations involve cold-start settings. Additional analyses indicate improved robustness and clearer diagnostics of individual bands' contributions. The findings support reasoning over relationships among frequency components and their reliability, extending the use of frequency information beyond static filtering or fixed reweighting.
summary.tldr: Structured Spectral Reasoning improves multimodal recommendations by separating, assessing, combining, and aligning graph-frequency information.

title: Structured Spectral Reasoning for Frequency-Adaptive Multimodal Recommendation

abstract: With advancements in reasoning capabilities, Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly employed for automated judgment tasks. While LLMs-as-Judges offer promise in automating evaluations, current approaches often rely on simplistic aggregation methods (e.g., majority voting), which can fail even when individual agents provide correct answers. To address this, we propose a multi-agent debate judge framework where agents collaboratively reason and iteratively refine their responses. We formalize the debate process mathematically, analyzing agent interactions and proving that debate amplifies correctness compared to static ensembles. To enhance efficiency, we introduce a stability detection mechanism that models judge consensus dynamics via a time-varying Beta-Binomial mixture, with adaptive stopping based on distributional similarity (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test). This mechanism models the judges' collective correct rate dynamics using a time-varying mixture of Beta-Binomial distributions and employs an adaptive stopping criterion based on distributional similarity (Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic). Experiments across multiple benchmarks and models demonstrate that our framework improves judgment accuracy over majority voting while maintaining computational efficiency.

paragraphs: This paper studies language models used as judges for automated evaluation. Combining several judges through majority voting can still produce a wrong decision even when some agents answer correctly. The proposed framework instead allows agents to debate, exchange reasoning, and revise their responses over successive rounds.

The authors formalize interactions during debate and prove a correctness-amplification result relative to static ensembles within their mathematical treatment. They also address the cost of repeated discussion. A time-varying mixture of Beta-Binomial distributions models the dynamics of the judges' collective correct rate, providing a statistical description of how the group's judgments evolve.

An adaptive stopping rule uses Kolmogorov-Smirnov distributional similarity to detect stability and determine when to end the debate. This makes the amount of discussion responsive to the observed dynamics. Across multiple benchmarks and models, experiments report higher judgment accuracy than majority voting while maintaining computational efficiency. The combined contribution is a collaborative evaluation procedure and a mechanism for limiting further rounds once the modeled process stabilizes.
summary.tldr: A debate framework improves reported LLM judgment accuracy over majority voting and uses statistical stability detection to stop discussion adaptively.

title: Multi-Agent Debate for LLM Judges with Adaptive Stability Detection

abstract: Variational quantum Eigensolver (VQE) is a leading candidate for harnessing quantum computers to advance quantum chemistry and materials simulations, yet its training efficiency deteriorates rapidly for large Hamiltonians. Two issues underlie this bottleneck: (i) the no-cloning theorem imposes a linear growth in circuit evaluations with the number of parameters per gradient step; and (ii) deeper circuits encounter barren plateaus (BPs), leading to exponentially increasing measurement overheads. To address these challenges, here we propose a deep learning framework, dubbed Titan, which identifies and freezes inactive parameters of a given ansätze at initialization for a specific class of Hamiltonians, reducing the optimization overhead without sacrificing accuracy. The motivation of Titan starts with our empirical findings that a subset of parameters consistently has negligible influence on training dynamics. Its design combines a theoretically grounded data construction strategy, ensuring each training example is informative and BP-resilient, with an adaptive neural architecture that generalizes across ansätze of varying sizes. Across benchmark transverse-field Ising models, Heisenberg models, and multiple molecule systems up to $30$ qubits, Titan achieves up to $3\times$ faster convergence and $40$–$60\%$ fewer circuit evaluations than state-of-the-art baselines, while matching or surpassing their estimation accuracy. By proactively trimming parameter space, Titan lowers hardware demands and offers a scalable path toward utilizing VQE to advance practical quantum chemistry and materials science.

paragraphs: Variational quantum eigensolvers face growing training costs as problems and circuits become larger. More parameters require more circuit evaluations per gradient step, while barren plateaus can greatly increase measurement overhead. TITAN addresses these costs by identifying parameters that can remain fixed during optimization.

The method starts from an empirical observation that some parameters consistently have negligible influence on training dynamics. A deep learning framework predicts and freezes inactive parameters at initialization for a specified class of Hamiltonians. Its training-data construction is theoretically grounded and designed to provide informative examples resilient to barren plateaus. Estimation accuracy matches or exceeds those comparisons. The findings support reducing optimization overhead by learning which parameters have little influence, with the demonstrated gains tied to the evaluated problem classes and circuit settings.
summary.tldr: TITAN predicts which quantum-circuit parameters can be frozen, reducing evaluated VQE training costs while maintaining or improving estimation accuracy.

title: TITAN: A Trajectory-Informed Technique for Adaptive Parameter Freezing in Large-Scale VQE

abstract: Maintaining robust 3D perception under dynamic and unpredictable test-time conditions remains a critical challenge for autonomous driving systems. Existing test-time adaptation (TTA) methods often fail in high-variance tasks like 3D object detection due to unstable optimization and sharp minima. While recent model merging strategies based on linear mode connectivity (LMC) offer improved stability by interpolating between fine-tuned checkpoints, they are computationally expensive, requiring repeated checkpoint access and multiple forward passes. In this paper, we introduce CodeMerge, a lightweight and scalable model merging framework that bypasses these limitations by operating in a compact latent space. Instead of loading full models, CodeMerge represents each checkpoint with a low-dimensional fingerprint derived from the source model’s penultimate features and constructs a key-value codebook. We compute merging coefficients using ridge leverage scores on these fingerprints, enabling efficient model composition without compromising adaptation quality. Our method achieves strong performance across challenging benchmarks, improving end-to-end 3D detection 14.9\% NDS on nuScenes-C and LiDAR-based detection by over 7.6\% mAP on nuScenes-to-KITTI, while benefiting downstream tasks such as online mapping, motion prediction and planning even without training. The code is released at \url{https://github.com/UQHTy/CodeMerge}.

They also report benefits for online mapping, motion prediction, and planning without training those downstream tasks. The findings support compact checkpoint representations as a practical basis for model composition that preserves adaptation quality while reducing computational demands.
summary.tldr: CodeMerge uses compact checkpoint fingerprints to guide efficient model merging for more robust 3D perception under changing deployment conditions.

title: CodeMerge: Codebook-Guided Model Merging for Robust Test-Time Adaptation in Autonomous Driving

abstract: Diffusion models show promise for dynamic scene deblurring; however, existing studies often fail to leverage the intrinsic nature of the blurring process within diffusion models, limiting their full potential. To address it, we present a Blur Diffusion Model (BlurDM), which seamlessly integrates the blur formation process into diffusion for image deblurring. Observing that motion blur stems from continuous exposure, BlurDM implicitly models the blur formation process through a dual-diffusion forward scheme, diffusing both noise and blur onto a sharp image. During the reverse generation process, we derive a dual denoising and deblurring formulation, enabling BlurDM to recover the sharp image by simultaneously denoising and deblurring, given pure Gaussian noise conditioned on the blurred image as input. Additionally, to efficiently integrate BlurDM into deblurring networks, we perform BlurDM in the latent space, forming a flexible prior generation network for deblurring. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BlurDM significantly and consistently enhances existing deblurring methods on four benchmark datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/Jin-Ting-He/BlurDM.

The paper starts from the observation that motion blur results from continuous exposure. It argues that existing diffusion approaches do not fully use this structure, leaving useful information about the degradation process underexploited.

The proposed forward process introduces both noise and blur into a sharp image. The authors then derive a reverse process that removes both together. Generation begins from Gaussian noise, with the observed blurred image supplying conditioning information. This connects the model’s restoration procedure to the paired degradations introduced during its forward process.

For efficient integration with deblurring networks, BlurDM operates in latent space and serves as a flexible prior generation network. Experiments on four benchmark datasets show significant, consistent improvements when it is incorporated into existing deblurring methods. The stated contribution is therefore both a formulation that explicitly incorporates blur formation and a practical component for strengthening restoration networks, with benefits demonstrated across the evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: BlurDM incorporates blur formation into diffusion and jointly removes blur and noise, improving existing deblurring methods on four benchmark datasets.

title: BlurDM: A Blur Diffusion Model for Image Deblurring

abstract: We introduce BayeSQP, a novel algorithm for general black-box optimization that merges the structure of sequential quadratic programming with concepts from Bayesian optimization. BayeSQP employs second-order Gaussian process surrogates for both the objective and constraints to jointly model the function values, gradients, and Hessian from only zero-order information. At each iteration, a local subproblem is constructed using the GP posterior estimates and solved to obtain a search direction. Crucially, the formulation of the subproblem explicitly incorporates uncertainty in both the function and derivative estimates, resulting in a tractable second-order cone program for high probability improvements under model uncertainty. A subsequent one-dimensional line search via constrained Thompson sampling selects the next evaluation point. Empirical results show that BayeSQP outperforms state-of-the-art methods in specific high-dimensional settings. Our algorithm offers a principled and flexible framework that bridges classical optimization techniques with modern approaches to black-box optimization.

paragraphs: BayeSQP tackles black-box optimization, where an algorithm can evaluate an objective and constraints without directly receiving their derivatives. It combines the local search structure of sequential quadratic programming with Bayesian models of uncertainty. The aim is to use estimated slopes and curvature to guide search even when only function evaluations are available.

The algorithm builds Gaussian process surrogates that jointly estimate function values, gradients, and Hessians for the objective and constraints. At each iteration, these estimates define a local optimization problem that produces a search direction. Crucially, that problem includes uncertainty in both values and derivatives. Experiments show advantages over state-of-the-art methods in specific high-dimensional settings. The contribution is a way to connect derivative-based optimization structure with uncertainty-aware search; the reported advantage is tied to those tested settings.
summary.tldr: BayeSQP estimates derivatives and their uncertainty from function evaluations to guide black-box optimization, with gains in specific high-dimensional settings.

title: BayeSQP: Bayesian Optimization through Sequential Quadratic Programming

abstract: Modern language models (LMs) exhibit strong deductive reasoning capabilities, yet standard evaluations emphasize correctness while overlooking a key aspect of human-like reasoning: *efficiency*. In real-world reasoning scenarios, much of the available information is irrelevant, and effective deductive inference requires identifying and ignoring such distractions. We propose a framework for assessing LM reasoning efficiency through the lens of logic programming, introducing a simple method to align proofs written in natural language---as generated by an LM---with shortest proofs found by executing the logic program. Efficiency is quantified by measuring how well a model avoids unnecessary inference. Empirically, we construct a dataset of math word problems injected with various number of irrelevant axioms that vary in semantic overlap with the goal theorem. We find that current LMs show marked accuracy declines under such conditions---even with minimal, domain-consistent distractions---and the proofs they generate frequently exhibit detours through irrelevant inferences.

paragraphs: A correct answer does not reveal whether a language model reached it efficiently. Reasoning can include unnecessary deductions, especially when the input contains plausible but irrelevant information. This paper develops an evaluation framework that measures a model's ability to avoid such detours, treating the selection of relevant information as part of reasoning quality.

The framework uses logic programming to obtain shortest proofs and aligns them with the natural-language proofs produced by a model. That comparison provides a reference for identifying unnecessary inference. The authors also construct math word problems with added irrelevant axioms, varying both the amount of distracting information and its semantic overlap with the goal.

The tested models lose substantial accuracy under these distractions, including cases with only a small amount of irrelevant information from the same domain. Their explanations also frequently pursue deductions that do not help establish the answer. These findings show why correctness alone can conceal weaknesses: the framework exposes both failed conclusions and inefficient paths through otherwise relevant-looking material.
summary.tldr: A logic-based evaluation finds that language models often follow irrelevant deductions and lose accuracy when reasoning problems contain distractions.

title: Are Language Models Efficient Reasoners? A Perspective from Logic Programming

abstract: We study strategic behavior of project proposers in the context of approval-based participatory budgeting (PB). In our model we assume that the votes are fixed and known and the proposers want to set as high project prices as possible, provided that their projects get selected and the prices are not below the minimum costs of their delivery. We study the existence of pure Nash equilibria (NE) in such games, focusing on the AV/Cost, Phragmen, and Method of Equal Shares rules. We also provide an experimental study of cost selection on real-life PB election data.

We study the existence of pure Nash equilibria (NE) in such games, focusing on the AV/Cost, Phragmen, and Method of Equal Shares rules. paragraphs: Participatory budgeting selects projects using public preferences and a limited budget. This paper studies the incentives of project proposers when they can choose the prices of their proposals. It assumes approval votes are already fixed and known, so the strategic decision concerns project pricing while voter preferences remain unchanged.

Each proposer wants the highest possible price that still allows their project to be selected. Prices must also cover a minimum delivery cost. These requirements create a tradeoff: raising a price is desirable for the proposer, but selection depends on the budgeting rule and the competing proposals. The analysis considers AV/Cost, Phragmen, and the Method of Equal Shares.

The theoretical question is whether these pricing games admit pure Nash equilibria: stable price choices where no proposer can improve their outcome through an individual change. The paper also studies cost selection experimentally using real participatory-budgeting election data. Its contribution examines project costs as strategic choices, making the funding rule's interaction with proposer incentives an explicit subject of analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper studies stable strategic project pricing under three participatory-budgeting rules when approval votes are fixed and known.

title: Strategic Cost Selection in Participatory Budgeting

abstract: Given a single in-the-wild human photo, it remains a challenging task to reconstruct a high-fidelity 3D human model. Existing methods face difficulties including a) the varying body proportions captured by in-the-wild human images; b) diverse personal belongings within the shot; and c) ambiguities in human postures and inconsistency in human textures. In addition, the scarcity of high-quality human data intensifies the challenge. To address these problems, we propose a Generalizable image-to-3D huMAN reconstruction framework, dubbed GeneMAN, building upon a comprehensive multi-source collection of high-quality human data, including 3D scans, multi-view videos, single photos, and our generated synthetic human data. GeneMAN encompasses three key modules. 1) Without relying on parametric human models (e.g., SMPL), GeneMAN first trains a human-specific text-to-image diffusion model and a view-conditioned diffusion model, serving as GeneMAN 2D human prior and 3D human prior for reconstruction, respectively. 2) With the help of the pretrained human prior models, the Geometry Initialization-&-Sculpting pipeline is leveraged to recover high-quality 3D human geometry given a single image. 3) To achieve high-fidelity 3D human textures, GeneMAN employs the Multi-Space Texture Refinement pipeline, consecutively refining textures in the latent and the pixel spaces. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that GeneMAN could generate high-quality 3D human models from a single image input, outperforming prior state-of-the-art methods. Notably, GeneMAN could reveal much better generalizability in dealing with in-the-wild images, often yielding high-quality 3D human models in natural poses with common items, regardless of the body proportions in the input images.

paragraphs: Recovering a detailed 3D person from one ordinary photograph is difficult because body proportions, poses, belongings, and surface appearance vary widely. GeneMAN addresses these challenges using human data from several sources: 3D scans, videos with multiple views, individual photographs, and generated synthetic examples. This collection supports specialized models for human reconstruction.

The framework first trains a human-focused text-to-image diffusion model and a view-conditioned diffusion model. These provide learned guidance about human appearance and 3D structure without relying on a parametric body model such as SMPL. A geometry initialization and sculpting pipeline then uses these priors to recover the person's shape from the input image.

A separate texture pipeline refines appearance successively in latent space and pixel space. Experiments report higher-quality reconstructions than prior leading methods and improved generalization to ordinary photographs. In particular, the system often produces detailed models of people in natural poses with common items across varying body proportions. The approach combines broad human-data coverage with distinct stages for geometric structure and surface detail.
summary.tldr: GeneMAN combines human-specific diffusion priors and staged refinement to reconstruct detailed 3D people from single photographs.

title: GeneMAN: Generalizable Single-Image 3D Human Reconstruction from Multi-Source Human Data

abstract: We introduce active generation of Pareto sets (A-GPS), a new framework for online discrete black-box multi-objective optimization (MOO). A-GPS learns a generative model of the Pareto set that supports a-posteriori conditioning on user preferences. The method employs a class probability estimator (CPE) to predict non-dominance relations and to condition the generative model toward high-performing regions of the search space. We also show that this non-dominance CPE implicitly estimates the probability of hypervolume improvement (PHVI). To incorporate subjective trade-offs, A-GPS introduces _preference direction vectors_ that encode user-specified preferences in objective space. At each iteration, the model is updated using both Pareto membership and alignment with these preference directions, producing an amortized generative model capable of sampling across the Pareto front without retraining. The result is a simple yet powerful approach that achieves high-quality Pareto set approximations, avoids explicit hypervolume computation, and flexibly captures user preferences. Empirical results on synthetic benchmarks and protein design tasks demonstrate strong sample efficiency and effective preference incorporation.

paragraphs: When several objectives compete, optimization often needs to produce a collection of useful compromises. A Pareto set contains candidates for which improving one objective requires sacrificing another. A-GPS learns to generate such candidates in discrete search spaces where objective values must be obtained through black-box evaluations. It also lets users express preferences after training, making the learned collection useful for different trade-offs.

The method uses a class probability estimator to predict non-dominance relations between candidates. Those predictions guide generation toward promising regions. The authors show that this estimator also implicitly estimates the probability of hypervolume improvement, allowing the approach to avoid explicitly computing hypervolume. Preference direction vectors describe which combinations of objectives a user favors.

During optimization, the model is updated using both Pareto membership and alignment with these directions. The resulting generator can sample different parts of the Pareto front without retraining for each preference. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and protein design tasks report strong sample efficiency and effective preference incorporation, supporting the value of sharing one learned generator across multiple desired compromises.
summary.tldr: A-GPS learns a reusable generator of promising objective trade-offs that can accommodate different user preferences without retraining.

title: Amortized Active Generation of Pareto Sets

abstract: Multi-Task Learning (MTL) in Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) is a promising approach for training a unified model capable of solving multiple Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) variants. However, existing Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based multi-task methods can only train light decoder models on small-scale problems, exhibiting limited generalization ability when solving large-scale problems. To overcome this limitation, this work introduces a novel multi-task learning method driven by knowledge distillation (MTL-KD), which enables efficient training of heavy decoder models with strong generalization ability. The proposed MTL-KD method transfers policy knowledge from multiple distinct RL-based single-task models to a single heavy decoder model, facilitating label-free training and effectively improving the model's generalization ability across diverse tasks. In addition, we introduce a flexible inference strategy termed Random Reordering Re-Construction (R3C), which is specifically adapted for diverse VRP tasks and further boosts the performance of the multi-task model. Experimental results on 6 seen and 10 unseen VRP variants with up to 1,000 nodes indicate that our proposed method consistently achieves superior performance on both uniform and real-world benchmarks, demonstrating robust generalization abilities. The code is available at [https://github.com/CIAM-Group/MTLKD](https://github.com/CIAM-Group/MTLKD).

paragraphs: Vehicle routing has multiple task variants, making a single solver that generalizes across them appealing. The paper identifies a training obstacle: existing reinforcement-learning approaches to multi-task routing are limited to lightweight decoders and small problems, with weaker generalization to larger instances. MTL-KD aims to train a more capable shared decoder efficiently.

The method transfers policy knowledge from several reinforcement-learning models, each trained for one task, into a single heavier decoder. This knowledge-distillation setup enables label-free training while combining expertise across routing tasks. The authors also introduce Random Reordering Re-Construction, an inference strategy designed to work flexibly across different vehicle-routing variants and improve the shared model's solutions.

Evaluation covers six seen and ten unseen variants, with problems containing up to 1,000 nodes. The method consistently achieves superior performance in the reported uniform and real-world benchmark comparisons. These results support the use of specialist policies as training guidance for a general solver, with evidence of transfer both to unfamiliar task variants and to larger routing problems.
summary.tldr: MTL-KD distills specialist routing policies into a larger shared decoder that generalizes across seen and unseen vehicle-routing variants.

title: MTL-KD: Multi-Task Learning Via Knowledge Distillation for Generalizable Neural Vehicle Routing Solver

abstract: We say that a classifier is $\text{\emph{adversarially robust}}$ to perturbations of norm $r$ if, with high probability over a point $x$ drawn from the input distribution, there is no point within distance $\le r$ from $x$ that is classified differently. The $\text{\emph{boundary volume}}$ is the probability that a point falls within distance $r$ of a point with a different label. This work studies the task of learning a hypothesis with small boundary volume, where the input is distributed as a subgaussian isotropic log-concave distribution over $\mathbb{R}^d$. Linear threshold functions are adversarially robust; they have boundary volume proportional to $r$. Such concept classes are efficiently learnable by polynomial regression, which produces a polynomial threshold function (PTF), but PTFs in general may have boundary volume $\Omega(1)$, even for $r \ll 1$. We give an algorithm that agnostically learns linear threshold functions and returns a classfier with boundary volume $O(r+\varepsilon)$ at radius of perturbation $r$. The time and sample complexity of $d^{\tilde{O}(1/\varepsilon^2)}$ matches the complexity of polynomial regression. Our algorithm augments the classic approach of polynomial regression with three additional steps:\ $\quad$ a) performing the $\ell_1$-error regression under $\ell_1$ noise sensitivity constraints,\ $\quad$ b) a structured partitioning and rounding step that returns a Boolean classifier with error $\mathrm{opt} + O(\varepsilon)$ and noise sensitivity $O(r+\varepsilon)$ simultaneously, and \ $\quad c)$ a local corrector that ``smooths'' a function with low noise sensitivity into a function that is adversarially robust.

paragraphs: A classifier can predict accurately yet change its answer under a very small input perturbation. This paper measures that vulnerability through boundary volume: the probability that an input lies within distance r of a point receiving a different label. It studies learning linear threshold functions when inputs follow a subgaussian, isotropic, log-concave distribution.

Linear threshold functions have boundary volume proportional to r under the stated setting. Standard polynomial regression can learn them efficiently, but its resulting polynomial threshold classifier may have substantial boundary volume even for tiny perturbations. The authors modify regression with noise-sensitivity constraints, then apply structured partitioning and rounding, followed by a local correction procedure that smooths the resulting classifier.

The algorithm agnostically learns with error within O(epsilon) of the best linear threshold function and returns a classifier with boundary volume O(r + epsilon). Its time and sample complexity match the stated polynomial-regression complexity. The result shows that, under the specified distribution assumptions, the learning procedure can preserve a meaningful robustness guarantee while retaining comparable computational requirements.
summary.tldr: Under specified log-concave input assumptions, a modified regression algorithm learns accurate classifiers with provably small adversarial boundary volume.

title: Robust learning of halfspaces under log-concave marginals

abstract: In semi-supervised segmentation, capturing meaningful semantic structures from unlabeled data is essential. This is particularly challenging in histopathology image analysis, where objects are densely distributed. To address this issue, we propose a semi-supervised segmentation framework designed to robustly identify and preserve relevant topological features. Our method leverages multiple perturbed predictions obtained through stochastic dropouts and temporal training snapshots, enforcing topological consistency across these varied outputs. This consistency mechanism helps distinguish biologically meaningful structures from transient and noisy artifacts. A key challenge in this process is to accurately match the corresponding topological features across the predictions in the absence of ground truth. To overcome this, we introduce a novel matching strategy that integrates spatial overlap with global structural alignment, minimizing discrepancies among predictions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach effectively reduces topological errors, resulting in more robust and accurate segmentations essential for reliable downstream analysis. Code is available at https://github.com/Melon-Xu/MATCH.

paragraphs: MATCH tackles semi-supervised segmentation of histopathology images, where densely packed objects make structural interpretation difficult. Unlabeled images can provide useful training information, but predictions may contain both meaningful structures and temporary artifacts. The framework focuses on preserving topological features that remain consistent across different predictions of the same data.

It produces varied predictions using stochastic dropout and model snapshots from different training times. Training then encourages agreement in their topological structure. A central difficulty is deciding which feature in one prediction corresponds to a feature in another when no ground-truth segmentation is available. MATCH addresses this with a matching strategy that combines spatial overlap and global structural alignment.

By establishing those correspondences, the method can reduce discrepancies across predictions and help separate persistent biological structure from noisy output. The authors report fewer topological errors and more accurate, robust segmentations in extensive experiments. The contribution makes structural consistency a source of supervision for unlabeled images, supporting the reliability of segmentations used in downstream histopathology analysis.
summary.tldr: MATCH learns from unlabeled histopathology images by matching and preserving consistent topological features across varied predictions.

title: MATCH: Multi-faceted Adaptive Topo-Consistency for Semi-Supervised Histopathology Segmentation

abstract: Training Transformer models on long sequences in a distributed setting poses significant challenges in terms of efficiency and scalability. Current methods are either constrained by the number of attention heads or excessive communication overheads. To address this problem, we propose StarTrail, a multi-dimensional concentric distributed training system for long sequences, fostering an efficient communication paradigm and providing additional tuning flexibility for communication arrangements. Specifically, StarTrail introduces an extra parallel dimension and divides the peer-to-peer communication into sub-rings to substantially reduce communication volume and avoid bandwidth bottlenecks. Through comprehensive experiments across diverse hardware environments and on both Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Computer Vision (CV) tasks, we demonstrate that our approach significantly surpasses state-of-the-art methods that support Long sequence lengths, achieving performance improvements of up to 77.12% on GPT-style models and up to 114.33% on DiT (Diffusion Transformer) models without affecting the computations results.

paragraphs: Distributing long-sequence Transformer training across hardware creates a communication problem as well as a computation problem. Existing approaches can be limited by the number of attention heads or by excessive data exchange. StarTrail changes how distributed workers communicate to improve efficiency and scalability for long inputs.

The system introduces an additional parallel dimension and organizes peer-to-peer exchanges into smaller sub-rings. This concentric arrangement reduces communication volume and helps avoid bandwidth bottlenecks. It also gives more flexibility in tuning communication arrangements, so the distributed organization can be adjusted across hardware environments.

Experiments span natural language processing and computer vision tasks on diverse hardware. The authors report performance improvements of up to 77.12% for GPT-style models and 114.33% for Diffusion Transformer models over state-of-the-art methods supporting long sequences, without changing computation results. These are gains in distributed training performance: the contribution is a more efficient way to execute the model's computations, making communication organization central to scaling long-sequence training.
summary.tldr: StarTrail reorganizes distributed communication into concentric sub-rings to accelerate long-sequence Transformer training without changing computation results.

title: StarTrail: Concentric Ring Sequence Parallelism for Efficient Near-Infinite-Context Transformer Model Training

abstract: Egocentric video-language pretraining has significantly advanced video representation learning. Humans perceive and interact with a fully 3D world, developing spatial awareness that extends beyond text-based understanding. However, most previous works learn from 1D text or 2D visual cues, such as bounding boxes, which inherently lack 3D understanding. To bridge this gap, we introduce EgoDTM, an Egocentric Depth- and Text-aware \textbf{M}odel, jointly trained through large-scale 3D-aware video pretraining and video-text contrastive learning. EgoDTM incorporates a lightweight 3D-aware decoder to efficiently learn 3D-awareness from pseudo depth maps generated by depth estimation models. To further facilitate 3D-aware video pretraining, we enrich the original brief captions with hand-object visual cues by organically combining several foundation models. Extensive experiments demonstrate EgoDTM's superior performance across diverse downstream tasks, highlighting its superior 3D-aware visual understanding. Code: \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EgoDTM}.

To bridge this gap, we introduce EgoDTM, an Egocentric Depth- and Text-aware \textbf{M}odel, jointly trained through large-scale 3D-aware video pretraining and video-text contrastive learning. paragraphs: First-person video captures interactions in a three-dimensional world, but video-language pretraining often relies on text and two-dimensional visual cues. Those signals provide descriptions and image locations without directly supplying depth. EgoDTM adds explicit depth-oriented supervision to help a video model learn spatial information alongside the correspondence between videos and language.

The authors also combine foundation models to enrich short captions with visual information about hands and objects.

Together, the depth maps and expanded captions provide complementary supervision for understanding interactions from the wearer's viewpoint. Experiments report superior performance across diverse downstream tasks, which the authors interpret as evidence of stronger 3D-aware visual understanding. title: EgoDTM: Towards 3D-Aware Egocentric Video-Language Pretraining

abstract: We study the adversarial Stochastic Shortest Path (SSP) problem with sparse costs under full-information feedback. In the known transition setting, existing bounds based on Online Mirror Descent (OMD) with negative-entropy regularization scale with $\sqrt{\log S A}$, where $SA$ is the size of the state-action space. While we show that this is optimal in the worst-case, this bound fails to capture the benefits of sparsity when only a small number $M \ll SA$ of state-action pairs incur cost. In fact, we also show that the negative-entropy is inherently non-adaptive to sparsity: it provably incurs regret scaling with $\sqrt{\log S}$ on sparse problems. Instead, we propose a novel family of $\ell_r$-norm regularizers ($r \in (1,2)$) that adapts to the sparsity and achieves regret scaling with $\sqrt{\log M}$ instead of $\sqrt{\log SA}$. We show this is optimal via a matching lower bound, highlighting that $M$ captures the effective dimension of the problem instead of $SA$. Finally, in the unknown transition setting the benefits of sparsity are limited: we prove that even on sparse problems, the minimax regret for any learner scales polynomially with $SA$.

paragraphs: This paper studies stochastic shortest-path learning with adversarial costs and full-information feedback. Its focus is sparsity: only M state-action pairs incur costs, even though the full space contains SA pairs. The question is whether learning guarantees can reflect the smaller number of costly pairs instead of the size of the entire problem.

When transition dynamics are known, standard online mirror descent with negative-entropy regularization has a square-root logarithmic dependence on SA. The authors show that this dependence is worst-case optimal, but that negative entropy cannot adapt adequately to sparse costs. They introduce a family of l_r-norm regularizers, with r between one and two, that replaces this dependence with the square root of log M.

A matching lower bound establishes optimality of the sparsity dependence. The distinction between known and unknown transitions is essential: when transitions must also be learned, the authors prove that minimax regret still depends polynomially on SA, even with sparse costs. Sparsity therefore reduces the effective dimension in the known-transition setting, with substantially more limited benefits in the unknown-transition setting.
summary.tldr: New regularizers exploit sparse costs optimally when transitions are known, while unknown transitions retain substantial state-action dependence.

title: Stochastic Shortest Path with Sparse Adversarial Costs

abstract: Language bias in Visual Question Answering (VQA) arises when models exploit spurious statistical correlations between question templates and answers, particularly in out-of-distribution scenarios, thereby neglecting essential visual cues and compromising genuine multimodal reasoning. Despite numerous efforts to enhance the robustness of VQA models, a principled understanding of how such bias originates and influences model behavior remains underdeveloped. In this paper, we address this gap through a comprehensive empirical and theoretical analysis, revealing that modality-specific gradient imbalances, which originate from the inherent heterogeneity of multimodal data, lead to skewed feature fusion and biased classifier weights. To alleviate these issues, we propose a novel Multi-Margin Collaborative Debiasing (MMCD) framework that adaptively integrates frequency-, confidence-, and difficulty-aware angular margins with a dynamic difficulty-aware contrastive learning mechanism, to dynamically reshape decision boundaries. Extensive experiments across multiple challenging VQA benchmarks confirm the consistent superiority of our proposed MMCD over state-of-the-art baselines in combating language bias.

paragraphs: A visual question-answering model can learn to guess from question wording instead of inspecting the image. Correlations between question templates and answers make this shortcut tempting, especially damaging performance when evaluation data differ from training data. This paper investigates how the imbalance develops and proposes a method to reduce it.

The authors’ empirical and theoretical analysis links language bias to unequal gradients across modalities. Differences inherent in multimodal data produce this imbalance, which then distorts feature fusion and classifier weights. Their Multi-Margin Collaborative Debiasing framework responds with adaptive angular margins that account for answer frequency, confidence, and difficulty.

The framework also uses contrastive learning whose behavior changes with difficulty, working alongside the margins to reshape decision boundaries. This connects the proposed explanation of bias with interventions in both representation learning and classification. Across multiple challenging VQA benchmarks, the authors report consistently better resistance to language bias than leading comparison methods. The contribution combines an account of the training dynamics behind the shortcut with a coordinated method for addressing it.
summary.tldr: MMCD addresses language shortcuts in visual question answering through adaptive classification margins and difficulty-aware contrastive learning.

title: Language‑Bias‑Resilient Visual Question Answering via Adaptive Multi‑Margin Collaborative Debiasing

abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have advanced robotic control by enabling end-to-end decision-making directly from multimodal inputs. However, their tightly coupled architectures expose novel security vulnerabilities. Unlike traditional adversarial perturbations, backdoor attacks represent a stealthier, persistent, and practically significant threat—particularly under the emerging Training-as-a-Service paradigm—but remain largely unexplored in the context of VLA models. To address this gap, we propose **BadVLA**, a backdoor attack method based on Objective-Decoupled Optimization, which for the first time exposes the backdoor vulnerabilities of VLA models. Specifically, it consists of a two-stage process: (1) explicit feature-space separation to isolate trigger representations from benign inputs, and (2) conditional control deviations that activate only in the presence of the trigger, while preserving clean-task performance. Empirical results on multiple VLA benchmarks demonstrate that BadVLA consistently achieves near-100\% attack success rates with minimal impact on clean task accuracy. Further analyses confirm its robustness against common input perturbations, task transfers, and model fine-tuning, underscoring critical security vulnerabilities in current VLA deployments. Our work offers the first systematic investigation of backdoor vulnerabilities in VLA models, highlighting an urgent need for secure and trustworthy embodied model design practices.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action models connect visual and language inputs directly to robotic decisions. BadVLA investigates whether these models can contain a persistent backdoor: a behavior that remains hidden during ordinary tasks but changes control when a particular trigger appears. The paper identifies this as a concern for systems whose training may be provided as a service.

Its approach separates the attack into two objectives. First, it makes trigger-related representations distinct from representations of benign inputs. Second, it introduces control deviations conditioned on that trigger while retaining performance on clean tasks. Separating these objectives is central to making the unwanted behavior selective and difficult to notice through ordinary task accuracy alone.

Across multiple VLA benchmarks, the authors report attack success rates close to 100% with little effect on clean-task accuracy. Further evaluations find that the attack withstands common input perturbations, task transfers, and model fine-tuning. These findings expose a security weakness in the evaluated models: strong ordinary performance can coexist with persistent, trigger-dependent failures in robotic control.
summary.tldr: BadVLA demonstrates persistent, trigger-dependent control failures in vision-language-action models while largely preserving ordinary task performance.

title: BadVLA: Towards Backdoor Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models via Objective-Decoupled Optimization

abstract: LLM-as-Benchmark-Generator methods have been widely studied as a supplement to human annotators for scalable evaluation, while the potential biases within this paradigm remain underexplored. In this work, we systematically define and validate the phenomenon of inflated performance in models evaluated on their self-generated benchmarks, referred to as self-bias, and attribute it to sub-biases arising from question domain, language style, and wrong labels. On this basis, we propose Silencer, a general framework that leverages the heterogeneity between multiple generators at both the sample and benchmark levels to neutralize bias and generate high-quality, self-bias-silenced benchmark. Experimental results across various settings demonstrate that Silencer can suppress self-bias to near zero, significantly improve evaluation effectiveness of the generated benchmark (with an average improvement from 0.655 to 0.833 in Pearson correlation with high-quality human-annotated benchmark), while also exhibiting strong generalizability.
