paragraphs: Language models can generate evaluation benchmarks at scale, supplementing human annotation. However, a model may appear unusually strong on a benchmark it created itself. This paper defines and validates that phenomenon as self-bias, then examines how question domains, language style, and incorrect labels contribute to inflated performance.

The proposed Silencer framework uses differences among multiple benchmark generators to counteract these biases. It operates at both the individual-sample level and the full-benchmark level. The central idea is that heterogeneity between generators can be used to neutralize preferences or errors associated with a single generator.

Across the evaluated settings, Silencer reduces self-bias to nearly zero and improves agreement with high-quality human-annotated benchmarks. The reported average Pearson correlation increases from 0.655 to 0.833, indicating that the generated evaluations track the human-annotated reference more closely. The authors also report strong generalizability. Together, these findings support combining diverse generators as a way to make automated benchmark construction more effective.
summary.tldr: Silencer combines heterogeneous benchmark generators to reduce self-bias and improve agreement with human-annotated evaluations.

title: Silencer: From Discovery to Mitigation of Self-Bias in LLM-as-Benchmark-Generator

abstract: Natural disasters cause devastating damage to communities and infrastructure every year. Effective disaster response is hampered by the difficulty of accessing affected areas during and after events. Remote sensing has allowed us to monitor natural disasters in a remote way. More recently there have been advances in computer vision and deep learning that help automate satellite imagery analysis, However, they remain limited by their narrow focus on specific disaster types, reliance on manual expert interpretation, and lack of datasets with sufficient temporal granularity or natural language annotations for tracking disaster progression. We present MONITRS, a novel multimodal dataset of $\sim$10,000 FEMA disaster events with temporal satellite imagery with natural language annotations from news articles, accompanied by geotagged locations, and question-answer pairs. We demonstrate that fine-tuning existing MLLMs on our dataset yields significant performance improvements for disaster monitoring tasks, establishing a new benchmark for machine learning-assisted disaster response systems.

paragraphs: Disaster monitoring is difficult when affected areas cannot be reached during or after an event. Satellite imagery helps observe those areas remotely, but automated analysis has often focused on particular disaster types or relied on expert interpretation. The paper also identifies a shortage of datasets combining sufficiently detailed time coverage with language descriptions of disaster progression.

MONITRS brings these forms of evidence together for approximately 10,000 FEMA disaster events. It combines satellite imagery over time with natural-language annotations drawn from news articles, geotagged locations, and question-answer pairs. This structure gives models visual observations alongside textual context and explicit questions, supporting the study of disaster monitoring as a multimodal task.

The authors fine-tune existing multimodal language models on the dataset and report significant improvements on disaster monitoring tasks. The contribution is both a training resource and a benchmark for evaluating machine-learning-assisted disaster response systems. Its combination of temporal observations and language directly addresses the dataset gaps motivating the work.
summary.tldr: MONITRS pairs satellite imagery over time with language and location data for about 10,000 disasters, improving evaluated monitoring models.

title: MONITRS: Multimodal Observations of Natural Incidents Through Remote Sensing

abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables large language models to perform few-shot learning by conditioning on labeled examples in the prompt. Despite its flexibility, ICL suffers from instability -- especially as prompt length increases with more demonstrations. To address this, we treat ICL as a source of weak supervision and propose a parameter-efficient method that disentangles demonstration-induced latent shifts from those of the query. An ICL-based teacher generates pseudo-labels on unlabeled queries, while a student predicts them using only the query input, updating a lightweight adapter. This captures demonstration effects in a compact, reusable form, enabling efficient inference while remaining composable with new demonstrations. Although trained on noisy teacher outputs, the student often outperforms its teacher through pseudo-label correction and coverage expansion, consistent with the weak-to-strong generalization effect. Empirically, our method improves generalization, stability, and efficiency across both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks, surpassing standard ICL and prior disentanglement methods.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model learn from labeled examples placed in its prompt, but its behavior can become unstable as more demonstrations lengthen that prompt. This paper treats those demonstrations as a source of training signals that can be transferred into a small adapter. The aim is to separate the influence of demonstrations from the information carried by the query itself.

An in-context learning teacher first produces labels for unlabeled queries. A student then learns to predict those labels while seeing only each query, updating a lightweight adapter rather than relying on the full demonstration prompt. This stores demonstration effects in a compact, reusable form. The resulting model can still be combined with new demonstrations.

Although the teacher's labels contain errors, the student often performs better than the teacher. The authors connect this to correcting pseudo-labels and expanding coverage, consistent with weak-to-strong generalization. Experiments report better generalization, stability, and efficiency on both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks, exceeding standard in-context learning and earlier disentanglement methods.
summary.tldr: A lightweight student adapter absorbs demonstration effects from an in-context teacher, improving efficiency and often surpassing its noisy teacher.

title: Disentangling Latent Shifts of In-Context Learning with Weak Supervision

abstract: Robust feature representations are essential for learning-based Multi-View Stereo (MVS), which relies on accurate feature matching. Recent MVS methods leverage Transformers to capture long-range dependencies based on local features extracted by conventional feature pyramid networks. However, the quadratic complexity of Transformer-based MVS methods poses challenges to balance performance and efficiency. Motivated by the global modeling capability and linear complexity of the Mamba architecture, we propose MVSMamba, the first Mamba-based MVS network. MVSMamba enables efficient global feature aggregation with minimal computational overhead. To fully exploit Mamba's potential in MVS, we propose a Dynamic Mamba module (DM-module) based on a novel reference-centered dynamic scanning strategy, which enables: (1) Efficient intra- and inter-view feature interaction from the reference to source views, (2) Omnidirectional multi-view feature representations, and (3) Multi-scale global feature aggregation. Extensive experimental results demonstrate MVSMamba outperforms state-of-the-art MVS methods on the DTU dataset and the Tanks-and-Temples benchmark with both superior performance and efficiency. The source code is available at https://github.com/JianfeiJ/MVSMamba.

paragraphs: Multi-view stereo depends on matching features accurately across images taken from different viewpoints. Recent methods use Transformers to combine local features with longer-range information, but their quadratic computational complexity makes efficiency harder to maintain. MVSMamba investigates Mamba as an alternative with global modeling capability and linear complexity.

The network's central component is a Dynamic Mamba module built around reference-centered dynamic scanning. This organizes feature interaction within images and between the reference and source views. It is designed to produce representations that incorporate multiple directions and aggregate global information at multiple scales. The scanning strategy adapts Mamba's processing to the relationships needed for multi-view matching.

Experiments on DTU and Tanks-and-Temples report better performance and efficiency than state-of-the-art multi-view stereo methods. The paper's contribution is therefore both an architectural adaptation and an empirical result: it shows how global feature aggregation using Mamba can support strong matching representations with minimal computational overhead in the evaluated multi-view stereo settings.
summary.tldr: MVSMamba uses reference-centered dynamic scanning to improve multi-view stereo feature aggregation, performance, and efficiency.

title: MVSMamba: Multi-View Stereo with State Space Model

abstract: We study offline policy optimization for infinite-horizon average-reward Markov decision processes (MDPs) with large or infinite state spaces. Specifically, we propose a pessimistic actor-critic algorithm that uses a computationally efficient linear function class for value function estimation. At the core of our method is a critic that computes a pessimistic estimate of the average reward under the current policy, as well as the corresponding policy gradient, by solving a fixed-point Bellman equation, rather than solving a successive sequence of regression problems as in finite horizon settings. This procedure reduces to solving a second-order cone program, which is computationally tractable. Our theoretical analysis is based on a weak partial data coverage assumption, which requires only that the offline data aligns well with the expected feature vector of a comparator policy. Under this condition, we show that our algorithm achieves the optimal sample complexity of O(\varepsilon^{-2}) for learning a near-optimal policy, up to model misspecification errors.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning a policy from an existing dataset when the objective is average reward over an infinite horizon. The setting permits large or infinite state spaces. The proposed actor-critic algorithm uses a linear function class to estimate values and adopts pessimistic reward estimates, making conservative evaluation central to policy optimization from offline data.

Its critic computes both an estimate of the current policy’s average reward and the associated policy gradient by solving a fixed-point Bellman equation. This avoids the successive regression problems used in finite-horizon settings. The resulting computation can be expressed as a second-order cone program, giving the critic a computationally tractable optimization formulation.

The learning guarantee depends on a weak partial data coverage condition: the offline data must align well with the expected feature vector of a comparator policy. Under that condition, the authors establish optimal sample complexity proportional to ε⁻² for obtaining a near-optimal policy, up to model misspecification errors. Both the coverage condition and the approximation error qualification are part of the stated guarantee.
summary.tldr: A pessimistic offline actor-critic algorithm achieves optimal average-reward sample complexity under a partial coverage assumption, up to model misspecification.

title: Offline Actor-Critic for Average Reward MDPs

abstract: Recent progress in large language models (LLMs) highlights the power of scaling test-time compute to achieve strong performance on complex tasks, such as mathematical reasoning and code generation. This raises a critical question: how should model training be modified to optimize performance under a subsequent test-time compute strategy and budget? To explore this, we focus on pass@N, a simple test-time strategy that searches for a correct answer in N independent samples. We show, surprisingly, that training with cross-entropy (CE) can be _misaligned_ with pass@N in that pass@N accuracy _decreases_ with longer CE training. We explain the origins of this misalignment in terms of model overconfidence induced by CE, and experimentally verify our prediction of overconfidence as an impediment to scaling test-time compute via pass@N. Furthermore we suggest a principled, modified training loss that is better aligned to pass@N by limiting model confidence and rescuing pass@N test performance. Our algorithm demonstrates improved mathematical reasoning on MATH and MiniF2F benchmarks under several scenarios: (1) providing answers to math questions both with and without Chain-of-Thought reasoning traces; and (2) proving theorems by searching over proof trees of varying shapes. Overall our work underscores the importance of co-designing two traditionally separate phases of LLM development: training-time protocols and test-time search and reasoning strategies.

paragraphs: A model trained to favor particular answers may not be best suited to a test-time procedure that searches across many attempts. This paper examines pass@N, which measures whether at least one of N independent samples is correct. It shows that longer cross-entropy training can reduce this measure, creating a mismatch between the training objective and the later search strategy.

The authors explain the mismatch through overconfidence induced by cross-entropy training and experimentally test that explanation. They propose a modified loss that limits model confidence to better align learning with pass@N. The purpose is to improve the usefulness of multiple sampled attempts under the subsequent test-time compute strategy.

The method improves mathematical reasoning on MATH and MiniF2F in several evaluated settings. These include answers generated with or without chain-of-thought traces and theorem proving through proof-tree searches of different shapes. The findings support designing training objectives together with inference-time search: an objective that improves conventional training behavior can still be poorly aligned with the way a model will eventually be used.
summary.tldr: Limiting confidence during fine-tuning improves reported mathematical reasoning when test-time search uses multiple samples, addressing a mismatch with cross-entropy training.

title: Rethinking Fine-Tuning when Scaling Test-Time Compute: Limiting Confidence Improves Mathematical Reasoning

abstract: AI agents have the potential to significantly alter the cybersecurity landscape. Here, we introduce the first framework to capture offensive and defensive cyber-capabilities in evolving real-world systems. Instantiating this framework with BountyBench, we set up 25 systems with complex, real-world codebases. To capture the vulnerability lifecycle, we define three task types: Detect (detecting a new vulnerability), Exploit (exploiting a given vulnerability), and Patch (patching a given vulnerability). For Detect, we construct a new success indicator, which is general across vulnerability types and provides localized evaluation. We manually set up the environment for each system, including installing packages, setting up server(s), and hydrating database(s). We add 40 bug bounties, which are vulnerabilities with monetary awards from \\$10 to \\$30,485, covering 9 of the OWASP Top 10 Risks. To modulate task difficulty, we devise a new strategy based on information to guide detection, interpolating from identifying a zero day to exploiting a given vulnerability. We evaluate 10 agents: Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI with o3-high and o4-mini, and custom agents with o3-high, GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5 Pro Preview, Claude 3.7 Sonnet Thinking, Qwen3 235B A22B, Llama 4 Maverick, and DeepSeek-R1. Given up to three attempts, the top-performing agents are OpenAI Codex CLI: o3-high (12.5% on Detect, mapping to \\$3,720; 90% on Patch, mapping to \\$14,152), Custom Agent with Claude 3.7 Sonnet Thinking (67.5% on Exploit), and OpenAI Codex CLI: o4-mini (90% on Patch, mapping to \\$14,422). OpenAI Codex CLI: o3-high, OpenAI Codex CLI: o4-mini, and Claude Code are more capable at defense, achieving higher Patch scores of 90%, 90%, and 87.5%, compared to Exploit scores of 47.5%, 32.5%, and 57.5% respectively; while the custom agents are relatively balanced between offense and defense, achieving Exploit scores of 17.5-67.5% and Patch scores of 25-60%.
originalAbstract: AI agents have the potential to significantly alter the cybersecurity landscape. Here, we introduce the first framework to capture offensive and defensive cyber-capabilities in evolving real-world systems. To capture the vulnerability lifecycle, we define three task types: Detect (detecting a new vulnerability), Exploit (exploiting a given vulnerability), and Patch (patching a given vulnerability). For Detect, we construct a new success indicator, which is general across vulnerability types and provides localized evaluation. We manually set up the environment for each system, including installing packages, setting up server(s), and hydrating database(s). We add 40 bug bounties, which are vulnerabilities with monetary awards from \\$10 to \\$30,485, covering 9 of the OWASP Top 10 Risks. To modulate task difficulty, we devise a new strategy based on information to guide detection, interpolating from identifying a zero day to exploiting a given vulnerability. We evaluate 10 agents: Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI with o3-high and o4-mini, and custom agents with o3-high, GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5 Pro Preview, Claude 3.7 Sonnet Thinking, Qwen3 235B A22B, Llama 4 Maverick, and DeepSeek-R1. Given up to three attempts, the top-performing agents are OpenAI Codex CLI: o3-high (12.5% on Detect, mapping to \\$3,720; 90% on Patch, mapping to \\$14,152), Custom Agent with Claude 3.7 Sonnet Thinking (67.5% on Exploit), and OpenAI Codex CLI: o4-mini (90% on Patch, mapping to \\$14,422). OpenAI Codex CLI: o3-high, OpenAI Codex CLI: o4-mini, and Claude Code are more capable at defense, achieving higher Patch scores of 90%, 90%, and 87.5%, compared to Exploit scores of 47.5%, 32.5%, and 57.5% respectively; while the custom agents are relatively balanced between offense and defense, achieving Exploit scores of 17.5-67.5% and Patch scores of 25-60%.

paragraphs: BountyBench evaluates AI agents on three stages of vulnerability work: discovering a vulnerability, exploiting a specified vulnerability, and patching one. It uses 25 systems with complex real-world codebases and 40 vulnerabilities associated with monetary awards ranging from $10 to $30,485. These cover nine OWASP Top 10 risk categories, connecting benchmark performance to concrete security problems.

The authors prepare each system’s operating environment and introduce a detection-success indicator that works across vulnerability types while localizing evaluation. They also vary how much information guides detection, allowing difficulty to range from finding an unknown vulnerability to exploiting a known one. Ten agents are evaluated with up to three attempts.

Codex CLI with o3-high leads detection at 12.5%, mapped to $3,720, while a custom Claude 3.7 Sonnet Thinking agent leads exploitation at 67.5%. Two Codex CLI configurations reach 90% patch success. The evaluated CLI agents perform better at patching than exploitation, whereas custom agents show a more balanced pattern. These monetary mappings describe benchmark outcomes rather than earnings.
summary.tldr: BountyBench evaluates vulnerability detection, exploitation, and patching in real codebases, revealing substantial differences between agents’ offensive and defensive performance.

title: BountyBench: Dollar Impact of AI Agent Attackers and Defenders on Real-World Cybersecurity Systems

abstract: Networks provide a ‘skeleton’ for the spread of contagions, like, information, ideas, behaviors and diseases. Many times networks over which contagions diffuse are unobserved and need to be inferred. Here we apply survival theory to develop general additive and multiplicative risk models under which the network inference problems can be solved efficiently by exploiting their convexity. Our additive risk model generalizes several existing network inference models. We show all these models are particular cases of our more general model. Our multiplicative model allows for modeling scenarios in which a node can either increase or decrease the risk of activation of another node, in contrast with previous approaches, which consider only positive risk increments. We evaluate the performance of our network inference algorithms on large synthetic and real cascade datasets, and show that our models are able to predict the length and duration of cascades in real data.

paragraphs: Information, ideas, behaviors, and diseases can spread through networks whose connections are not directly observed. This paper uses survival theory to infer such networks from propagation data. It develops additive and multiplicative risk models, describing how activity at one node relates to the risk that another node becomes active.

The additive formulation provides a common model containing several existing network inference approaches as special cases. The multiplicative formulation adds the ability to represent influences that either increase or decrease another node's activation risk. This extends the range of interactions beyond the positive risk increments considered by previous approaches. Both formulations yield inference problems whose convexity can be exploited for efficient solution.

The authors evaluate their inference algorithms on large synthetic and real cascade datasets. They also show that the models can predict cascade length and duration in real data. These results connect network reconstruction with observable propagation behavior. The contribution combines a unifying model family, a way to represent opposing influences, and computationally tractable inference.
summary.tldr: Survival-based risk models enable efficient network inference, including influences that suppress activation, and predict cascade length and duration in real data.

title: Modeling Information Propagation with Survival Theory

abstract: We derive sharp bounds on the generalization error of a generic linear classifier trained by empirical risk minimization on randomly-projected data. We make no restrictive assumptions (such as sparsity or separability) on the data: Instead we use the fact that, in a classification setting, the question of interest is really ‘what is the effect of random projection on the predicted class labels?’ and we therefore derive the exact probability of ‘label flipping’ under Gaussian random projection in order to quantify this effect precisely in our bounds.
originalAbstract: We derive sharp bounds on the generalization error of a generic linear classifier trained by empirical risk minimization on randomly-projected data. We make no restrictive assumptions (such as sparsity or separability) on the data: Instead we use the fact that, in a classification setting, the question of interest is really ‘what is the effect of random projection on the predicted class labels?’ and we therefore derive the exact probability of ‘label flipping’ under Gaussian random projection in order to quantify this effect precisely in our bounds.

paragraphs: Random projection changes the representation of data before a classifier is trained. This paper asks how that change affects prediction on unseen examples for a generic linear classifier trained by empirical risk minimization. The authors derive sharp generalization-error bounds without requiring restrictive data properties such as sparsity or separability.

The analysis centers on predicted class labels. For classification, a geometric change matters especially when it moves an example across a decision boundary and changes its assigned label. The authors derive the exact probability of this label-flipping event under Gaussian random projection. That probability gives a precise way to quantify the effect of the projection in their bounds.

The contribution therefore links projection directly to the decision the classifier makes, rather than treating preservation of geometry as the only question. The absence of sparsity and separability assumptions broadens the stated data setting. The result remains specifically an analysis of linear empirical-risk classifiers and Gaussian projection effects; it quantifies generalization error rather than claiming that projection always preserves every label.
summary.tldr: Exact label-flipping probabilities under Gaussian random projection yield sharp generalization bounds for linear classifiers without sparsity or separability assumptions.

title: Sharp Generalization Error Bounds for Randomly-projected Classifiers

abstract: In this paper, we present a method that combines the merits of Bayesian nonparametrics, specifically stick-breaking priors, and large-margin kernel machines in the context of sequential data classification. The proposed model postulates a set of (theoretically) infinite interdependent large-margin classifiers as model components, that robustly capture local nonlinearity of complex data. The postulated large-margin classifiers are connected in the context of a Markov-switching construction that allows for capturing complex temporal dynamics in the modeled datasets. Appropriate stick-breaking priors are imposed over the component switching mechanism of our model to allow for data-driven determination of the optimal number of component large-margin classifiers, under a standard nonparametric Bayesian inference scheme. Efficient model training is performed under the maximum entropy discrimination (MED) framework, which integrates the large-margin principle with Bayesian posterior inference. We evaluate our method using several real-world datasets, and compare it to state-of-the-art alternatives.

paragraphs: Sequential classification must account for both complex relationships within observations and changes over time. This paper combines large-margin kernel classifiers with Bayesian nonparametric modeling to address both. Its model contains a theoretically infinite collection of interdependent classifier components, intended to capture local nonlinear structure in complex data.

A Markov-switching construction connects the components, allowing the active classification behavior to follow temporal dynamics. Stick-breaking priors govern this switching mechanism and let Bayesian inference determine how many components to use from the data. The infinite formulation therefore supplies flexibility in model size, while component selection is driven by the observations.

Training uses maximum entropy discrimination, a framework that combines the large-margin principle with Bayesian posterior inference. The authors describe the training as efficient and evaluate the method on several real-world datasets against state-of-the-art alternatives. The paper's stated contribution is this integrated model of nonlinear classification, temporal switching, and adaptable component count. The abstract reports the evaluation but does not specify a comparative performance outcome.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian nonparametric Markov-switching model combines large-margin classifiers with temporal dynamics and a data-driven number of components.

title: Infinite Markov-Switching Maximum Entropy Discrimination Machines

abstract: Exchangeable graph models (ExGM) subsume a number of popular network models. The mathematical object that characterizes an ExGM is termed a graphon. Finding scalable estimators of graphons, provably consistent, remains an open issue. In this paper, we propose a histogram estimator of a graphon that is provably consistent and numerically efficient. The proposed estimator is based on a sorting-and-smoothing (SAS) algorithm, which first sorts the empirical degree of a graph, then smooths the sorted graph using total variation minimization. The consistency of the SAS algorithm is proved by leveraging sparsity concepts from compressed sensing.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate the structure underlying an exchangeable graph model, a family that includes several popular network models. That structure is represented by a mathematical object called a graphon. The central challenge is to construct an estimator that is computationally practical and has a proof that its estimates become accurate as the available information grows.

The proposed solution is a histogram estimator built through a sorting-and-smoothing procedure. It first orders the graph according to empirical node degrees, giving the observed network an organized arrangement. It then smooths the sorted graph using total variation minimization. These two stages turn the estimation problem into a concrete computational procedure rather than leaving consistency as an abstract statistical objective.

The authors prove consistency using sparsity ideas from compressed sensing and describe the estimator as numerically efficient. The contribution connects a simple sequence of operations with a formal statistical guarantee. This makes sorting and smoothing a theoretically supported approach to graphon estimation within the paper’s framework.
summary.tldr: A sorting-and-smoothing algorithm provides a numerically efficient, provably consistent histogram estimator of graphons.

title: A Consistent Histogram Estimator for Exchangeable Graph Models

abstract: We propose two new algorithms for the sparse reinforcement learning problem based on different formulations. The first algorithm is an off-line method based on the alternating direction method of multipliers for solving a constrained formulation that explicitly controls the projected Bellman residual. The second algorithm is an online stochastic approximation algorithm that employs the regularized dual averaging technique, using the Lagrangian formulation. The convergence of both algorithms are established. We demonstrate the performance of these algorithms through two classical examples.
originalAbstract: We propose two new algorithms for the sparse reinforcement learning problem based on different formulations. The first algorithm is an off-line method based on the alternating direction method of multipliers for solving a constrained formulation that explicitly controls the projected Bellman residual. The second algorithm is an online stochastic approximation algorithm that employs the regularized dual averaging technique, using the Lagrangian formulation. The convergence of both algorithms are established. We demonstrate the performance of these algorithms through two classical examples.

paragraphs: The paper proposes two algorithms for sparse reinforcement learning, using different optimization formulations. The pair addresses offline and online computation. Its organizing idea is that the learning problem can be approached through convex optimization tools, with the formulation determining how the relevant error and regularization are handled.

The offline algorithm uses the alternating direction method of multipliers. It solves a constrained problem that explicitly controls the projected Bellman residual, a measure of mismatch in the projected value-learning relation. The online algorithm instead uses stochastic approximation with regularized dual averaging, working from a Lagrangian formulation of the problem.

The authors establish convergence for both algorithms and demonstrate their performance on two classical examples. This supplies theoretical support for both computational approaches alongside illustrative empirical evidence. The contribution is the combination of two formulations and corresponding solvers: one makes residual control explicit through a constraint, while the other supports online updates through its stochastic approximation scheme. The stated findings establish convergence and demonstrate performance without asserting universal superiority for either algorithm.
summary.tldr: Two convergent sparse reinforcement learning algorithms use constrained offline optimization and regularized online stochastic approximation.

title: Sparse Reinforcement Learning via Convex Optimization

abstract: Many supervised learning problems involve learning from samples whose labels are corrupted in some way. For example, each sample may have some constant probability of being incorrectly labelled (learning with label noise), or one may have a pool of unlabelled samples in lieu of negative samples (learning from positive and unlabelled data). This paper uses class-probability estimation to study these and other corruption processes belonging to the mutually contaminated distributions framework (Scott et al., 2013), with three conclusions. First, one can optimise balanced error and AUC without knowledge of the corruption process parameters. Second, given estimates of the corruption parameters, one can minimise a range of classification risks. Third, one can estimate the corruption parameters using only corrupted data. Experiments confirm the efficacy of class-probability estimation in learning from corrupted labels.
originalAbstract: Many supervised learning problems involve learning from samples whose labels are corrupted in some way. For example, each sample may have some constant probability of being incorrectly labelled (learning with label noise), or one may have a pool of unlabelled samples in lieu of negative samples (learning from positive and unlabelled data). This paper uses class-probability estimation to study these and other corruption processes belonging to the mutually contaminated distributions framework (Scott et al., 2013), with three conclusions. First, one can optimise balanced error and AUC without knowledge of the corruption process parameters. Second, given estimates of the corruption parameters, one can minimise a range of classification risks. Third, one can estimate the corruption parameters using only corrupted data. Experiments confirm the efficacy of class-probability estimation in learning from corrupted labels.

paragraphs: The paper studies binary classification when the observed labels do not directly represent the desired clean learning problem. Examples include labels that can be flipped and training sets containing positive examples plus unlabeled data instead of explicit negatives. The authors examine these cases within the mutually contaminated distributions framework using class-probability estimation.

The analysis separates what can be learned without knowing the corruption mechanism from what requires estimates of its parameters. Balanced error and AUC can be optimized without those parameters. A broader range of classification risks can be minimized when parameter estimates are available. These are distinct results, so the parameter-free conclusion does not extend automatically to every risk considered.

The authors also show that the corruption parameters themselves can be estimated using corrupted data alone. This connects the conditional risk-minimization result to a way of obtaining the needed information from the available observations. Experiments support the effectiveness of class-probability estimation across the studied corruption settings. The overall contribution is a framework linking probability estimates, evaluation objectives, and information about label corruption.
summary.tldr: Class-probability estimation supports learning from corrupted labels, including parameter-free optimization of balanced error and AUC.

title: Learning from Corrupted Binary Labels via Class-Probability Estimation

abstract: We consider the problem of sequentially making decisions that are rewarded by “successes” and “failures” which can be predicted through an unknown relationship that depends on a partially controllable vector of attributes for each instance. The learner takes an active role in selecting samples from the instance pool. The goal is to maximize the probability of success, either after the offline training phase or minimizing regret in online learning. Our problem is motivated by real-world applications where observations are time consuming and/or expensive. With the adaptation of an online Bayesian linear classifier, we develop a knowledge-gradient type policy to guide the experiment by maximizing the expected value of information of labeling each alternative, in order to reduce the number of expensive physical experiments. We provide a finite-time analysis of the estimated error and demonstrate the performance of the proposed algorithm on both synthetic problems and benchmark UCI datasets.

The learner takes an active role in selecting samples from the instance pool. Our problem is motivated by real-world applications where observations are time consuming and/or expensive. With the adaptation of an online Bayesian linear classifier, we develop a knowledge-gradient type policy to guide the experiment by maximizing the expected value of information of labeling each alternative, in order to reduce the number of expensive physical experiments. paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions whose observed outcomes are successes or failures. Success depends on an unknown relationship involving instance attributes, some of which can be controlled. The learner actively chooses which instances to observe, making sample selection consequential when observations require substantial time or expense.

The authors adapt an online Bayesian linear classifier and develop a knowledge-gradient policy. The policy chooses experiments according to the expected value of the information obtained by labeling each alternative. This ties the next observation to how useful it is expected to be for subsequent decisions, with the aim of reducing the number of costly physical experiments.

The framework considers both maximizing success probability after offline training and minimizing regret during online learning. The paper supplies a finite-time analysis of estimated error and evaluates performance on synthetic problems and benchmark UCI datasets. These contributions combine a probabilistic prediction model, an information-based experiment-selection rule, and theoretical and empirical analysis for learning from binary feedback.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian knowledge-gradient policy selects binary-outcome experiments by their expected information value for future decisions.

title: The Knowledge Gradient for Sequential Decision Making with Stochastic Binary Feedbacks

abstract: Humans have an impressive ability to reason about new concepts and experiences from just a single example. In particular, humans have an ability for one-shot generalization: an ability to encounter a new concept, understand its structure, and then be able to generate compelling alternative variations of the concept. We develop machine learning systems with this important capacity by developing new deep generative models, models that combine the representational power of deep learning with the inferential power of Bayesian reasoning. We develop a class of sequential generative models that are built on the principles of feedback and attention. These two characteristics lead to generative models that are among the state-of-the art in density estimation and image generation. We demonstrate the one-shot generalization ability of our models using three tasks: unconditional sampling, generating new exemplars of a given concept, and generating new exemplars of a family of concepts. In all cases our models are able to generate compelling and diverse samples—having seen new examples just once—providing an important class of general-purpose models for one-shot machine learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies one-shot generalization: encountering a new concept once and then generating plausible variations of it. Its motivation is the human ability to infer useful structure from a single example. The authors develop deep generative models that combine neural-network representations with Bayesian reasoning to pursue this ability in machine learning.

Their models generate sequentially and are built around feedback and attention. These characteristics support a class of generative models reported to be among the state of the art in density estimation and image generation. The approach connects the quality of the generative model to its ability to produce variations after limited exposure to new examples.

The demonstrations cover unconditional sampling, generating new examples of a given concept, and generating examples from a family of concepts. Across these tasks, the authors report compelling, diverse samples and demonstrate generalization after seeing new examples only once. The contribution is a class of general-purpose generative models with demonstrated one-shot capabilities across the reported tasks.
summary.tldr: Sequential generative models using feedback and attention demonstrate diverse generation from newly encountered examples seen only once.

title: One-Shot Generalization in Deep Generative Models

abstract: We introduce a principled approach for simultaneous mapping and clustering (SMAC) for establishing consistent maps across heterogeneous object collections (e.g., 2D images or 3D shapes). Our approach takes as input a heterogeneous object collection and a set of maps computed between some pairs of objects, and outputs a homogeneous object clustering together with a new set of maps possessing optimal intra- and inter-cluster consistency. Our approach is based on the spectral decomposition of a data matrix storing all pairwise maps in its blocks. We additionally provide tight theoretical guarantees on the exactness of SMAC under established noise models. We also demonstrate the usefulness of the approach on synthetic and real datasets.
originalAbstract: We introduce a principled approach for simultaneous mapping and clustering (SMAC) for establishing consistent maps across heterogeneous object collections (e.g., 2D images or 3D shapes). Our approach takes as input a heterogeneous object collection and a set of maps computed between some pairs of objects, and outputs a homogeneous object clustering together with a new set of maps possessing optimal intra- and inter-cluster consistency. Our approach is based on the spectral decomposition of a data matrix storing all pairwise maps in its blocks. We additionally provide tight theoretical guarantees on the exactness of SMAC under established noise models. We also demonstrate the usefulness of the approach on synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: SMAC addresses collections of heterogeneous objects, such as images or three-dimensional shapes, for which some pairwise maps have already been computed. The task is to organize the objects into homogeneous groups while making the relationships among them consistent. The method treats grouping and map estimation as a joint problem.

Its input consists of the object collection and available maps between selected pairs. It produces both a clustering and a revised set of maps with optimal consistency within and between clusters. The method assembles pairwise maps as blocks of a data matrix and uses spectral decomposition of that matrix to carry out the joint analysis.

The authors provide tight theoretical guarantees for exactness under established noise models and demonstrate usefulness on synthetic and real datasets. The guarantees tie exact recovery to the modeled noise setting. The broader contribution is a single spectral approach that links which objects belong together with how their maps should agree, allowing those two aspects of structure to be resolved together.
summary.tldr: SMAC jointly clusters heterogeneous objects and improves map consistency through spectral decomposition, with exactness guarantees under specified noise models.

title: SMAC: Simultaneous Mapping and Clustering Using Spectral Decompositions

abstract: For data-driven decision-making, one promising approach, called predictive optimization, is to solve maximization problems i n which the objective function to be maximized is estimated from data. Predictive optimization, however, suffers from the problem of a calculated optimal solution’s being evaluated too optimistically, i.e., the value of the objective function is overestimated. This paper investigates such optimistic bias and presents two methods for correcting it. The first, which is analogous to cross-validation, successfully corrects the optimistic bias but results in underestimation of the true value. Our second method employs resampling techniques to avoid both overestimation and underestimation. We show that the second method, referred to as the parameter perturbation method, achieves asymptotically unbiased estimation. Empirical results for both artificial and real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed approach successfully corrects the optimistic bias.
originalAbstract: For data-driven decision-making, one promising approach, called predictive optimization, is to solve maximization problems i n which the objective function to be maximized is estimated from data. Predictive optimization, however, suffers from the problem of a calculated optimal solution’s being evaluated too optimistically, i.e., the value of the objective function is overestimated. This paper investigates such optimistic bias and presents two methods for correcting it. The first, which is analogous to cross-validation, successfully corrects the optimistic bias but results in underestimation of the true value. Our second method employs resampling techniques to avoid both overestimation and underestimation. We show that the second method, referred to as the parameter perturbation method, achieves asymptotically unbiased estimation. Empirical results for both artificial and real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed approach successfully corrects the optimistic bias.

paragraphs: Predictive optimization chooses a decision by maximizing an objective estimated from data. The resulting best-looking decision can receive an overly optimistic evaluation: its estimated objective value exceeds its true value. This paper studies that optimism and develops corrections aimed at evaluating the selected solution more accurately.

The first correction resembles cross-validation. It removes the optimistic bias but goes too far in the opposite direction, underestimating the true objective value. This distinction matters because eliminating overestimation alone does not ensure an accurate evaluation. A correction can replace one systematic error with another.

The second approach, called parameter perturbation, uses resampling to address both directions of bias. The authors prove that it is asymptotically unbiased, meaning the bias vanishes in the relevant large-sample limit rather than necessarily being zero for every finite dataset. Experiments on artificial and real-world data show successful correction of optimism. The contribution concerns estimating the value of a data-selected decision more faithfully.
summary.tldr: Parameter perturbation uses resampling to correct optimistic evaluations in predictive optimization and achieves asymptotically unbiased estimation.

title: Unbiased Objective Estimation in Predictive Optimization

abstract: In many real-world problems, there is the possibility to configure, to a limited extent, some environmental parameters to improve the performance of a learning agent. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, Configurable Markov Decision Processes (Conf-MDPs), to model this new type of interaction with the environment. Furthermore, we provide a new learning algorithm, Safe Policy-Model Iteration (SPMI), to jointly and adaptively optimize the policy and the environment configuration. After having introduced our approach and derived some theoretical results, we present the experimental evaluation in two explicative problems to show the benefits of the environment configurability on the performance of the learned policy.
originalAbstract: In many real-world problems, there is the possibility to configure, to a limited extent, some environmental parameters to improve the performance of a learning agent. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, Configurable Markov Decision Processes (Conf-MDPs), to model this new type of interaction with the environment. Furthermore, we provide a new learning algorithm, Safe Policy-Model Iteration (SPMI), to jointly and adaptively optimize the policy and the environment configuration. After having introduced our approach and derived some theoretical results, we present the experimental evaluation in two explicative problems to show the benefits of the environment configurability on the performance of the learned policy.

paragraphs: A learning agent’s performance depends both on its behavior and on the environment in which it acts. In some problems, a limited set of environmental parameters can also be adjusted. This paper introduces Configurable Markov Decision Processes to represent that additional opportunity within the learning problem.

The accompanying algorithm, Safe Policy-Model Iteration, jointly and adaptively optimizes the agent’s policy and the environment configuration. A policy determines how the agent acts; the configuration determines the adjustable aspects of its surroundings. Treating them together makes their interaction part of the optimization, allowing the learning process to consider improvements through either kind of choice.

The authors derive theoretical results for the approach and evaluate it on two illustrative problems. Those experiments show benefits from environmental configurability for the learned policy’s performance. The contribution therefore concerns settings where some environmental control is actually available: it provides a framework and algorithm for using that control alongside policy learning, with experimental evidence that the combination can be useful.
summary.tldr: Configurable Markov Decision Processes let an agent jointly improve its policy and the adjustable parts of its environment.

title: Configurable Markov Decision Processes

abstract:
We consider the problem of Bayesian optimization (BO) in one dimension, under a Gaussian process prior and Gaussian sampling noise. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that, under fairly mild technical assumptions on the kernel, the best possible cumulative regret up to time $T$ behaves as $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ and $O(\sqrt{T\log T})$. This gives a tight characterization up to a $\sqrt{\log T}$ factor, and includes the first non-trivial lower bound for noisy BO. Our assumptions are satisfied, for example, by the squared exponential and Matérn-$
u$ kernels, with the latter requiring $
u > 2$. Our results certify the near-optimality of existing bounds (Srinivas et al. , 2009) for the SE kernel, while proving them to be strictly suboptimal for the Matérn kernel with $
u > 2$.

We consider the problem of Bayesian optimization (BO) in one dimension, under a Gaussian process prior and Gaussian sampling noise. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that, under fairly mild technical assumptions on the kernel, the best possible cumulative regret up to time $T$ behaves as $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ and $O(\sqrt{T\log T})$. This gives a tight characterization up to a $\sqrt{\log T}$ factor, and includes the first non-trivial lower bound for noisy BO. Our assumptions are satisfied, for example, by the squared exponential and Matérn-$
u$ kernels, with the latter requiring $
u > 2$. Our results certify the near-optimality of existing bounds (Srinivas et al. , 2009) for the SE kernel, while proving them to be strictly suboptimal for the Matérn kernel with $
u > 2$.

paragraphs: This paper studies the theoretical limits of Bayesian optimization for a one-dimensional function observed with Gaussian noise under a Gaussian process prior. It measures cumulative regret, the accumulated shortfall from choosing points below the optimum. The question is how quickly this total can grow even when the optimization strategy is as effective as possible.

Under technical assumptions on the kernel, the best achievable cumulative regret has a lower bound of order square root of T and an upper bound of order square root of T log T. The bounds differ only by a square-root-logarithmic factor. The lower bound is presented as the first nontrivial one for noisy Bayesian optimization.

The assumptions cover the squared exponential kernel and Matérn kernels with smoothness parameter greater than two. For the squared exponential case, the results establish near-optimality of existing bounds. For the stated Matérn case, they show that earlier bounds are strictly suboptimal. The contribution therefore both identifies a near-tight achievable scale and clarifies where previous analyses were loose.
summary.tldr: Nearly matching regret bounds characterize one-dimensional noisy Bayesian optimization under stated Gaussian-process kernel assumptions.

title: Tight Regret Bounds for Bayesian Optimization in One Dimension

abstract: We present POLITEX (POLicy ITeration with EXpert advice), a variant of policy iteration where each policy is a Boltzmann distribution over the sum of action-value function estimates of the previous policies, and analyze its regret in continuing RL problems. We assume that the value function error after running a policy for $\tau$ time steps scales as $\epsilon(\tau) = \epsilon_0 + O(\sqrt{d/\tau})$, where $\epsilon_0$ is the worst-case approximation error and $d$ is the number of features in a compressed representation of the state-action space. We establish that this condition is satisfied by the LSPE algorithm under certain assumptions on the MDP and policies. Under the error assumption, we show that the regret of POLITEX in uniformly mixing MDPs scales as $O(d^{1/2}T^{3/4} + \epsilon_0T)$, where $O(\cdot)$ hides logarithmic terms and problem-dependent constants. Thus, we provide the first regret bound for a fully practical model-free method which only scales in the number of features, and not in the size of the underlying MDP. Experiments on a queuing problem confirm that POLITEX is competitive with some of its alternatives, while preliminary results on Ms Pacman (one of the standard Atari benchmark problems) confirm the viability of POLITEX beyond linear function approximation.

summary.tldr: POLITEX combines past value estimates into policies and obtains feature-dependent regret bounds under mixing and evaluation-error assumptions.

title: POLITEX: Regret Bounds for Policy Iteration using Expert Prediction

abstract: Improving the robustness of deep neural networks (DNNs) to adversarial examples is an important yet challenging problem for secure deep learning. Across existing defense techniques, adversarial training with Projected Gradient Decent (PGD) is amongst the most effective. Adversarial training solves a min-max optimization problem, with the inner maximization generating adversarial examples by maximizing the classification loss, and the outer minimization finding model parameters by minimizing the loss on adversarial examples generated from the inner maximization. A criterion that measures how well the inner maximization is solved is therefore crucial for adversarial training. In this paper, we propose such a criterion, namely First-Order Stationary Condition for constrained optimization (FOSC), to quantitatively evaluate the convergence quality of adversarial examples found in the inner maximization. With FOSC, we find that to ensure better robustness, it is essential to use adversarial examples with better convergence quality at the later stages of training. Yet at the early stages, high convergence quality adversarial examples are not necessary and may even lead to poor robustness. Based on these observations, we propose a dynamic training strategy to gradually increase the convergence quality of the generated adversarial examples, which significantly improves the robustness of adversarial training. Our theoretical and empirical results show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

This paper examines the quality of the inner search. It asks how well the attack optimization has converged, and how that quality should change over the course of training.

The authors introduce the First-Order Stationary Condition for constrained optimization as a quantitative measure of convergence quality. Using this criterion, they find that better-converged adversarial examples are essential for better robustness later in training. Its practical implication is that the inner optimization deserves a training schedule of its own: the quality of adversarial examples should be considered together with the stage at which they are used.
summary.tldr: Gradually increasing adversarial-example convergence quality improves robustness, reflecting different needs early and late in training.

title: On the Convergence and Robustness of Adversarial Training

abstract: Automating algorithm configuration is growing increasingly necessary as algorithms come with more and more tunable parameters. It is common to tune parameters using machine learning, optimizing algorithmic performance (runtime or solution quality, for example) using a training set of problem instances from the specific domain at hand. We investigate a fundamental question about these techniques: how large should the training set be to ensure that a parameter’s average empirical performance over the training set is close to its expected, future performance? We answer this question for algorithm configuration problems that exhibit a widely-applicable structure: the algorithm’s performance as a function of its parameters can be approximated by a “simple” function. We show that if this approximation holds under the L$\infty$-norm, we can provide strong sample complexity bounds, but if the approximation holds only under the Lp-norm for p < $\infty$, it is not possible to provide meaningful sample complexity bounds in the worst case. We empirically evaluate our bounds in the context of integer programming, obtaining sample complexity bounds that are up to 700 times smaller than the previously best-known bounds.

paragraphs: Automatically tuning an algorithm means choosing parameters based on performance on training instances. The practical question is how many instances are needed before that observed performance reliably represents expected future performance. This paper studies configuration problems where performance, viewed as a function of the parameters, can be approximated by a simpler function.

The crucial distinction is the type of approximation. When the approximation is uniformly accurate under the L-infinity norm, the authors obtain strong sample-complexity bounds. If accuracy holds only under an Lp norm with finite p, meaningful worst-case sample-complexity bounds are not possible on that basis. Thus, a uniformly controlled error offers a guarantee that an averaged error measure alone does not provide.

The authors evaluate their bounds in integer programming and obtain sample-complexity bounds up to 700 times smaller than previously best-known ones. This is an improvement in the theoretical training-set requirements evaluated there, rather than a claim of a corresponding runtime speedup. The work explains why the precise form of performance-function approximability matters when justifying parameter selection from data.
summary.tldr: Uniform approximation enables strong algorithm-configuration sample bounds, while finite-Lp approximation alone cannot support meaningful bounds in the worst case.

title: Refined bounds for algorithm configuration: The knife-edge of dual class approximability

abstract: There is a recent surge of interest in designing deep architectures based on the update steps in traditional algorithms, or learning neural networks to improve and replace traditional algorithms. While traditional algorithms have certain stopping criteria for outputting results at different iterations, many algorithm-inspired deep models are restricted to a “fixed-depth” for all inputs. Similar to algorithms, the optimal depth of a deep architecture may be different for different input instances, either to avoid “over-thinking”, or because we want to compute less for operations converged already. In this paper, we tackle this varying depth problem using a steerable architecture, where a feed-forward deep model and a variational stopping policy are learned together to sequentially determine the optimal number of layers for each input instance. Training such architecture is very challenging. We provide a variational Bayes perspective and design a novel and effective training procedure which decomposes the task into an oracle model learning stage and an imitation stage. Experimentally, we show that the learned deep model along with the stopping policy improves the performances on a diverse set of tasks, including learning sparse recovery, few-shot meta learning, and computer vision tasks.

paragraphs: Many neural architectures borrow their structure from iterative algorithms but use the same fixed number of layers for every input. Traditional algorithms can stop when further iterations are unnecessary. This paper brings a similar capability to deep models, motivated by the possibility that some inputs need less computation or that additional processing can amount to over-thinking.

The proposed steerable architecture learns a feed-forward prediction model together with a variational stopping policy. The policy sequentially decides how many layers to use for each input. Because jointly learning prediction and stopping is challenging, the authors develop a variational Bayes perspective and a training procedure divided into an oracle-model learning stage and an imitation stage.

Experiments show improved performance across sparse recovery, few-shot meta-learning, and computer vision tasks. The contribution is a way to make depth an input-dependent learned decision while training the underlying predictor alongside it. The results support adaptive stopping across the tested applications, with the stopping policy serving as part of the model’s decision process rather than a single fixed depth chosen for all cases.
summary.tldr: A jointly learned predictor and stopping policy adapt network depth to each input and improve performance across several evaluated tasks.

title: Learning To Stop While Learning To Predict

abstract: We introduce a new non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) method for ordinal data, called OrdNMF. Ordinal data are categorical data which exhibit a natural ordering between the categories. In particular, they can be found in recommender systems, either with explicit data (such as ratings) or implicit data (such as quantized play counts). OrdNMF is a probabilistic latent factor model that generalizes Bernoulli-Poisson factorization (BePoF) and Poisson factorization (PF) applied to binarized data. Contrary to these methods, OrdNMF circumvents binarization and can exploit a more informative representation of the data. We design an efficient variational algorithm based on a suitable model augmentation and related to variational PF. In particular, our algorithm preserves the scalability of PF and can be applied to huge sparse datasets. We report recommendation experiments on explicit and implicit datasets, and show that OrdNMF outperforms BePoF and PF applied to binarized data.

paragraphs: Recommendation data often contain ordered categories, such as ratings or play counts grouped into levels. Converting these observations into binary indicators discards distinctions between the levels. OrdNMF is a probabilistic non-negative matrix factorization model designed to retain that ordering and use the more informative representation directly.

The model generalizes Bernoulli-Poisson factorization and Poisson factorization applied to binarized observations. Its latent-factor formulation provides a way to represent recommendation data while preserving their ordinal character. The authors also develop an efficient variational inference algorithm using a suitable augmentation of the model, connecting the computation to variational Poisson factorization.

A key practical result is that the algorithm retains the scalability of Poisson factorization and can handle very large sparse datasets. Recommendation experiments cover both explicit and implicit feedback, and OrdNMF outperforms the two stated approaches when they operate on binarized data. The findings support preserving ordered feedback while maintaining a computational approach suited to sparse recommendation settings.
summary.tldr: OrdNMF preserves ordered recommendation feedback and improves reported results over binarized factorization methods while retaining scalability.

title: Ordinal Non-negative Matrix Factorization for Recommendation

abstract: The field of algorithms has seen a push for fairness, or the removal of inherent bias, in recent history. In data summarization, where a much smaller subset of a data set is chosen to represent the whole of the data, fairness can be introduced by guaranteeing each "demographic group" a specific portion of the representative subset. Specifically, this paper examines this fair variant of the k-centers problem, where a subset of the data with cardinality k is chosen to minimize distance to the rest of the data. Previous papers working on this problem presented both a 3-approximation algorithm with a super-linear runtime and a linear-time algorithm whose approximation factor is exponential in the number of demographic groups. This paper combines the best of each algorithm by presenting a linear-time algorithm with a guaranteed 3-approximation factor and provides empirical evidence of both the algorithm’s runtime and effectiveness.

paragraphs: Data summarization selects a small group of examples to represent a larger dataset. This paper studies a fair version of the k-centers problem, where the representative set must contain specified portions from each demographic group. The goal is to satisfy those representation requirements while keeping the dataset close to the chosen centers.

Earlier algorithms offered different compromises between speed and approximation quality. One guaranteed a solution within a factor of three of the optimum but required superlinear runtime. Another ran in linear time, but its approximation factor grew exponentially with the number of demographic groups. These tradeoffs made it difficult to obtain both efficient computation and a strong quality guarantee.

The proposed algorithm, presented through maximum matching, combines linear runtime with a guaranteed factor-three approximation. Empirical results also support its runtime and effectiveness. The contribution is a precise algorithmic improvement for the specified fairness constraint: demographic representation can be enforced while retaining both a constant approximation factor and linear-time processing.
summary.tldr: A fair k-centers algorithm combines demographic representation constraints with linear runtime and a factor-three approximation guarantee.

title: Fair k-Centers via Maximum Matching

abstract: PCA with Outliers is the fundamental problem of identifying an underlying low-dimensional subspace in a data set corrupted with outliers. A large body of work is devoted to the information-theoretic aspects of this problem. However, from the computational perspective, its complexity is still not well-understood. We study this problem from the perspective of parameterized complexity by investigating how parameters like the dimension of the data, the subspace dimension, the number of outliers and their structure, and approximation error, influence the computational complexity of the problem. Our algorithmic methods are based on techniques of randomized linear algebra and algebraic geometry.

paragraphs: PCA with outliers seeks a low-dimensional subspace underlying data that also contain corrupted observations. The challenge has both a recovery aspect and a computational aspect: knowing that the underlying structure can be identified does not by itself explain how difficult the required computation will be. This paper focuses on that computational question.

The authors use parameterized complexity to examine how different features of the problem affect difficulty. These include the dimension of the original data, the dimension of the desired subspace, the number and structure of outliers, and the permitted approximation error. Considering these quantities separately gives a more detailed view than treating dataset size as the only source of computational cost.

The algorithmic methods draw on randomized linear algebra and algebraic geometry. The contribution concerns fixed-parameter and approximation algorithms, organizing the search for a useful subspace around the parameters that govern the problem. Its significance is a computational perspective on robust dimensionality reduction: the structure of the instance and the accuracy requested are central parts of assessing algorithmic difficulty.
summary.tldr: The paper studies how dimensions, outlier properties, and approximation error shape the computational difficulty of PCA with outliers.

title: Fixed-Parameter and Approximation Algorithms for PCA with Outliers

abstract: We propose improved fixed-design confidence bounds for the linear logistic model. Our bounds significantly improve upon the state-of-the-art bound by Li et al. (2017) via recent developments of the self-concordant analysis of the logistic loss (Faury et al., 2020). Specifically, our confidence bound avoids a direct dependence on $1/\kappa$, where $\kappa$ is the minimal variance over all arms’ reward distributions. In general, $1/\kappa$ scales exponentially with the norm of the unknown linear parameter $\theta^*$. Instead of relying on this worst case quantity, our confidence bound for the reward of any given arm depends directly on the variance of that arm’s reward distribution. We present two applications of our novel bounds to pure exploration and regret minimization logistic bandits improving upon state-of-the-art performance guarantees. For pure exploration we also provide a lower bound highlighting a dependence on $1/\kappa$ for a family of instances.

paragraphs: In logistic bandit problems, decisions depend on estimating rewards and understanding the uncertainty in those estimates. This paper improves fixed-design confidence bounds for the linear logistic model. Earlier bounds depended directly on the inverse of the smallest reward variance across all arms, a quantity that can grow exponentially with the unknown parameter's norm.

Using self-concordant analysis of logistic loss, the authors replace that direct worst-case dependence with a bound tied to the reward variance of the particular arm being assessed. This makes the confidence statement more specific to the arm instead of letting a single global minimum variance determine the bound.

The authors apply the result to both pure exploration, where learning is the objective, and regret minimization, where choices must also earn rewards. Both applications improve stated performance guarantees. A complementary lower bound shows that inverse-minimum-variance dependence still arises for a family of pure-exploration instances. The improvement therefore refines uncertainty analysis without claiming that this difficult dependence disappears from every related learning problem.
summary.tldr: Arm-specific variance yields sharper logistic confidence bounds and better bandit guarantees, while a lower bound preserves a worst-case dependence for some exploration problems.

title: Improved Confidence Bounds for the Linear Logistic Model and Applications to Bandits

abstract: Social learning is a key component of human and animal intelligence. By taking cues from the behavior of experts in their environment, social learners can acquire sophisticated behavior and rapidly adapt to new circumstances. This paper investigates whether independent reinforcement learning (RL) agents in a multi-agent environment can learn to use social learning to improve their performance. We find that in most circumstances, vanilla model-free RL agents do not use social learning. We analyze the reasons for this deficiency, and show that by imposing constraints on the training environment and introducing a model-based auxiliary loss we are able to obtain generalized social learning policies which enable agents to: i) discover complex skills that are not learned from single-agent training, and ii) adapt online to novel environments by taking cues from experts present in the new environment. In contrast, agents trained with model-free RL or imitation learning generalize poorly and do not succeed in the transfer tasks. By mixing multi-agent and solo training, we can obtain agents that use social learning to gain skills that they can deploy when alone, even out-performing agents trained alone from the start.

paragraphs: An agent sharing an environment with an expert could potentially learn useful behavior by watching what that expert does. This paper investigates whether independent reinforcement learning agents acquire that ability. In most circumstances studied, ordinary model-free agents do not make use of social learning, so the presence of knowledgeable peers alone is insufficient.

The authors analyze this deficiency and combine constraints on the training environment with a model-based auxiliary loss. The resulting policies learn how to use social information across situations. They discover complex skills absent from single-agent training and adapt during interaction with unfamiliar environments by taking cues from experts present there.

In the transfer tasks, the compared model-free and imitation-learning agents generalize poorly and do not succeed. Mixing multi-agent training with solo training also allows socially acquired skills to remain useful when an agent is alone. Those agents can even outperform agents trained alone from the beginning, showing that social learning can support later independent performance.
summary.tldr: Training constraints and a model-based auxiliary loss enable agents to learn from experts, adapt to new environments, and retain skills for solo use.

title: Emergent Social Learning via Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The recent work by Rendle et al. (2020), based on empirical observations, argues that matrix-factorization collaborative filtering (MCF) compares favorably to neural collaborative filtering (NCF), and conjectures the dot product’s superiority over the feed-forward neural network as similarity function. In this paper, we address the comparison rigorously by answering the following questions: 1. what is the limiting expressivity of each model; 2. under the practical gradient descent, to which solution does each optimization path converge; 3. how would the models generalize under the inductive and transductive learning setting. Our results highlight the similar expressivity for the overparameterized NCF and MCF as kernelized predictors, and reveal the relation between their optimization paths. We further show their different generalization behaviors, where MCF and NCF experience specific tradeoff and comparison in the transductive and inductive collaborative filtering setting. Lastly, by showing a novel generalization result, we reveal the critical role of correcting exposure bias for model evaluation in the inductive setting. Our results explain some of the previously observed conflicts, and we provide synthetic and real-data experiments to shed further insights to this topic.

paragraphs: The paper revisits whether matrix-factorization collaborative filtering is preferable to neural collaborative filtering. Earlier empirical observations favored matrix factorization and suggested that a dot product might be a better similarity function than a feed-forward network. The authors investigate that comparison through representational capacity, gradient-descent optimization, and generalization.

Their results show similar expressivity for overparameterized versions of the two model families when viewed as kernelized predictors. They also reveal a relationship between their optimization paths. This connects the models at the level of what they can express and how training proceeds, rather than judging them only through observed predictive performance.

Generalization produces a more differentiated picture, with tradeoffs across inductive and transductive collaborative filtering settings. The paper additionally establishes a result highlighting the importance of correcting exposure bias when evaluating models in the inductive setting. Synthetic and real-data experiments provide further insight. Together, the findings explain some earlier conflicting observations and make the comparison depend on the learning and evaluation setting, rather than establishing one model family as universally superior.
summary.tldr: Theory links neural and matrix-factorization recommenders while revealing setting-dependent generalization tradeoffs and the importance of correcting exposure bias.

title: Rethinking Neural vs. Matrix-Factorization Collaborative Filtering: the Theoretical Perspectives

abstract: What is the best way to exploit extra data – be it unlabeled data from the same task, or labeled data from a related task – to learn a given task? This paper formalizes the question using the theory of reference priors. Reference priors are objective, uninformative Bayesian priors that maximize the mutual information between the task and the weights of the model. Such priors enable the task to maximally affect the Bayesian posterior, e.g., reference priors depend upon the number of samples available for learning the task and for very small sample sizes, the prior puts more probability mass on low-complexity models in the hypothesis space. This paper presents the first demonstration of reference priors for medium-scale deep networks and image-based data. We develop generalizations of reference priors and demonstrate applications to two problems. First, by using unlabeled data to compute the reference prior, we develop new Bayesian semi-supervised learning methods that remain effective even with very few samples per class. Second, by using labeled data from the source task to compute the reference prior, we develop a new pretraining method for transfer learning that allows data from the target task to maximally affect the Bayesian posterior. Empirical validation of these methods is conducted on image classification datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/grasp-lyrl/deep_reference_priors
