paragraphs: This paper asks how extra data should influence learning a target task, whether that data is unlabeled or comes with labels from a related task. It frames the question through Bayesian reference priors: priors chosen to maximize mutual information between the task and model weights, allowing task data to strongly influence the resulting posterior.

A distinctive feature is that these priors depend on the amount of data available for learning. With very small sample sizes, they assign more probability to lower-complexity models. The authors demonstrate reference priors for medium-scale deep networks using images and develop generalizations that support two ways of using additional data.

For semi-supervised learning, unlabeled data helps construct the prior, yielding methods reported to remain effective with very few examples per class. For transfer learning, labeled source-task data defines a prior intended to let the target task maximally influence the posterior. Image classification experiments validate both applications. The contribution is a Bayesian formulation of how pretraining information and target-task evidence should interact.
summary.tldr: Deep reference priors provide a Bayesian way to use unlabeled or source-task data while preserving the target task’s influence on learning.

title: Deep Reference Priors: What is the best way to pretrain a model?

abstract: Impressive results in natural language processing (NLP) based on the Transformer neural network architecture have inspired researchers to explore viewing offline reinforcement learning (RL) as a generic sequence modeling problem. Recent works based on this paradigm have achieved state-of-the-art results in several of the mostly deterministic offline Atari and D4RL benchmarks. However, because these methods jointly model the states and actions as a single sequencing problem, they struggle to disentangle the effects of the policy and world dynamics on the return. Thus, in adversarial or stochastic environments, these methods lead to overly optimistic behavior that can be dangerous in safety-critical systems like autonomous driving. In this work, we propose a method that addresses this optimism bias by explicitly disentangling the policy and world models, which allows us at test time to search for policies that are robust to multiple possible futures in the environment. We demonstrate our method’s superior performance on a variety of autonomous driving tasks in simulation.

paragraphs: Treating offline reinforcement learning as sequence prediction lets models learn patterns across recorded states and actions. However, a high-return sequence can reflect both good decisions and favorable events outside the agent’s control. The paper argues that modeling everything together makes it difficult to distinguish these contributions, encouraging overly optimistic decisions when environments are stochastic or adversarial.

The proposed method explicitly separates the policy model from the model of the world. This distinction lets the system reason separately about which actions it can choose and which environmental outcomes it may face. At test time, it searches for policies that remain robust across multiple possible futures, rather than relying on a favorable predicted continuation.

The authors demonstrate superior performance on several simulated autonomous-driving tasks. These findings support separating decision-making from environmental prediction when uncertainty matters. The evidence is specifically about performance in simulation; the central methodological contribution is a way to address optimism caused by confusing controllable actions with uncertain world dynamics.
summary.tldr: Separating policy and world models helps sequence-based reinforcement learning search for decisions that withstand multiple possible futures.

title: Addressing Optimism Bias in Sequence Modeling for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We propose two linear bandits algorithms with per-step complexity sublinear in the number of arms $K$. The algorithms are designed for applications where the arm set is extremely large and slowly changing. Our key realization is that choosing an arm reduces to a maximum inner product search (MIPS) problem, which can be solved approximately without breaking regret guarantees. Existing approximate MIPS solvers run in sublinear time. We extend those solvers and present theoretical guarantees for online learning problems, where adaptivity (i.e., a later step depends on the feedback in previous steps) becomes a unique challenge. We then explicitly characterize the tradeoff between the per-step complexity and regret. For sufficiently large $K$, our algorithms have sublinear per-step complexity and $\widetilde O(\sqrt{T})$ regret. Empirically, we evaluate our proposed algorithms in a synthetic environment and a real-world online movie recommendation problem. Our proposed algorithms can deliver a more than 72 times speedup compared to the linear time baselines while retaining similar regret.

Their per-step computation grows sublinearly with the number of arms, addressing the cost of examining a very large collection of choices.

The central observation is that arm selection can be expressed as maximum inner product search. Approximate solvers can handle this search in sublinear time, but using them inside an online learning algorithm introduces a challenge: later searches depend on feedback from earlier decisions. The authors extend the solvers and establish guarantees that account for this adaptivity.

The analysis explicitly characterizes a tradeoff between computation and regret. For sufficiently many arms, the algorithms combine sublinear per-step complexity with regret scaling roughly as the square root of the time horizon, up to logarithmic factors. Experiments in a synthetic environment and movie recommendation report more than a 72-fold speedup over linear-time baselines while retaining similar regret.
summary.tldr: Approximate maximum inner product search enables faster linear-bandit decisions over very large action sets while preserving theoretical regret guarantees.

title: Linear Bandit Algorithms with Sublinear Time Complexity

abstract: We propose a new method, dubbed One Class Signed Distance Function (OCSDF), to perform One Class Classification (OCC) by provably learning the Signed Distance Function (SDF) to the boundary of the support of any distribution. The distance to the support can be interpreted as a normality score, and its approximation using 1-Lipschitz neural networks provides robustness bounds against $l2$ adversarial attacks, an under-explored weakness of deep learning-based OCC algorithms. As a result, OCSDF comes with a new metric, certified AUROC, that can be computed at the same cost as any classical AUROC. We show that OCSDF is competitive against concurrent methods on tabular and image data while being way more robust to adversarial attacks, illustrating its theoretical properties. Finally, as exploratory research perspectives, we theoretically and empirically show how OCSDF connects OCC with image generation and implicit neural surface parametrization.

paragraphs: One-class classification identifies whether an observation is consistent with the distribution being modeled. This paper proposes One Class Signed Distance Function, or OCSDF, which learns a signed distance to the boundary of that distribution's support. The distance provides a geometric normality score, connecting classification to how an observation relates to the region supported by the data distribution.

The authors give a provable learning result and approximate the distance function using 1-Lipschitz neural networks. This restriction on how quickly network outputs can change provides robustness bounds against attacks measured in the l2 distance. They also introduce certified AUROC, a robustness-aware evaluation metric that can be computed at the same cost as ordinary AUROC.

Experiments on tabular and image data show competitive classification performance and substantially greater adversarial robustness than the compared methods, illustrating the theoretical properties. The paper additionally explores connections to image generation and implicit neural surface parameterization through theoretical and empirical results. Those connections are presented as exploratory directions, extending the geometric viewpoint beyond its primary one-class classification task.
summary.tldr: OCSDF learns a geometric normality score with 1-Lipschitz networks, yielding certified robustness bounds and competitive one-class classification results.

title: Robust One-Class Classification with Signed Distance Function using 1-Lipschitz Neural Networks

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated an impressive ability to perform arithmetic and symbolic reasoning tasks, when provided with a few examples at test time ("few-shot prompting"). Much of this success can be attributed to prompting methods such as "chain-of-thought", which employ LLMs for both understanding the problem description by decomposing it into steps, as well as solving each step of the problem. While LLMs seem to be adept at this sort of step-by-step decomposition, LLMs often make logical and arithmetic mistakes in the solution part, even when the problem is decomposed correctly. In this paper, we present Program-Aided Language models (PAL): a novel approach that uses the LLM to read natural language problems and generate programs as the intermediate reasoning steps, but offloads the solution step to a runtime such as a Python interpreter. With PAL, decomposing the natural language problem into runnable steps remains the only learning task for the LLM, while solving is delegated to the interpreter. We demonstrate this synergy between a neural LLM and a symbolic interpreter across 13 mathematical, symbolic, and algorithmic reasoning tasks from BIG-Bench Hard and others. In all these natural language reasoning tasks, generating code using an LLM and reasoning using a Python interpreter leads to more accurate results than much larger models. For example, PAL using Codex achieves state-of-the-art few-shot accuracy on GSM8K, surpassing PaLM which uses chain-of-thought by absolute 15% top-1.

paragraphs: Language models can break a reasoning problem into sensible steps and still make mistakes when carrying out arithmetic or logic. Program-aided language models, or PAL, separates these responsibilities. The language model reads the problem and expresses the reasoning steps as a runnable program, while an interpreter performs the computation.

The approach therefore combines language understanding with program execution within one solution process.

Across those tasks, the combination produces more accurate answers than much larger models. On GSM8K, PAL with Codex achieves reported state-of-the-art few-shot accuracy and exceeds PaLM using chain-of-thought by 15 absolute percentage points in top-1 accuracy.
summary.tldr: PAL improves reasoning accuracy by having language models generate programs and an interpreter execute the solution steps.

title: PAL: Program-aided Language Models

abstract: In practical federated learning (FL) systems, the communication cost between the clients and the central server can often be a bottleneck. In this paper, we focus on biased gradient compression in non-convex FL problems. In the classical distributed learning, the method of error feedback (EF) is a common technique to remedy the downsides of biased gradient compression, but the performance of EF in FL still lacks systematic investigation. In this work, we study a compressed FL scheme with error feedback, named Fed-EF, with two variants depending on the global model optimizer. While directly applying biased compression in FL leads to poor convergence, we show that Fed-EF is able to match the convergence rate of the full-precision FL counterpart with a linear speedup w.r.t. the number of clients. Experiments verify that Fed-EF achieves the same performance as the full-precision FL approach, at the substantially reduced communication cost. Moreover, we develop a new analysis of the EF under partial participation (PP), an important scenario in FL. Under PP, the convergence rate of Fed-EF exhibits an extra slow-down factor due to a so-called “stale error compensation” effect, which is also justified in our experiments. Our results provide insights on a theoretical limitation of EF, and possible directions for improvements.

paragraphs: Communication between clients and a central server can bottleneck federated learning. Compressing gradients reduces that traffic, but biased compression can distort optimization and lead to poor convergence. This paper studies whether error feedback, which compensates for compression errors, can address that problem in federated learning with non-convex objectives.

The authors analyze Fed-EF, a compressed federated learning scheme with two variants distinguished by the server's optimizer. They show that it can match the convergence rate of the corresponding full-precision method while achieving linear speedup with the number of clients. Experiments likewise report matching performance with substantially less communication, supporting the value of retaining and compensating for compression error.

The analysis also examines partial participation, where only some clients contribute at a time. Here, accumulated error compensation can become stale, introducing an additional slowdown factor into convergence. Experiments support this effect. The findings identify both a strong case for error feedback and a specific limitation that arises when participation is intermittent.
summary.tldr: Fed-EF can preserve full-precision convergence with compressed communication, but partial client participation introduces a slowdown from stale error compensation.

title: Analysis of Error Feedback in Federated Non-Convex Optimization with Biased Compression: Fast Convergence and Partial Participation

abstract: Current benchmarks for evaluating neural code models focus on only a small subset of programming languages, excluding many popular languages such as Go or Rust. To ameliorate this issue, we present the BabelCode framework for execution-based evaluation of any benchmark in any language. BabelCode enables new investigations into the qualitative performance of models’ memory, runtime, and individual test case results. Additionally, we present a new code translation dataset called Translating Python Programming Puzzles (TP3) from the Python Programming Puzzles (Schuster et al., 2021) benchmark that involves translating expert-level python functions to any language. With both BabelCode and the TP3 benchmark, we investigate if balancing the distributions of 14 languages in a training dataset improves a large language model’s performance on low-resource languages. Training a model on a balanced corpus results in, on average, 12.34% higher $pass@k$ across all tasks and languages compared to the baseline. We find that this strategy achieves 66.48% better $pass@k$ on low-resource languages at the cost of only a 12.94% decrease to high-resource languages. In our three translation tasks, this strategy yields, on average, 30.77% better low-resource $pass@k$ while having 19.58% worse high-resource $pass@k$.

paragraphs: Code-model benchmarks often cover only a narrow selection of programming languages. This paper introduces BabelCode, a framework for execution-based evaluation across benchmarks and languages, with visibility into memory use, runtime, and individual test outcomes. For low-resource languages, the reported pass@k improvement is 66.48%, accompanied by a 12.94% decrease for high-resource languages. Across three translation tasks, the corresponding averages are a 30.77% improvement and a 19.58% decrease. These findings make the training-distribution tradeoff concrete: broader support can benefit less represented languages substantially, while reducing performance on better represented ones in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: BabelCode and TP3 enable broader code-model evaluation, revealing that balanced language training improves low-resource performance with high-resource tradeoffs.

title: Measuring the Impact of Programming Language Distribution

abstract: For infinite action contextual bandits, smoothed regret and reduction to regression results in state-of-the-art online performance with computational cost independent of the action set: unfortunately, the resulting data exhaust does not have well-defined importance-weights. This frustrates the execution of downstream data science processes such as offline model selection. In this paper we describe an online algorithm with an equivalent smoothed regret guarantee, but which generates well-defined importance weights: in exchange, the online computational cost increases, but only to order smoothness (i.e., still independent of the action set). This removes a key obstacle to adoption of smoothed regret in production scenarios.
originalAbstract: For infinite action contextual bandits, smoothed regret and reduction to regression results in state-of-the-art online performance with computational cost independent of the action set: unfortunately, the resulting data exhaust does not have well-defined importance-weights. This frustrates the execution of downstream data science processes such as offline model selection. In this paper we describe an online algorithm with an equivalent smoothed regret guarantee, but which generates well-defined importance weights: in exchange, the online computational cost increases, but only to order smoothness (i.e., still independent of the action set). This removes a key obstacle to adoption of smoothed regret in production scenarios.

paragraphs: Contextual bandit algorithms choose actions using the current context and learn from the outcomes. With infinitely many possible actions, a useful approach combines smoothed regret guarantees with reduction to regression, keeping computation independent of action-set size. The paper identifies a practical problem with the resulting interaction data: it lacks well-defined importance weights needed by downstream analyses such as offline model selection.

The proposed online algorithm preserves an equivalent smoothed regret guarantee while generating data with well-defined importance weights. The contribution therefore concerns both the quality of online decisions and the usability of the records those decisions produce. It makes data reuse part of the algorithm's design, rather than treating logged interactions as an automatically adequate resource for later analysis.

This improvement has a computational tradeoff. Online cost increases to an order governed by smoothness, but remains independent of the action set. The result removes a specific obstacle to using smoothed-regret methods in production: obtaining strong online guarantees need not leave subsequent offline model-selection processes without the importance weights they require.
summary.tldr: An infinite-action contextual bandit algorithm preserves smoothed regret guarantees while producing importance-weighted data usable for downstream analysis.

title: Infinite Action Contextual Bandits with Reusable Data Exhaust

abstract: We introduce a modality-agnostic neural compression algorithm based on a functional view of data and parameterised as an Implicit Neural Representation (INR). Bridging the gap between latent coding and sparsity, we obtain compact latent representations non-linearly mapped to a soft gating mechanism. This allows the specialisation of a shared INR network to each data item through subnetwork selection. After obtaining a dataset of such latent representations, we directly optimise the rate/distortion trade-off in a modality-agnostic space using neural compression. Variational Compression of Implicit Neural Representations (VC-INR) shows improved performance given the same representational capacity pre quantisation while also outperforming previous quantisation schemes used for other INR techniques.Our experiments demonstrate strong results over a large set of diverse modalities using the same algorithm without any modality-specific inductive biases. We show results on images, climate data, 3D shapes and scenes as well as audio and video, introducing VC-INR as the first INR-based method to outperform codecs as well-known and diverse as JPEG 2000, MP3 and AVC/HEVC on their respective modalities.

paragraphs: VC-INR compresses data by treating each item as a function represented by an implicit neural network. Its aim is to use a common compression method across different kinds of data. Rather than assigning an entirely separate network to every item, it specializes a shared network through compact latent representations.

Those latent representations are mapped nonlinearly into soft gates that select subnetworks. This connects compact coding with sparsity: the code determines which parts of the shared representation serve a particular item. After learning these codes, the method applies neural compression directly in their shared space, optimizing the trade-off between storage rate and reconstruction distortion.

The authors report better performance at equal representational capacity before quantization, along with improvements over earlier INR quantization schemes. Experiments span images, climate data, 3D shapes and scenes, audio, and video without modality-specific inductive biases. The reported comparisons include outperforming JPEG 2000, MP3, and AVC/HEVC on their respective modalities, demonstrating the breadth of the approach in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: VC-INR uses compact codes to specialize and compress shared neural representations across diverse data modalities.

title: Modality-Agnostic Variational Compression of Implicit Neural Representations

abstract: Global modeling-based image restoration frameworks have become popular. However, they often require a high memory footprint and do not consider task-specific degradation. Our work presents an alternative approach to global modeling that is more efficient for image restoration. The key insights which motivate our study are two-fold: 1) Fourier transform is capable of disentangling image degradation and content component to a certain extent, serving as the image degradation prior, and 2) Fourier domain innately embraces global properties, where each pixel in the Fourier space is involved with all spatial pixels. While adhering to the “spatial interaction + channel evolution” rule of previous studies, we customize the core designs with Fourier spatial interaction modeling and Fourier channel evolution. Our paradigm, Fourmer, achieves competitive performance on common image restoration tasks such as image de-raining, image enhancement, image dehazing, and guided image super-resolution, while requiring fewer computational resources. The code for Fourmer will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: Image restoration can benefit from modeling relationships across an entire image, but existing global approaches often consume substantial memory and overlook the particular degradation being corrected. Fourmer develops a more efficient way to model this global information. Its design draws on two properties of the Fourier representation of images.

First, Fourier transforms can separate degradation from image content to some extent, providing useful prior information about the restoration problem. Second, each location in Fourier space involves information from all spatial pixels, making global interactions inherent to the representation. The separation claim is partial: the motivation does not require degradation and content to become perfectly isolated.

Fourmer retains a design organized around spatial interaction and channel evolution, but implements both through customized Fourier-based components. The authors report competitive performance on image de-raining, enhancement, dehazing, and guided super-resolution while using fewer computational resources. These results suggest that Fourier-domain structure can support useful global restoration without the resource demands of the global modeling approaches considered in the paper.
summary.tldr: Fourmer uses Fourier-based spatial and channel modeling to achieve competitive image restoration with fewer computational resources.

title: Fourmer: An Efficient Global Modeling Paradigm for Image Restoration

abstract: We study regret minimization for reinforcement learning (RL) in Latent Markov Decision Processes (LMDPs) with context in hindsight. We design a novel model-based algorithmic framework which can be instantiated with both a model-optimistic and a value-optimistic solver. We prove an $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{\mathsf{Var}^\star M \Gamma S A K})$ regret bound where $\tilde{O}$ hides logarithm factors, $M$ is the number of contexts, $S$ is the number of states, $A$ is the number of actions, $K$ is the number of episodes, $\Gamma \le S$ is the maximum transition degree of any state-action pair, and $\mathsf{Var}^\star$ is a variance quantity describing the determinism of the LMDP. The regret bound only scales logarithmically with the planning horizon, thus yielding the first (nearly) horizon-free regret bound for LMDP. This is also the first problem-dependent regret bound for LMDP. Key in our proof is an analysis of the total variance of alpha vectors (a generalization of value functions), which is handled with a truncation method. We complement our positive result with a novel $\Omega(\sqrt{\mathsf{Var}^\star M S A K})$ regret lower bound with $\Gamma = 2$, which shows our upper bound minimax optimal when $\Gamma$ is a constant for the class of variance-bounded LMDPs. Our lower bound relies on new constructions of hard instances and an argument inspired by the symmetrization technique from theoretical computer science, both of which are technically different from existing lower bound proof for MDPs, and thus can be of independent interest.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning in latent Markov decision processes with context available in hindsight. It asks how much regret a learner accumulates and how that cost depends on environmental variability and planning length. The authors develop a model-based framework that supports both model-optimistic and value-optimistic solvers.

Their regret bound depends on a variance quantity describing how deterministic the environment is, together with the numbers of contexts, states, actions, episodes, and the maximum transition degree. Crucially, planning horizon appears only through logarithmic factors. The result therefore identifies both an achievable learning guarantee and a matching difficulty scale under that stated restriction.
summary.tldr: A model-based framework achieves variance-dependent regret with only logarithmic horizon dependence for latent decision processes with context in hindsight.

title: Horizon-Free and Variance-Dependent Reinforcement Learning for Latent Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Deep neural networks have been found to be vulnerable to adversarial noise. Recent works show that exploring the impact of adversarial noise on intrinsic components of data can help improve adversarial robustness. However, the pattern closely related to human perception has not been deeply studied. In this paper, inspired by the cognitive science, we investigate the interference of adversarial noise from the perspective of image phase, and find ordinarily-trained models lack enough robustness against phase-level perturbations. Motivated by this, we propose a joint adversarial defense method: a phase-level adversarial training mechanism to enhance the adversarial robustness on the phase pattern; an amplitude-based pre-processing operation to mitigate the adversarial perturbation in the amplitude pattern. Experimental results show that the proposed method can significantly improve the robust accuracy against multiple attacks and even adaptive attacks. In addition, ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of our defense strategy.
originalAbstract: Deep neural networks have been found to be vulnerable to adversarial noise. Recent works show that exploring the impact of adversarial noise on intrinsic components of data can help improve adversarial robustness. However, the pattern closely related to human perception has not been deeply studied. In this paper, inspired by the cognitive science, we investigate the interference of adversarial noise from the perspective of image phase, and find ordinarily-trained models lack enough robustness against phase-level perturbations. Motivated by this, we propose a joint adversarial defense method: a phase-level adversarial training mechanism to enhance the adversarial robustness on the phase pattern; an amplitude-based pre-processing operation to mitigate the adversarial perturbation in the amplitude pattern. Experimental results show that the proposed method can significantly improve the robust accuracy against multiple attacks and even adaptive attacks. In addition, ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of our defense strategy.

paragraphs: Adversarial noise can disrupt a neural network even when the changes are subtle. This paper investigates that disruption through image phase, motivated by its relationship to human perception. The authors find that ordinarily trained models have insufficient robustness to perturbations at the phase level, identifying a particular weakness within image representations.

Their defense combines two mechanisms aimed at different components of the image. Phase-level adversarial training strengthens robustness to changes in phase patterns. An amplitude-based preprocessing operation mitigates perturbations in amplitude patterns. The design links the observed phase vulnerability to a training intervention while also addressing the other image component through preprocessing.

Experiments report substantial improvements in robust accuracy against multiple attacks, including adaptive attacks. Ablation studies further support the effectiveness of the defense strategy. The contribution is both an investigation of where adversarial interference occurs and a joint response based on that investigation. Its reported success concerns the attacks evaluated, demonstrating the usefulness of considering phase and amplitude separately when building the defense.
summary.tldr: Combining phase-level adversarial training with amplitude-based preprocessing improves robust accuracy against the evaluated attacks, including adaptive attacks.

title: Phase-aware Adversarial Defense for Improving Adversarial Robustness

abstract: Zhang et al. (ICML 2021, PLMR 139, pp. 12447–12457) introduced probabilistic generating circuits (PGCs) as a probabilistic model to unify probabilistic circuits (PCs) and determinantal point processes (DPPs). At a first glance, PGCs store a distribution in a very different way, they compute the probability generating polynomial instead of the probability mass function and it seems that this is the main reason why PGCs are more powerful than PCs or DPPs. However, PGCs also allow for negative weights, whereas classical PCs assume that all weights are nonnegative. One main insight of this work is that the negative weights are the cause for the power of PGCs and not the different representation. PGCs are PCs in disguise: we show how to transform any PGC on binary variables into a PC with negative weights with only polynomial blowup. PGCs were defined by Zhang et al. only for binary random variables. As our second main result, we show that there is a good reason for this: we prove that PGCs for categorical variables with larger image size do not support tractable marginalization unless NP=P. On the other hand, we show that we can model categorical variables with larger image size as PC with negative weights computing set-multilinear polynomials. These allow for tractable marginalization. In this sense, PCs with negative weights strictly subsume PGCs.

paragraphs: Probabilistic generating circuits represent distributions through probability-generating polynomials. They were introduced to unify probabilistic circuits and determinantal point processes. Their apparent additional power might seem to come from this representation. This paper identifies a different source: generating circuits permit negative weights, whereas classical probabilistic circuits require nonnegative weights.

The authors show that any generating circuit over binary variables can be converted into a probabilistic circuit with negative weights, with only polynomial growth in size. This establishes that the alternative polynomial representation is not the essential source of expressiveness in that setting. Allowing signed weights is the key distinction.

The paper also examines variables with more than two possible values. It proves that extending generating circuits to these categorical variables does not preserve tractable marginalization unless NP equals P. In contrast, probabilistic circuits with negative weights that compute set-multilinear polynomials can represent such variables while retaining tractable marginalization. In this sense, the signed probabilistic-circuit framework strictly contains the generating-circuit framework and clarifies its computational boundary.
summary.tldr: Negative weights explain generating circuits’ expressive power, while signed probabilistic circuits extend further with tractable categorical marginalization.

title: Probabilistic Generating Circuits - Demystified

abstract: Identification and analysis of symmetrical patterns in the natural world have led to significant discoveries across various scientific fields, such as the formulation of gravitational laws in physics and advancements in the study of chemical structures. In this paper, we focus on exploiting Euclidean symmetries inherent in certain cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems and prevalent in many applications. We begin by formally characterizing a subclass of Markov games with a general notion of symmetries that admits the existence of symmetric optimal values and policies. Motivated by these properties, we design neural network architectures with symmetric constraints embedded as an inductive bias for multi-agent actor-critic methods. This inductive bias results in superior performance in various cooperative MARL benchmarks and impressive generalization capabilities such as zero-shot learning and transfer learning in unseen scenarios with repeated symmetric patterns.

paragraphs: Some cooperative multi-agent problems contain Euclidean symmetries: different spatial arrangements can share the same underlying decision structure. This paper investigates how to exploit those symmetries in reinforcement learning. The aim is to make the model’s architecture reflect relationships already present in the task, giving learning a useful structural starting point.

The authors first characterize a subclass of Markov games with symmetries that admit symmetric optimal values and policies. This theoretical result motivates actor-critic neural networks with symmetry constraints embedded in their design. The constraints act as an inductive bias, guiding the networks toward behavior consistent with the relevant transformations.

Across cooperative multi-agent benchmarks, the resulting methods achieve better performance and strong generalization, including zero-shot and transfer learning in unseen scenarios with repeated symmetric patterns. The connection between theory and architecture is central: the symmetry constraints are motivated by properties established for a particular game class. The reported transfer benefits concern situations where those recurring patterns provide reusable structure for the agents’ decisions.
summary.tldr: Symmetry-constrained actor-critic networks improve cooperative multi-agent learning and transfer in settings with recurring Euclidean structure.

title: $\rm E(3)$-Equivariant Actor-Critic Methods for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Many algorithms have been recently proposed for causal machine learning. Yet, there is little to no theory on their quality, especially considering finite samples. In this work, we propose a theory based on generalization bounds that provides such guarantees. By introducing a novel change-of-measure inequality, we are able to tightly bound the model loss in terms of the deviation of the treatment propensities over the population, which we show can be empirically limited. Our theory is fully rigorous and holds even in the face of hidden confounding and violations of positivity. We demonstrate our bounds on semi-synthetic and real data, showcasing their remarkable tightness and practical utility.

In this work, we propose a theory based on generalization bounds that provides such guarantees. By introducing a novel change-of-measure inequality, we are able to tightly bound the model loss in terms of the deviation of the treatment propensities over the population, which we show can be empirically limited. Our theory is fully rigorous and holds even in the face of hidden confounding and violations of positivity. We demonstrate our bounds on semi-synthetic and real data, showcasing their remarkable tightness and practical utility.

paragraphs: Causal machine learning needs guarantees about how well models perform with finite data, not just methods for fitting them. This paper develops generalization bounds for causal regression to address that need. The goal is to place a rigorous upper bound on model loss while accounting for how treatment assignment varies across the population.

The technical contribution is a new change-of-measure inequality. It allows the authors to bound loss in terms of deviations in treatment propensities, which describe the chances of receiving treatment. They also show that these deviations can be bounded empirically. This links the theoretical guarantee to a quantity that can be constrained using data.

The theory remains valid in the presence of hidden confounding and violations of positivity, two difficulties explicitly addressed by the paper. The authors demonstrate the bounds on semi-synthetic and real datasets and report tight, practically useful results. The contribution is therefore a way to quantify model loss under challenging causal conditions; the stated guarantees concern these bounds rather than an assertion that those conditions disappear.
summary.tldr: New generalization bounds quantify causal regression loss and remain valid with hidden confounding and positivity violations.

title: Generalization Bounds for Causal Regression: Insights, Guarantees and Sensitivity Analysis

abstract: Algorithmic decision-making in practice must be fair for legal, ethical, and societal reasons. To achieve this, prior research has contributed various approaches that ensure fairness in machine learning predictions, while comparatively little effort has focused on fairness in decision-making, specifically off-policy learning. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for fair off-policy learning: we learn decision rules from observational data under different notions of fairness, where we explicitly assume that observational data were collected under a different – potentially discriminatory – behavioral policy. Importantly, our framework applies to different fairness notions for off-policy learning, where fairness is formalized based on actions or policy values. As our main contribution, we propose a neural network-based framework to learn optimal policies under different fairness notions. We further provide theoretical guarantees in the form of generalization bounds for the finite-sample version of our framework. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through extensive numerical experiments using both simulated and real-world data. Altogether, our work enables algorithmic decision-making in a wide array of practical applications where fairness must be ensured.

paragraphs: This paper studies fairness when learning a decision policy from observational records. The data are explicitly assumed to come from a different behavioral policy, which may itself be discriminatory. That setting matters because learning a new decision rule involves evidence shaped by earlier decisions, rather than observations collected under the policy now being developed.

The proposed neural network framework learns optimal policies under different definitions of fairness. Those definitions can concern the actions a policy takes or the values associated with the policy. This distinction lets the framework address fairness at different points in decision-making, rather than treating fairness solely as a property of predictions.

The authors provide generalization bounds for the finite-sample framework and evaluate it using simulated and real-world data. The experiments demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness in the studied settings, while the theoretical results address how learning from a finite dataset relates to broader performance. Together, these contributions connect explicit fairness requirements with policy learning from records produced by a potentially discriminatory predecessor.
summary.tldr: A neural framework learns policies under action-based or value-based fairness requirements from data collected by a potentially discriminatory policy.

title: Fair Off-Policy Learning from Observational Data

abstract: Distribution shifts pose significant challenges for model calibration and model selection tasks in the unsupervised domain adaptation problem—a scenario where the goal is to perform well in a distribution shifted domain without labels. In this work, we tackle difficulties coming from distribution shifts by developing a novel importance weighted group accuracy estimator. Specifically, we present a new perspective of addressing the model calibration and model selection tasks by estimating the group accuracy. Then, we formulate an optimization problem for finding an importance weight that leads to an accurate group accuracy estimation with theoretical analyses. Our extensive experiments show that our approach improves state-of-the-art performances by 22% in the model calibration task and 14% in the model selection task.

In this work, we tackle difficulties coming from distribution shifts by developing a novel importance weighted group accuracy estimator. paragraphs: When a model moves to a different data distribution, its confidence and its relative standing against other models can become unreliable. Unsupervised domain adaptation makes this especially difficult because the target domain has no labels. This paper addresses both confidence calibration and model selection through a shared question: how accurately does the model perform on groups of examples?

The proposed method estimates group accuracy using importance weights. These weights account for distribution differences when forming the estimate. The authors formulate an optimization problem to find weights that produce accurate group accuracy estimates and provide theoretical analysis of that formulation. Group accuracy thus becomes the common quantity supporting two otherwise distinct evaluation tasks.

In extensive experiments, the authors report improvements over state-of-the-art performance of 22% for calibration and 14% for model selection. These are the improvements stated for the evaluated tasks, rather than percentage-point gains in classification accuracy. The results suggest that better estimation of group-level correctness can help both adjust confidence and choose models under distribution shift without target labels.
summary.tldr: Importance-weighted estimates of group accuracy improve calibration and model selection when target-domain labels are unavailable.

title: IW-GAE: Importance weighted group accuracy estimation for improved calibration and model selection in unsupervised domain adaptation

abstract: We introduce Cell2Sentence (C2S), a novel method to directly adapt large language models to a biological context, specifically single-cell transcriptomics. By transforming gene expression data into "cell sentences," C2S bridges the gap between natural language processing and biology. We demonstrate cell sentences enable the fine-tuning of language models for diverse tasks in biology, including cell generation, complex cell-type annotation, and direct data-driven text generation. Our experiments reveal that GPT-2, when fine-tuned with C2S, can generate biologically valid cells based on cell type inputs, and accurately predict cell types from cell sentences. This illustrates that language models, through C2S fine-tuning, can acquire a significant understanding of single-cell biology while maintaining robust text generation capabilities. C2S offers a flexible, accessible framework to integrate natural language processing with transcriptomics, utilizing existing models and libraries for a wide range of biological applications.

paragraphs: Cell2Sentence adapts language models to single-cell transcriptomics by converting gene expression measurements into sequences called cell sentences. This representation gives biological data a form that language models can use directly during fine-tuning. The central idea is to connect existing language-model machinery with tasks involving the molecular characteristics of individual cells.

The authors demonstrate this approach on several tasks, including generating cell representations, assigning complex cell-type labels, and producing text directly from biological data. In their experiments, GPT-2 fine-tuned with Cell2Sentence generates biologically valid cells when given cell-type inputs and accurately predicts cell types from cell sentences. These are complementary uses of the same biological representation.

The findings suggest that this fine-tuning approach can teach a language model substantial information about single-cell biology while preserving strong text generation abilities. Its practical appeal is the ability to use existing models and libraries for biological applications. The paper therefore presents a flexible representation framework that connects biological prediction and generation with natural-language capabilities.
summary.tldr: Cell2Sentence turns gene expression data into sequences that let language models learn cell-type prediction, cell generation, and biology-related text generation.

title: Cell2Sentence: Teaching Large Language Models the Language of Biology

abstract: Transfer learning is a critical part of real-world machine learning deployments and has been extensively studied in experimental works with overparameterized neural networks. However, even in the simplest setting of linear regression a notable gap still exists in the theoretical understanding of transfer learning. In-distribution research on high-dimensional linear regression has led to the identification of a phenomenon known as benign overfitting, in which linear interpolators overfit to noisy training labels and yet still generalize well. This behavior occurs under specific conditions on the source covariance matrix and input data dimension. Therefore, it is natural to wonder how such high-dimensional linear models behave under transfer learning. We prove the first non-asymptotic excess risk bounds for benignly-overfit linear interpolators in the transfer learning setting. From our analysis, we propose a taxonomy of beneficial and malignant covariate shifts based on the degree of overparameterization. We follow our analysis with empirical studies that show these beneficial and malignant covariate shifts for linear interpolators on real image data, and for fully-connected neural networks in settings where the input data dimension is larger than the training sample size.

paragraphs: A high-dimensional linear model can fit noisy training labels exactly and still predict well, a phenomenon called benign overfitting. This behavior depends on conditions involving the source data's covariance and dimensionality. The paper asks what happens when such a model is transferred to inputs with a different distribution.

The authors prove non-asymptotic excess-risk bounds for benignly overfit linear interpolators under transfer learning. These bounds address finite settings rather than relying only on limiting behavior. Their analysis leads to a classification of beneficial and malignant covariate shifts, with the distinction depending on the degree of overparameterization.

Empirical studies illustrate both kinds of shift for linear interpolators using real image data. The authors also observe them for fully connected neural networks when input dimensionality exceeds the number of training examples. The result helps explain why a change in input distribution can have different consequences for models that fit their training data perfectly. The theoretical guarantees concern linear interpolators, while the neural-network findings provide a separate empirical extension.
summary.tldr: Finite-sample theory identifies how covariate shifts can help or harm benignly overfit linear models depending on overparameterization.

title: Minimum-Norm Interpolation Under Covariate Shift

abstract: It has long been challenging to recover the underlying dynamic 3D scene representations from a monocular RGB video. Existing works formulate this problem into finding a single most plausible solution by adding various constraints such as depth priors and strong geometry constraints, ignoring the fact that there could be infinitely many 3D scene representations corresponding to a single dynamic video. In this paper, we aim to learn all plausible 3D scene configurations that match the input video, instead of just inferring a specific one. To achieve this ambitious goal, we introduce a new framework, called OSN. The key to our approach is a simple yet innovative object scale network together with a joint optimization module to learn an accurate scale range for every dynamic 3D object. This allows us to sample as many faithful 3D scene configurations as possible. Extensive experiments show that our method surpasses all baselines and achieves superior accuracy in dynamic novel view synthesis on multiple synthetic and real-world datasets. Most notably, our method demonstrates a clear advantage in learning fine-grained 3D scene geometry.

paragraphs: A single-camera video can be consistent with infinitely many underlying dynamic three-dimensional scenes. Methods that seek one plausible reconstruction typically add depth or geometry constraints to select a solution. OSN instead aims to represent the range of plausible scene configurations that agree with the observed video.

The central mechanism combines an object scale network with joint optimization to learn a scale range for each moving three-dimensional object. These ranges allow the framework to sample many configurations consistent with the input. Treating scale as a range makes ambiguity part of the representation, rather than forcing the method to commit immediately to a single configuration.

Experiments on multiple synthetic and real-world datasets report better dynamic novel-view synthesis accuracy than all evaluated baselines. The authors particularly emphasize improved recovery of fine-grained scene geometry. These findings support the usefulness of representing alternative configurations for reconstruction and rendering. Learning all plausible scenes is the framework’s stated goal; the reported mechanism enables sampling many faithful configurations rather than establishing exhaustive recovery of every possibility.
summary.tldr: OSN learns object-scale ranges to sample multiple plausible dynamic 3D scenes from one video, improving novel-view synthesis and fine geometry in evaluations.

title: OSN: Infinite Representations of Dynamic 3D Scenes from Monocular Videos

abstract: Among various acquisition functions (AFs) in Bayesian optimization (BO), Gaussian process upper confidence bound (GP-UCB) and Thompson sampling (TS) are well-known options with established theoretical properties regarding Bayesian cumulative regret (BCR). Recently, it has been shown that a randomized variant of GP-UCB achieves a tighter BCR bound compared with GP-UCB, which we call the tighter BCR bound for brevity. Inspired by this study, this paper first shows that TS achieves the tighter BCR bound. On the other hand, GP-UCB and TS often practically suffer from manual hyperparameter tuning and over-exploration issues, respectively. Therefore, we analyze yet another AF called a probability of improvement from the maximum of a sample path (PIMS). We show that PIMS achieves the tighter BCR bound and avoids the hyperparameter tuning, unlike GP-UCB. Furthermore, we demonstrate a wide range of experiments, focusing on the effectiveness of PIMS that mitigates the practical issues of GP-UCB and TS.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization uses an acquisition function to choose which candidate to evaluate next. This paper studies the theoretical and practical behavior of several such rules, focusing on Bayesian cumulative regret. A recent randomized version of Gaussian process upper confidence bound had obtained a tighter regret bound, motivating the authors to investigate whether other approaches achieve it.

They first prove that Thompson sampling also satisfies this tighter bound. They then analyze PIMS, an acquisition function based on probability of improvement relative to the maximum of a sampled function path. PIMS receives the same tighter regret guarantee and avoids the hyperparameter tuning associated with the GP-UCB acquisition rule.

The practical motivation is that GP-UCB can require manual tuning, while Thompson sampling can explore excessively. A broad set of experiments supports PIMS as a way to mitigate these issues. The paper therefore contributes both a stronger analysis of an established sampling method and a theoretically supported alternative whose evaluation addresses practical difficulties in selecting where to sample next.
summary.tldr: Thompson sampling and PIMS receive tighter Bayesian regret bounds, while PIMS also reduces acquisition-rule tuning and mitigates over-exploration in experiments.

title: Posterior Sampling-Based Bayesian Optimization with Tighter Bayesian Regret Bounds

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables multiple devices to collaboratively train a shared model while ensuring data privacy. The selection of participating devices in each training round critically affects both the model performance and training efficiency, especially given the vast heterogeneity in training capabilities and data distribution across devices. To deal with these challenges, we introduce a novel device selection solution called FedRank, which is based on an end-to-end, ranking-based model that is pre-trained by imitation learning against state-of-the-art analytical approaches. It not only considers data and system heterogeneity at runtime but also adaptively and efficiently chooses the most suitable clients for model training. Specifically, FedRank views client selection in FL as a ranking problem and employs a pairwise training strategy for the smart selection process. Additionally, an imitation learning-based approach is designed to counteract the cold-start issues often seen in state-of-the-art learning-based approaches. Experimental results reveal that FedRank boosts model accuracy by 5.2% to 56.9%, accelerates the training convergence up to $2.01 \times$ and saves the energy consumption up to 40.1%.

paragraphs: Federated learning coordinates multiple devices to train a shared model. Choosing which devices participate in each round affects both model quality and efficiency because devices differ in computing capabilities and data distributions. FedRank addresses this selection problem by learning how to rank potential participants.

The method uses an end-to-end ranking model trained with pairwise comparisons. At runtime, it considers both data differences and system differences to adaptively choose suitable clients. These ranges and maxima describe the evaluated outcomes rather than guaranteed gains for every deployment. The approach matters because participant selection becomes a learned ranking decision that can account for heterogeneous devices, while imitation provides guidance before the selector has developed its own experience.
summary.tldr: FedRank uses imitation-pretrained client ranking to improve federated-learning accuracy, convergence speed, and energy use in experiments.

title: Ranking-based Client Imitation Selection for Efficient Federated Learning

abstract: In real-world scenarios, the application of reinforcement learning is significantly challenged by complex non-stationarity. Most existing methods attempt to model changes in the environment explicitly, often requiring impractical prior knowledge of environments. In this paper, we propose a new perspective, positing that non-stationarity can propagate and accumulate through complex causal relationships during state transitions, thereby compounding its sophistication and affecting policy learning. We believe that this challenge can be more effectively addressed by implicitly tracing the causal origin of non-stationarity. To this end, we introduce the Causal-Origin REPresentation (COREP) algorithm. COREP primarily employs a guided updating mechanism to learn a stable graph representation for the state, termed as causal-origin representation. By leveraging this representation, the learned policy exhibits impressive resilience to non-stationarity. We supplement our approach with a theoretical analysis grounded in the causal interpretation for non-stationary reinforcement learning, advocating for the validity of the causal-origin representation. Experimental results further demonstrate the superior performance of COREP over existing methods in tackling non-stationarity problems. The code is available at https://github.com/PKU-RL/COREP.

The Causal-Origin REPresentation algorithm, or COREP, uses a guided updating mechanism to learn a stable graph representation of the state. The representation is intended to implicitly trace the causal origin of non-stationarity. Policy learning then uses this representation, with the aim of maintaining useful behavior despite changes in the environment.

The authors provide theoretical analysis grounded in their causal interpretation and report experimental performance above existing methods on the non-stationarity problems evaluated. These findings support the use of causal-origin representations for resilient policy learning. The contribution combines a proposed explanation of how environmental change becomes complex with an algorithm that acts on that explanation, shifting attention toward learning a stable state representation.
summary.tldr: COREP learns a stable graph representation intended to trace the causal origins of environmental change and improve reinforcement-learning resilience.

title: Tackling Non-Stationarity in Reinforcement Learning via Causal-Origin Representation

abstract: While language models (LMs) have shown potential across a range of decision-making tasks, their reliance on simple acting processes limits their broad deployment as autonomous agents. In this paper, we introduce Language Agent Tree Search (LATS) – the first general framework that synergizes the capabilities of LMs in reasoning, acting, and planning. By leveraging the in-context learning ability of LMs, we integrate Monte Carlo Tree Search into LATS to enable LMs as agents, along with LM-powered value functions and self-reflections for proficient exploration and enhanced decision-making. A key feature of our approach is the incorporation of an environment for external feedback, which offers a more deliberate and adaptive problem-solving mechanism that surpasses the constraints of existing techniques. Our experimental evaluation across diverse domains, including programming, interactive question-answering (QA), web navigation, and math, validates the effectiveness and generality of LATS in decision-making while maintaining competitive or improved reasoning performance. Notably, LATS achieves state-of-the-art pass@1 accuracy (92.7%) for programming on HumanEval with GPT-4 and demonstrates gradient-free performance (average score of 75.9) comparable to gradient-based fine-tuning for web navigation on WebShop with GPT-3.5. Code can be found at https://github.com/lapisrocks/LanguageAgentTreeSearch

Language-model-powered value functions help assess alternatives, while self-reflections contribute to exploration and decision-making. An external environment supplies feedback, giving the agent information beyond its own proposed reasoning. These components let the search adapt as it considers actions and their outcomes, connecting internal evaluation with responses from the task environment.

summary.tldr: LATS combines tree search, language-model evaluation, self-reflection, and environmental feedback to improve agent decision-making.

title: Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning in Language Models

abstract: Few-shot class-incremental learning (FSCIL) is proposed to continually learn from novel classes with only a few samples after the (pre-)training on base classes with sufficient data. However, this remains a challenge. In contrast, humans can easily recognize novel classes with a few samples. Cognitive science demonstrates that an important component of such human capability is compositional learning. This involves identifying visual primitives from learned knowledge and then composing new concepts using these transferred primitives, making incremental learning both effective and interpretable. To imitate human compositional learning, we propose a cognitive-inspired method for the FSCIL task. We define and build a compositional model based on set similarities, and then equip it with a primitive composition module and a primitive reuse module. In the primitive composition module, we propose to utilize the Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) similarity to approximate the similarity between primitive sets, allowing the training and evaluation based on primitive compositions. In the primitive reuse module, we enhance primitive reusability by classifying inputs based on primitives replaced with the closest primitives from other classes. Experiments on three datasets validate our method, showing it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods with improved interpretability. Our code is available at https://github.com/Zoilsen/Comp-FSCIL.

paragraphs: Few-shot class-incremental learning asks a model to keep learning new categories from only a handful of examples after initially training on well-represented categories. This paper approaches the problem through composition: previously learned visual primitives can be reused and combined to describe new categories. The motivation comes from accounts of how people assemble new concepts from familiar components.

The proposed model compares sets of primitives and contains two complementary modules. The composition module uses Centered Kernel Alignment to approximate similarity between primitive sets, allowing training and evaluation to operate on combinations of components. The reuse module classifies inputs after replacing primitives with the closest primitives from other classes, encouraging components to remain useful across category boundaries.

Experiments on three datasets show improvements over the state-of-the-art methods considered, along with improved interpretability. The approach matters because it gives learning from scarce examples an explicit structure: new categories can draw on reusable visual knowledge instead of depending entirely on their own limited samples. Its interpretation of categories as compositions also provides a clearer account of how previously learned information contributes to new recognition decisions.
summary.tldr: A compositional model reuses visual primitives to learn new classes from few examples, improving reported accuracy and interpretability.

title: Compositional Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning

abstract: Digital twins are models of real-world systems that can simulate their dynamics in response to potential actions. In complex settings, the state and action variables, and available data and knowledge relevant to a system can constantly change, requiring digital twins to continuously update with these changes to remain relevant. Current approaches struggle in this regard, as they require fixed, well-defined modelling environments, and they cannot adapt to novel variables without re-designs, or incorporate new information without re-training. To address this, we frame digital twinning as an in-context learning problem using large language models, enabling seamless updates to the twin at inference time. We develop CALM-DT, a Context-Adaptive Language Model-based Digital Twin that can accurately simulate across diverse state-action spaces using in-context learning alone by utilising fine-tuned encoders for sample retrieval. We empirically demonstrate CALM-DT’s competitive performance with existing digital twin approaches, and its unique ability to adapt to changes in its modelling environment without parameter updates.

paragraphs: A digital twin simulates how a real system responds to possible actions. Keeping that simulation relevant becomes difficult when the available variables, actions, data, or knowledge change. The paper addresses this changing environment, where conventional approaches can require redesign to handle new variables or retraining to incorporate new information.

The authors formulate digital twinning as in-context learning with a language model. Their system, CALM-DT, uses information supplied at inference time to simulate across different state and action spaces. Fine-tuned encoders retrieve samples for the model's context. This makes retrieval and context construction central to how the twin adapts, while the adaptation itself takes place without updating model parameters.

Experiments show competitive simulation performance compared with existing digital-twin approaches and demonstrate adaptation to changes in the modeling environment. The result supports a different way of maintaining a twin: updating the information available during inference can accommodate changes that would otherwise call for changes to the trained model. The method still uses fine-tuned retrieval encoders as part of its design.
summary.tldr: CALM-DT uses retrieved examples and language-model context to adapt digital twins to changing environments without parameter updates during adaptation.

title: Continuously Updating Digital Twins using Large Language Models

abstract: Neural ordinary differential equations (NODEs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in modeling time series. However, existing NODE- based methods often focus solely on the surface-level dynamics derived from observed states, which limits their ability to capture more complex underlying behaviors. To overcome this challenge, we propose KoNODE, a Koopman-driven NODE framework that explicitly models the evolution of ODE parameters over time to encode deep-level information. KoNODE captures the essential yet simple intrinsic linear dynamics that govern the surface dynamics by employing Koopman operators. Our framework operates at three hierarchical levels: the observed state dynamics, the parameter dynamics, and the Koopman linear dynamics, representing the fundamental driving rules of the state dynamics. The proposed approach offers significant improvements in two critical time series tasks: long-term prediction (enabled by the simple linear dynamics) and generalization to new data (driven by the evolving ODE parameters). We validate KoNODE through experiments on synthetic data from complex dynamic systems and real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in practical scenarios.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations model how a time series evolves continuously. Existing approaches often concentrate on dynamics visible in the observed states. KoNODE aims to capture a deeper source of changing behavior by explicitly allowing the parameters of the differential equation themselves to evolve over time.

The framework organizes this modeling into three levels: observed state dynamics, parameter dynamics, and underlying linear dynamics represented through Koopman operators. The evolving parameters encode information beyond the observed state trajectory, while the Koopman component captures simple intrinsic dynamics that drive the more complex behavior at the surface.

The paper links the linear dynamics to better long-term prediction and the evolving equation parameters to improved generalization to new data. Experiments on synthetic complex dynamical systems and real-world datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution is this hierarchical treatment of change: the model represents both how observed states move and how the parameters governing that movement evolve, using a linear dynamical component at the deepest level.
summary.tldr: KoNODE combines evolving differential-equation parameters with Koopman linear dynamics to improve long-term time-series prediction and generalization.

title: KoNODE: Koopman-Driven Neural Ordinary Differential Equations with Evolving Parameters for Time Series Analysis

abstract: Causal discovery, i.e., inferring underlying causal relationships from observational data, is highly challenging for AI systems. In a time series modeling context, traditional causal discovery methods mainly consider constrained scenarios with fully observed variables and/or data from stationary time-series. We develop a causal discovery approach to handle a wide class of nonstationary time series that are conditionally stationary, where the nonstationary behaviour is modeled as stationarity conditioned on a set of latent state variables. Named State-Dependent Causal Inference (SDCI), our approach is able to recover the underlying causal dependencies, with provable identifiablity for the state-dependent causal structures. Empirical experiments on nonlinear particle interaction data and gene regulatory networks demonstrate SDCI’s superior performance over baseline causal discovery methods. Improved results over non-causal RNNs on modeling NBA player movements demonstrate the potential of our method and motivate the use of causality-driven methods for forecasting.

paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships from observations becomes harder when a time series changes its behavior over time. Traditional approaches often restrict attention to fully observed variables, stationary data, or both. This paper studies a broader setting in which apparent nonstationarity can be explained by underlying, unobserved state variables.

Its key modeling condition is conditional stationarity: once the latent state is accounted for, the relevant behavior is stationary. State-Dependent Causal Inference, or SDCI, uses this structure to recover causal dependencies that depend on the state. The paper provides an identifiability result for these state-dependent causal structures, giving a theoretical basis for their recovery within the proposed setting.

Experiments on nonlinear particle interactions and gene regulatory networks report better causal discovery than baseline methods. On NBA player movements, SDCI also improves modeling results over non-causal recurrent neural networks. Together, these findings connect the structural recovery problem to forecasting, supporting the potential usefulness of causal modeling when changing behavior has the conditional structure the method assumes.
summary.tldr: SDCI discovers state-dependent causal relationships in nonstationary time series whose behavior becomes stationary when conditioned on latent states.

title: Causal Discovery from Conditionally Stationary Time Series

abstract: Recent breakthroughs in solving reasoning, math and coding problems with Large Language Models (LLMs) have been enabled by investing substantial computation budgets at inference time. Therefore, inference speed is one of the most critical properties of LLM architectures, and there is a growing need for LLMs that are efficient and fast at inference. Recently, LLMs built on the xLSTM architecture have emerged as a powerful alternative to Transformers, offering linear compute scaling with sequence length and constant memory usage, both highly desirable properties for efficient inference. However, such xLSTM-based LLMs have yet to be scaled to larger models and assessed and compared with respect to inference speed and efficiency. In this work, we introduce xLSTM 7B, a 7-billion-parameter LLM that combines xLSTM’s architectural benefits with targeted optimizations for fast and efficient inference. Our experiments demonstrate that xLSTM 7B achieves performance on downstream tasks comparable to other similar-sized LLMs, while providing significantly faster inference speeds and greater efficiency compared to Llama- and Mamba-based LLMs. These results establish xLSTM 7B as the fastest and most efficient 7B LLM, offering a solution for tasks that require large amounts of test-time computation. Our work highlights xLSTM’s potential as a foundational architecture for methods building on heavy use of LLM inference. Our model weights, model code and training code are open-source. Model: https://huggingface.co/NX-AI/xLSTM-7b Code: https://github.com/NX-AI/xlstm and https://github.com/NX-AI/xlstm-jax.

paragraphs: When language-model applications spend substantial computation during inference, generation speed becomes especially important. This paper introduces xLSTM 7B, a seven-billion-parameter recurrent language model designed for that setting. It combines the xLSTM architecture with targeted optimizations intended to make inference faster and more efficient at this model scale.

The architectural motivation is that xLSTM offers computation that scales linearly with sequence length and constant memory usage. The paper moves beyond those desirable scaling properties to assess a larger model’s actual performance and inference efficiency. This connects an architectural argument about resource use with measurements of a concrete language model.

The experiments report downstream performance comparable to other similarly sized language models, alongside substantially faster and more efficient inference than the Llama- and Mamba-based models compared. The authors characterize xLSTM 7B as the fastest and most efficient seven-billion-parameter model on the basis of these results. summary.tldr: xLSTM 7B combines recurrent architecture and inference optimizations, reporting comparable task performance with faster inference than the Llama- and Mamba-based models compared.

title: xLSTM 7B: A Recurrent LLM for Fast and Efficient Inference

abstract: Parallel data collection has redefined Reinforcement Learning (RL), unlocking unprecedented efficiency and powering breakthroughs in large-scale real-world applications. In this paradigm, $N$ identical agents operate in $N$ replicas of an environment simulator, accelerating data collection by a factor of $N$. A critical question arises: Does specializing the policies of the parallel agents hold the key to surpass the $N$ factor acceleration? In this paper, we introduce a novel learning framework that maximizes the entropy of collected data in a parallel setting. Our approach carefully balances the entropy of individual agents with inter-agent diversity, effectively minimizing redundancies. The latter idea is implemented with a centralized policy gradient method, which shows promise when evaluated empirically against systems of identical agents, as well as synergy with batch RL techniques that can exploit data diversity. Finally, we provide an original concentration analysis that shows faster rates for specialized parallel sampling distributions, which supports our methodology and may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Running reinforcement-learning agents in parallel speeds up data collection, but identical agents may repeatedly gather similar experiences. This paper asks whether specializing their policies can make parallel collection more useful than simply increasing the number of copies. The focus is on diversity in the collected data, alongside the volume of experience.

The proposed framework maximizes data entropy by balancing two considerations: how broadly each individual agent explores and how different the agents are from one another. A centralized policy-gradient method implements the diversity component. This balance aims to reduce redundant experiences while retaining exploration within each agent’s own behavior.

Empirical comparisons with identical-agent systems show promise, including compatibility with batch reinforcement-learning techniques that can benefit from diverse data. The authors also provide a concentration analysis showing faster rates for specialized parallel sampling distributions. That theoretical result supports the sampling strategy, while the experimental claims remain qualified: the abstract does not establish a universal speedup beyond the number of parallel agents.
summary.tldr: Specializing parallel agents to balance individual exploration and collective diversity shows promise for reducing redundant reinforcement-learning data.

title: Enhancing Diversity In Parallel Agents: A Maximum State Entropy Exploration Story

abstract: Wearable devices record physiological and behavioral signals that can improve health predictions. While foundation models are increasingly used for such predictions, they have been primarily applied to low-level sensor data, despite behavioral data often being more informative due to their alignment with physiologically relevant timescales and quantities. We develop foundation models of such behavioral signals using over 2.5B hours of wearable data from 162K individuals, systematically optimizing architectures and tokenization strategies for this unique dataset. Evaluated on 57 health-related tasks, our model shows strong performance across diverse real-world applications including individual-level classification and time-varying health state prediction. The model excels in behavior-driven tasks like sleep prediction, and improves further when combined with representations of raw sensor data. These results underscore the importance of tailoring foundation model design to wearables and demonstrate the potential to enable new health applications.
