paragraphs: Wearable devices provide both low-level sensor readings and information about behavior. The paper focuses on the latter, arguing that behavioral signals can be especially informative because their quantities and timescales often match processes relevant to physiology. This motivates building foundation models directly around behavior, expanding the information used for health prediction.

The authors develop these models using more than 2.5 billion hours of wearable data from 162,000 people. They systematically examine model architectures and tokenization strategies, meaning the ways the data is divided into units the model can process. This design work addresses the particular structure of wearable behavioral information rather than assuming any foundation model design will serve equally well.

Evaluation spans 57 health-related tasks, including classifying individuals and predicting health states that change over time. The model performs strongly across these applications and particularly well on behavior-driven tasks such as sleep prediction. Combining its representations with representations of raw sensor data improves performance further, suggesting that the two sources provide complementary information for the evaluated health predictions.
summary.tldr: Foundation models trained on wearable behavioral data perform strongly across health prediction tasks and benefit further from raw sensor representations.

title: Beyond Sensor Data: Foundation Models of Behavioral Data from Wearables Improve Health Predictions

abstract: While Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning for Large Language Models (LLMs), its performance often falls short of Full Fine-Tuning (Full FT). Current methods optimize LoRA by initializing with static singular value decomposition (SVD) subsets, leading to suboptimal leveraging of pre-trained knowledge. Another path for improving LoRA is incorporating a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture. However, weight misalignment and complex gradient dynamics make it challenging to adopt SVD prior to the LoRA MoE architecture. To mitigate these issues, we propose Great LoRA Mixture-of-Expert (GOAT), a framework that (1) adaptively integrates relevant priors using an SVD-structured MoE, and (2) aligns optimization with full fine-tuned MoE by deriving a theoretical scaling factor. We demonstrate that proper scaling, without modifying the architecture or training algorithms, boosts LoRA MoE’s efficiency and performance. Experiments across 25 datasets, including natural language understanding, commonsense reasoning, image classification, and natural language generation, demonstrate GOAT’s state-of-the-art performance, closing the gap with Full FT. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Facico/GOAT-PEFT

paragraphs: Low-Rank Adaptation reduces how many parameters must be trained when adapting a model, but its performance often trails full fine-tuning. Existing improvements use fixed subsets from singular value decomposition to initialize adaptation or introduce multiple experts. Combining those ideas is difficult because the weights and optimization dynamics can become misaligned.

GOAT addresses both the selection of prior knowledge and the alignment of training. It uses an SVD-structured mixture of experts to adaptively incorporate relevant information from pretrained weights. It also derives a theoretical scaling factor that aligns optimization with a fully fine-tuned mixture of experts. The paper shows that appropriate scaling can improve LoRA expert models without changing their architecture or training algorithms.

Experiments cover 25 datasets spanning language understanding, commonsense reasoning, image classification, and language generation. The authors report state-of-the-art performance and a closing of the gap with full fine-tuning. The findings emphasize that parameter-efficient adaptation depends on both which pretrained information is used and how the resulting updates are scaled.
summary.tldr: GOAT combines adaptive SVD-based experts with theoretically motivated scaling to improve LoRA and close its performance gap with full fine-tuning.

title: Make LoRA Great Again: Boosting LoRA with Adaptive Singular Values and Mixture-of-Experts Optimization Alignment

abstract: We consider the Euclidean bi-chromatic matching problem in the dynamic setting, where the goal is to efficiently process point insertions and deletions while maintaining a high-quality solution. Computing the minimum cost bi-chromatic matching is one of the core problems in geometric optimization that has found many applications, most notably in estimating Wasserstein distance between two distributions. In this work, we present the first fully dynamic algorithm for Euclidean bi-chromatic matching with sublinear update time. For any fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, our algorithm achieves $O(1/\varepsilon)$-approximation and handles updates in $O(n^{\varepsilon})$ time. Our experiments show that our algorithm enables effective monitoring of the distributional drift in the Wasserstein distance on real and synthetic data sets, while outperforming the runtime of baseline approximations by orders of magnitudes.

Computing the minimum cost bi-chromatic matching is one of the core problems in geometric optimization that has found many applications, most notably in estimating Wasserstein distance between two distributions. In this work, we present the first fully dynamic algorithm for Euclidean bi-chromatic matching with sublinear update time. For any fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, our algorithm achieves $O(1/\varepsilon)$-approximation and handles updates in $O(n^{\varepsilon})$ time. paragraphs: Euclidean bichromatic matching pairs points from two groups while seeking a low total matching cost. In a dynamic setting, points can be inserted or deleted, so the solution must be maintained as the underlying data change. This matters for applications such as estimating Wasserstein distance between distributions and monitoring how those distributions drift over time.

The paper presents the first fully dynamic algorithm for this problem with sublinear update time. For any fixed positive ε, it provides an O(1/ε) approximation with O(n^ε) time per update. The parameter exposes a tradeoff between the approximation guarantee and the exponent governing update cost; choosing ε below one gives the stated sublinear dependence on problem size.

Experiments on real and synthetic datasets show that the algorithm can effectively monitor distributional drift through Wasserstein distance. The reported runtime exceeds baseline approximation methods by orders of magnitude in speed. The contribution combines a theoretical update guarantee with evidence that maintaining an approximate matching can make changing distributions substantially cheaper to track.
summary.tldr: A fully dynamic approximate matching algorithm supports sublinear updates and fast Wasserstein-based distribution-drift monitoring.

title: Fully Dynamic Euclidean Bi-Chromatic Matching in Sublinear Update Time

abstract: Deep learning has been extensively employed as a powerful function approximator for modeling physics-based problems described by partial differential equations (PDEs). Despite their popularity, standard deep learning models often demand prohibitively large computational resources and yield limited accuracy when scaling to large-scale, high-dimensional physical problems. Their black-box nature further hinders their application in industrial problems where interpretability and high precision are critical. To overcome these challenges, this paper introduces Interpolating Neural Network-Tensor Decomposition (INN-TD), a scalable and interpretable framework that has the merits of both machine learning and finite element methods for modeling large-scale physical systems. title: Interpolating Neural Network-Tensor Decomposition (INN-TD): a scalable and interpretable approach for large-scale physics-based problems

abstract: Decoding with autoregressive language models traditionally occurs sequentially, generating one token after another. Recent attempts to introduce parallelism require a pre-determined structure in the generated content to implement parallel generation, such as by pattern-matching on bullet points. In this work, we present a new technique to automate parallel generation by dynamically exploiting the semantic independence of generation outputs to implement asynchronous decoding. We introduce an annotation language Pasta-Lang for language models to initiate asynchronous decoding at inference time. We also develop an accompanying Pasta-Lang interpreter that performs on-the-fly asynchronous decoding, effectively implementing parallel generation and speeding up inference. We present an instruction-finetuning dataset with Pasta-Lang-annotated responses for teaching LLMs to annotate semantic independence with Pasta-Lang as well as the methodology for creating the dataset. Our evaluation shows using the interpreter with a Pasta-Lang-equipped model achieves significant speedup while maintaining the same generation quality.

paragraphs: Autoregressive language models normally generate one token after another, limiting opportunities to produce multiple parts of a response simultaneously. This paper introduces a way for models to identify semantic independence within their own output and initiate parallel generation dynamically. It moves beyond approaches that require predetermined structures, such as recognizable bullet points, to organize parallel work.

The method introduces Pasta-Lang, an annotation language through which a model requests asynchronous decoding. An accompanying interpreter reads those annotations during inference and carries out the parallel generation. The model supplies information about which parts can be generated independently, while the interpreter turns those annotations into an execution strategy as generation proceeds.

To teach this behavior, the authors provide an instruction-fine-tuning dataset containing Pasta-Lang-annotated responses and describe how to create it. Evaluations report significant speedups with the interpreter and a Pasta-Lang-equipped model while preserving generation quality. The contribution therefore combines learned decisions about semantic independence with a runtime that can use those decisions to accelerate response production.
summary.tldr: Pasta-Lang teaches models to mark semantically independent output for asynchronous generation, delivering reported speedups without reducing generation quality.

title: Learning to Keep a Promise: Scaling Language Model Decoding Parallelism with Learned Asynchronous Decoding

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in contextual knowledge understanding. In this paper, we show for the first time that these concentrated massive values consistently emerge in specific regions of attention queries (Q) and keys (K) while not having such patterns in values (V) in various modern transformer-based LLMs. Through extensive experiments, we further demonstrate that these massive values play a critical role in interpreting contextual knowledge (i.e., knowledge obtained from the current context window) rather than in retrieving parametric knowledge stored within the model’s parameters. Our further investigation of quantization strategies reveals that ignoring these massive values leads to a pronounced drop in performance on tasks requiring rich contextual understanding, aligning with our analysis. Finally, we trace the emergence of concentrated massive values and find that such concentration is caused by Rotary Positional Encoding (RoPE) and it appears since very first layers. These findings shed new light on how Q and K operate in LLMs and offer practical insights for model design and optimization. The code is available at https://github.com/MingyuJ666/Rope_with_LLM.

paragraphs: This paper investigates unusually large numerical values concentrated in particular regions of attention queries and keys. The authors observe the pattern across various modern transformer language models, while finding no corresponding pattern in attention values. Here, the word values can mean numerical magnitudes or the separate V component of attention, so that distinction matters.

Experiments connect these large query and key entries to understanding knowledge supplied in the current context window, rather than retrieving knowledge stored in model parameters. The authors also examine quantization and report a pronounced performance decline on context-intensive tasks when quantization strategies ignore these entries. Their numerical size therefore corresponds to a consequential role in the evaluated models.

The investigation traces the concentration to Rotary Positional Encoding, or RoPE, and finds it beginning in the earliest layers. Together, the findings link a positional encoding mechanism, a specific attention pattern, and contextual understanding. They also provide a practical reason to account for these concentrated magnitudes when designing quantization strategies and optimizing models.
summary.tldr: Experiments link RoPE-induced large query and key values to contextual understanding and show that ignoring them during quantization harms context-intensive tasks.

title: Massive Values in Self-Attention Modules are the Key to Contextual Knowledge Understanding

abstract: Protein’s backbone flexibility is a crucial property that heavily influences its functionality. Recent work in the field of protein diffusion probabilistic modelling has leveraged Normal Mode Analysis (NMA) and, for the first time, introduced information about large scale protein motion into the generative process. However, obtaining molecules with both the desired dynamics and designable quality has proven challenging. In this work, we present NMA-tune, a new method that introduces the dynamics information to the protein design stage. NMA-tune uses a trainable component to condition the backbone generation on the lowest normal mode of oscillation. We implement NMA-tune as a plug-and-play extension to RFdiffusion, show that the proportion of samples with high quality structure and the desired dynamics is improved as compared to other methods without the trainable component, and we show the presence of the targeted modes in the Molecular Dynamics simulations.

paragraphs: A protein’s function depends partly on how its backbone can move, so designing a useful structure also involves its flexibility. Earlier protein diffusion models introduced large-scale motion information through Normal Mode Analysis. Obtaining generated backbones with both the desired dynamics and suitable structural quality, however, remained challenging.

NMA-tune introduces a trainable component that conditions backbone generation on the lowest normal mode of oscillation. This mode provides the motion information used during design. Implemented as a plug-and-play extension to RFdiffusion, the method makes dynamics conditioning a learned part of the generation process.

The authors report a higher proportion of samples that combine high-quality structures with the desired dynamics compared with methods lacking the trainable component. Molecular Dynamics simulations also show the targeted modes in generated structures. These results support using learned dynamics conditioning to improve the joint design objective: producing backbones with desirable structural properties and the intended motion behavior. The simulation findings provide additional evidence that the targeted dynamics appear beyond the conditioning representation itself.
summary.tldr: NMA-tune adds learned motion conditioning to RFdiffusion, improving the proportion of protein backbones with both high structural quality and desired dynamics.

title: NMA-tune: Generating Highly Designable and Dynamics Aware Protein Backbones

abstract: While deep learning has witnessed remarkable achievements in a wide range of applications, its substantial computational cost imposes limitations on application scenarios of neural networks. To alleviate this problem, low-rank compression is proposed as a class of efficient and hardware-friendly network compression methods, which reduce computation by replacing large matrices in neural networks with products of two small ones. In this paper, we implement low-rank networks by inserting a sufficiently narrow linear layer without bias between each of two adjacent nonlinear layers. We prove that low-rank Swish networks with a fixed depth are capable of approximating any function from the Hölder ball $\mathcal{C}^{\beta, R}([0,1]^d)$ within an arbitrarily small error where $\beta$ is the smooth parameter and $R$ is the radius. Our proposed constructive approximation ensures that the width of linear hidden layers required for approximation is no more than one-third of the width of nonlinear layers, which implies that the computational cost can be decreased by at least one-third compared with a network with the same depth and width of nonlinear layers but without narrow linear hidden layers. Our theoretical finding can offer a theoretical basis for low-rank compression from the perspective of universal approximation theory.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether reducing the cost of a neural network must weaken its ability to represent smooth functions. It studies low-rank compression, where a large weight matrix is replaced by a product of smaller matrices. The proposed network implements this structure by placing narrow, bias-free linear layers between adjacent nonlinear layers.

The central result concerns fixed-depth networks using the Swish activation. The authors prove that these networks can approximate any function in a specified Hölder ball on a unit cube to arbitrarily small error. This function class is defined by smoothness and radius parameters, so the guarantee concerns a mathematically specified family of smooth functions.

Their construction needs linear hidden layers no wider than one-third of the nonlinear layers. This implies at least a one-third reduction in computational cost relative to a network with the same depth and nonlinear-layer widths but without those narrow layers. The contribution is a constructive approximation guarantee: substantial low-rank structure can coexist with strong representational capability.
summary.tldr: Fixed-depth, low-rank Swish networks can approximate a specified class of smooth functions arbitrarily well while reducing computational cost.

title: Approximation to Smooth Functions by Low-Rank Swish Networks

abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has proven highly effective for enhancing complex reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Yet, it struggles in complex spatial reasoning tasks. Nonetheless, human cognition extends beyond language alone, enabling the remarkable capability to think in both words and images. Inspired by this mechanism, we propose a new reasoning paradigm, Multimodal Visualization-of-Thought (MVoT). It enables visual thinking in MLLMs by generating image visualizations of their reasoning traces. To ensure high-quality visualization, we introduce token discrepancy loss into autoregressive MLLMs. This innovation significantly improves both visual coherence and fidelity. We validate this approach through several dynamic spatial reasoning tasks. Experimental results reveal that MVoT demonstrates competitive performance across tasks. Moreover, it exhibits robust and reliable improvements in the most challenging scenarios where CoT fails. Ultimately, MVoT establishes new possibilities for complex reasoning tasks where visual thinking can effectively complement verbal reasoning.

MVoT creates image visualizations of a model's reasoning traces, giving spatial reasoning an explicit visual component. To improve those visualizations, the authors introduce token discrepancy loss into autoregressive multimodal language models. They report that this training innovation substantially improves visual coherence and fidelity, supporting the quality of the images used during the reasoning process.

The findings support visual thinking as a useful complement to verbal reasoning for these tasks, with the strongest stated benefits concentrated in particularly challenging spatial situations.
summary.tldr: MVoT adds generated visual reasoning traces to multimodal models, improving performance on challenging spatial reasoning tasks.

title: Imagine While Reasoning in Space: Multimodal Visualization-of-Thought

abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) has been demonstrated to improve the generalization performance of overparameterized models by seeking flat minima on the loss landscape through optimizing model parameters that incur the largest loss within a neighborhood. Nevertheless, such min-max formulations are computationally challenging especially when the problem is highly non-convex. Additionally, focusing only on the worst-case local solution while ignoring potentially many other local solutions may be suboptimal when searching for flat minima. In this work, we propose Tilted SAM (TSAM), a smoothed generalization of SAM inspired by exponential tilting that effectively assigns higher priority to local solutions that incur larger losses. TSAM is parameterized by a tilt hyperparameter $t$ and reduces to SAM as $t$ approaches infinity. We show that TSAM is smoother than SAM and thus easier to optimize, and it explicitly favors flatter minima. We develop algorithms motivated by the discretization of Hamiltonian dynamics to solve TSAM. Empirically, TSAM arrives at flatter local minima and results in superior test performance than the baselines of SAM and ERM across a range of image and text tasks.

paragraphs: Sharpness-Aware Minimization seeks parameters that perform well even at the highest-loss point in a nearby neighborhood. This can favor flat regions of the loss landscape, but its worst-case optimization is difficult in highly nonconvex problems. The paper also questions whether focusing exclusively on the single worst local outcome makes the best use of nearby information.

Tilted SAM replaces that focus with a smoothed objective based on exponential tilting. Nearby solutions with higher losses receive greater priority, controlled by a tilt parameter. As that parameter approaches infinity, the objective reduces to SAM. The authors show that the tilted objective is smoother, easier to optimize, and explicitly favors flatter minima.

They develop optimization algorithms motivated by discretized Hamiltonian dynamics. Across the evaluated image and text tasks, TSAM reaches flatter local minima and achieves better test performance than SAM and empirical risk minimization. These findings support a graded emphasis on high-loss neighboring solutions as a useful alternative to optimizing only the local worst case.
summary.tldr: Tilted SAM smooths sharpness-aware optimization by weighting nearby high-loss solutions, improving reported test performance across image and text tasks.

title: Tilted Sharpness-Aware Minimization

abstract: Estimation and inference for the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a cornerstone of causal inference and often serves as the foundation for developing procedures for more complicated settings. Although traditionally analyzed in a batch setting, recent advances in martingale theory have paved the way for adaptive methods that can enhance the power of downstream inference. Despite these advances, progress in understanding and developing adaptive algorithms remains in its early stages. Existing work either focus on asymptotic analyses that overlook exploration-exploitation trade-offs relevant in finite-sample regimes or rely on simpler but suboptimal estimators. In this work, we address these limitations by studying adaptive sampling procedures that take advantage of the asymptotically optimal Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting (AIPW) estimator. Our analysis uncovers challenges obscured by asymptotic approaches and introduces a novel algorithmic design principle reminiscent of optimism in multi-armed bandits. This principled approach enables our algorithm to achieve significant theoretical and empirical gains compared to previous methods. Our findings mark a step forward in the advancement of adaptive causal inference methods in theory and practice.

summary.tldr: The paper combines adaptive sampling with AIPW estimation using an optimism-inspired principle that improves theoretical and empirical performance.

title: Optimistic Algorithms for Adaptive Estimation of the Average Treatment Effect

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable reasoning capabilities across diverse domains. Recent studies have shown that increasing test-time computation enhances LLMs’ reasoning capabilities. This typically involves extensive sampling at inference time guided by an external LLM verifier, resulting in a two-player system. Despite external guidance, the effectiveness of this system demonstrates the potential of a single LLM to tackle complex tasks. Thus, we pose a new research problem: Can we internalize the searching capabilities to fundamentally enhance the reasoning abilities of a single LLM? This work explores an orthogonal direction focusing on post-training LLMs for autoregressive searching (i.e., an extended reasoning process with self-reflection and self-exploration of new strategies). To achieve this, we propose the Chain-of-Action-Thought (COAT) reasoning and a two-stage training paradigm: 1) a small-scale format tuning stage to internalize the COAT reasoning format and 2) a large-scale self-improvement stage leveraging reinforcement learning. Our approach results in Satori, a 7B LLM trained on open-source models and data. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that Satori achieves state-of-the-art performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks while exhibits strong generalization to out-of-domain tasks. Code, data, and models are fully open-sourced.

summary.tldr: Satori uses format tuning and reinforcement learning to teach a single language model reasoning with self-reflection and exploration of alternative strategies.

title: Satori: Reinforcement Learning with Chain-of-Action-Thought Enhances LLM Reasoning via Autoregressive Search

abstract: Though typically represented by the discrete node and edge attributes, the graph topological information can be sufficiently captured by the graph spectrum in a continuous space. It is believed that incorporating the continuity of graph topological information into the generative process design could establish a superior paradigm for graph generative modeling. Motivated by such prior and recent advancements in the generative paradigm, we propose Graph Bayesian Flow Networks (GraphBFN) in this paper, a principled generative framework that designs an alternative generative process emphasizing the dynamics of topological information. Unlike recent discrete-diffusion-based methods, GraphBFNemploys the continuous counts derived from sampling infinite times from a categorical distribution as latent to facilitate a smooth decomposition of topological information, demonstrating enhanced effectiveness. To effectively realize the concept, we further develop an advanced sampling strategy and new time-scheduling techniques to overcome practical barriers and boost performance. Through extensive experimental validation on both generic graph and molecular graph generation tasks, GraphBFN could consistently achieve superior or competitive performance with significantly higher training and sampling efficiency.

title: Smooth Interpolation for Improved Discrete Graph Generative Models

abstract: Motion transfer is to transfer pose in driving video to object of source image, so that object of source image moves. Although great progress has been made recently in unsupervised motion transfer, many unsupervised methods still struggle to accurately model large displacement motions when large motion differences occur between source and driving images. To solve the problem, we propose an unsupervised anytime interpolation based large displacement motion transfer method, which can generate a series of anytime interpolated images between source and driving images. By decomposing large displacement motion into many small displacement motions, difficulty of large displacement motion estimation is reduced. In the process, we design a selector that can select optimal interpolated image from generated interpolated images for downstream tasks. Since there are no real images as labels in the interpolation process, we propose a bidirectional training strategy. Some constraints are added to optimal interpolated image to generate a reasonable interpolated image. To encourage network to generate high-quality images, a pre-trained Vision Transformer model is used to design constraint losses. Finally, experiments show that compared with the large displacement motion between source and driving images, small displacement motion between interpolated and driving images is easier to realize motion transfer. Compared with existing state-of-art methods, our method has significant improvements in motion-related metrics.

paragraphs: Motion transfer animates an object from a source image using poses from a driving video. Large differences between source and driving poses are difficult for existing unsupervised methods to model. This paper addresses that difficulty by generating intermediate images, turning a large displacement into a sequence of smaller motion changes.

Additional constraint losses use a pretrained Vision Transformer to encourage image quality.

The experiments support the central premise: transferring motion across the smaller gap between an interpolated image and a driving image is easier than handling the original large gap. The method also reports significant improvements in motion-related metrics over existing state-of-the-art approaches. Interpolation thus serves as an intermediate computational step for making difficult motion transfer more manageable.
summary.tldr: The method improves large-displacement motion transfer by learning intermediate images that reduce the motion gap to the driving pose.

title: Large Displacement Motion Transfer with Unsupervised Anytime Interpolation

abstract: Document-level relation extraction (RE) aims to extract comprehensive correlations between entities and relations from documents. Most of existing works conduct transfer learning on pre-trained language models (PLMs), which allows for richer contextual representation to improve the performance. However, such PLMs-based methods suffer from incorporating structural knowledge, such as entity-entity interactions. Moreover, current works struggle to infer the implicit relations between entities across different sentences, which results in poor prediction. To deal with the above issues, we propose a novel and effective framework, named DocKS-RAG, which introduces extra structural knowledge and semantic information to further enhance the performance of document-level RE. Specifically, we construct a Document-level Knowledge Graph from the observable documentation data to better capture the structural information between entities and relations. Then, a Sentence-level Semantic Retrieval-Augmented Generation mechanism is designed to consider the similarity in different sentences by retrieving the relevant contextual semantic information. Furthermore, we present a hybrid-prompt tuning method on large language models (LLMs) for specific document-level RE tasks. Finally, extensive experiments conducted on two benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed framework enhances all the metrics compared with state-of-the-art methods.

Some relationships are implicit or span multiple sentences, making sentence-local evidence insufficient. DocKS-RAG combines structural and semantic information to address these difficulties. It builds a document-level knowledge graph from the available document data to represent connections between entities and relations. A sentence-level retrieval-augmented generation mechanism then retrieves relevant contextual information using similarities between sentences. Hybrid prompt tuning adapts a large language model to the relation extraction task.

These components give the model complementary evidence: the graph organizes relationships, while retrieval supplies related language context from elsewhere in the document. Experiments on two benchmark datasets report improvements across all evaluated metrics compared with state-of-the-art methods. The stated results support combining document structure, contextual retrieval, and task-specific prompting for more comprehensive relation extraction.
summary.tldr: DocKS-RAG combines document knowledge graphs, sentence-level retrieval, and hybrid prompt tuning to improve relation extraction.

title: DocKS-RAG: Optimizing Document-Level Relation Extraction through LLM-Enhanced Hybrid Prompt Tuning

abstract: We introduce a novel resampling criterion using lift scores, for improving compositional generation in diffusion models. By leveraging the lift scores, we evaluate whether generated samples align with each single condition and then compose the results to determine whether the composed prompt is satisfied. Our key insight is that lift scores can be efficiently approximated using only the original diffusion model, requiring no additional training or external modules. We develop an optimized variant that achieves relatively lower computational overhead during inference while maintaining effectiveness. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that lift scores significantly improved the condition alignment for compositional generation across 2D synthetic data, CLEVR position tasks, and text-to-image synthesis. Our code is available at github.com/rainorangelemon/complift.

paragraphs: Compositional generation asks a model to satisfy several conditions together. A generated sample may match parts of a request while missing the complete combination. This paper introduces a resampling criterion based on lift scores, using separate checks of the individual conditions to assess whether their composition has been satisfied.

The key practical insight is that these scores can be approximated efficiently using the original diffusion model itself. The approach does not require another training stage or an external module to assess condition alignment. The authors also develop an optimized version that reduces inference overhead relative to their approach while maintaining its effectiveness.

Experiments cover two-dimensional synthetic data, CLEVR position tasks, and text-to-image synthesis. Across these settings, the authors report significant improvements in how well generated samples align with composed conditions. The contribution is a way to guide resampling using the model's own information about individual requirements, with an optimized variant that makes the added inference work less costly.
summary.tldr: Lift-score resampling improves diffusion models' adherence to combined conditions using the original model without additional training or external modules.

title: Improving Compositional Generation with Diffusion Models Using Lift Scores

abstract: This paper introduces two novel criteria: one for feature selection and another for feature elimination in the context of best subset selection, which is a benchmark problem in statistics and machine learning. From the perspective of optimization, we revisit the classical selection and elimination criteria in traditional best subset selection algorithms, revealing that these classical criteria capture only partial variations of the objective function after the entry or exit of features. By formulating and solving optimization subproblems for feature entry and exit exactly, new selection and elimination criteria are proposed, proved as the optimal decisions for the current entry-and-exit process compared to classical criteria. Replacing the classical selection and elimination criteria with the proposed ones generates a series of enhanced best subset selection algorithms. These generated algorithms not only preserve the theoretical properties of the original algorithms but also achieve significant meta-gains without increasing computational cost across various scenarios and evaluation metrics on multiple tasks such as compressed sensing and sparse regression.

paragraphs: Best subset selection seeks a useful collection of features, and many algorithms build that collection by repeatedly adding or removing features. This paper revisits the rules used to make those decisions. Its central observation is that classical selection and elimination criteria account for only part of the change in the optimization objective after a feature enters or leaves.

The authors formulate optimization subproblems for feature entry and exit and solve them exactly. These solutions produce two replacement criteria, one for adding features and another for removing them. The resulting decisions are proved optimal for the current entry or exit process. This is a statement about each decision within that process, rather than a claim that every complete subset search reaches a global optimum.

Replacing existing criteria yields enhanced versions of multiple subset-selection algorithms while preserving their theoretical properties. Across tasks including compressed sensing and sparse regression, the paper reports substantial gains across different evaluation measures without increasing computational cost. The contribution therefore improves a shared decision mechanism used by several algorithms.
summary.tldr: Exact feature-entry and feature-exit criteria improve existing subset-selection algorithms without increasing their computational cost.

title: Best Subset Selection: Optimal Pursuit for Feature Selection and Elimination

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a transformative AI paradigm, profoundly influencing broad aspects of daily life. Despite their remarkable performance, LLMs exhibit a fundamental limitation: hallucination—the tendency to produce misleading outputs that appear plausible. This inherent unreliability poses significant risks, particularly in high-stakes domains where trustworthiness is essential.On the other hand, Formal Methods (FMs), which share foundations with symbolic AI, provide mathematically rigorous techniques for modeling, specifying, reasoning, and verifying the correctness of systems. These methods have been widely employed in mission-critical domains such as aerospace, defense, and cybersecurity. However, the broader adoption of FMs remains constrained by significant challenges, including steep learning curves, limited scalability, and difficulties in adapting to the dynamic requirements of daily applications.To build trustworthy AI agents, we argue that the integration of LLMs and FMs is necessary to overcome the limitations of both paradigms. LLMs offer adaptability and human-like reasoning but lack formal guarantees of correctness and reliability. FMs provide rigor but need enhanced accessibility and automation to support broader adoption from LLMs.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that trustworthy AI agents require language models and formal methods to work together. Language models offer adaptability and human-like reasoning, but they can also generate plausible, misleading outputs. That unreliability creates particular concern in settings where correctness has high stakes.

Formal methods provide mathematically rigorous ways to describe systems, specify requirements, reason about behavior, and verify correctness. They already have applications in mission-critical areas such as aerospace, defense, and cybersecurity. Their wider use faces substantial obstacles, including difficult learning curves, scalability limits, and trouble accommodating changing requirements in everyday applications.

The authors present integration as necessary to overcome the complementary weaknesses of the two approaches. Formal methods contribute rigor that language models lack, while language models could improve the accessibility and automation needed for broader use of formal methods. The paper’s central position is that developing trustworthy agents should bring these capabilities together, addressing both the reliability of AI behavior and the practical usability of verification.
summary.tldr: The authors argue that trustworthy agents need language models’ adaptability combined with the mathematical rigor of formal methods.

title: Position: Trustworthy AI Agents Require the Integration of Large Language Models and Formal Methods

abstract: Influence functions are a standard tool for data debugging and unlearning, but they become impractical for high-query subset workloads such as large-$K$ cross-validation, repeated resampling, or interactive what-if analysis as each subset query typically requires an expensive inverse-curvature solve. We introduce Clustered Influence Functions (CiF), which turns subset influence into an amortized subset oracle. We build a compact cache once by clustering training gradients, solve a damped Generalised Gauss-Newton system only for cluster means, and answer new subset queries by a linear recombination using cluster membership counts. This yields per-query cost of $O(Cp)$ linear in the cache size $C$, and the number of model parameters $p$. We further provide a diagnostic error bound that decomposes approximation error into a clustering scatter term and a solver residual term, making the accuracy-compute tradeoff explicit through the cache budget and solver tolerance. Evaluations across MNIST, CIFAR-10 show that CiF matches per-query influence rankings while significantly reducing the total runtime in high-$Q$ regimes, enabling influence-based workflows that are otherwise computationally prohibitive.

paragraphs: Influence functions help estimate how training data affects a model, supporting tasks such as data debugging and unlearning. Their cost becomes especially troublesome when users repeatedly ask about different subsets of data. Each new subset can require another expensive computation involving the model’s curvature, making repeated what-if analysis difficult.

Clustered Influence Functions shares that work across queries. It groups training gradients into clusters, solves a damped Generalised Gauss-Newton system for each cluster mean, and stores the results. A new subset query then combines cached results according to how many members of each cluster the subset contains. Its per-query cost is O(Cp), where C is the cache size and p is the number of model parameters.

The paper also separates approximation error into variation within clusters and residual error from the numerical solver. This exposes how cache size and solver tolerance affect the accuracy–compute trade-off. On MNIST and CIFAR-10, the method matches per-query influence rankings while substantially reducing total runtime when many queries are made.
summary.tldr: Clustered Influence Functions caches shared computations to make repeated training-data influence queries substantially cheaper.

title: Clustered Influence Functions

abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) has shown notable success in accelerating the post-training of large language models (LLMs). However, its decoupled data generation and training paradigm introduces a fundamental distributional mismatch between data generated by stale behavior policies and current policy, leading to unstable training and degraded performance. To address this challenge, we propose D-ARL, a Distribution-matched Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning framework that selects high-quality asynchronous samples whose distributions are well aligned with the current policy for policy optimization. Specifically, D-ARL maintains a replay buffer that collects samples from the most recent $K$ behavior policies and proposes a variance-guided metric to select distribution-matched data. During training, D-ARL introduces a multi-behavior policy optimization algorithm to leverage the multi-source nature of the selected samples for policy update. Experiments on six widely used reasoning benchmarks show that D-ARL outperforms state-of-the-art asynchronous methods, achieving an average improvement of 6.4% in reasoning performance and 34.7% in sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Asynchronous reinforcement learning speeds up language-model post-training by separating the generation of training examples from model updates. That separation creates a moving-target problem: examples may come from older versions of the model, whose behavior differs from the current version. The paper addresses the resulting mismatch, which can destabilize training and weaken reasoning performance.

D-ARL keeps a replay buffer containing samples from the most recent K behavior policies. Rather than treating all available samples as equally suitable, it uses a variance-guided measure to select high-quality examples whose distributions align with the current policy. A multi-behavior policy optimization algorithm then accounts for the selected data coming from several policy versions.

Across six reasoning benchmarks, the authors report average improvements of 6.4% in reasoning performance and 34.7% in sample efficiency over state-of-the-art asynchronous methods. The contribution connects sample selection with the update rule: both are designed around the fact that asynchronous data have multiple, changing sources. The reported results show benefits from explicitly managing that mismatch during training.
summary.tldr: D-ARL improves asynchronous language-model reinforcement learning by selecting samples that better match the current policy.

title: D-ARL: A Distribution-Matched Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning Framework for Language Reasoning

abstract: We propose causal preference elicitation, a Bayesian framework for expert-in-the-loop causal discovery that actively queries local edge relations to concentrate a posterior over directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). From any black-box observational posterior, we model noisy expert judgments with a three-way likelihood over edge existence and direction. Posterior inference uses a flexible particle approximation, and queries are selected by an efficient expected information gain criterion on the expert’s categorical response. Experiments on synthetic graphs, protein signaling data, and a human gene perturbation benchmark show faster posterior concentration and improved recovery of directed effects under tight query budgets.

From any black-box observational posterior, we model noisy expert judgments with a three-way likelihood over edge existence and direction. Posterior inference uses a flexible particle approximation, and queries are selected by an efficient expected information gain criterion on the expert’s categorical response. paragraphs: Causal discovery can leave uncertainty about whether two variables are connected and which direction the connection takes. This paper proposes using expert judgments to refine that uncertainty through targeted questions. Its Bayesian framework maintains a distribution over possible directed acyclic graphs, allowing multiple causal explanations to remain under consideration.

The method starts from any black-box posterior obtained from observational data. It models noisy expert answers with a three-way likelihood covering local edge existence and direction, then updates a flexible particle approximation of the graph posterior. Questions are selected using expected information gain: the method favors queries whose possible categorical answers are expected to reduce uncertainty efficiently.

Experiments on synthetic graphs, protein signaling data, and a human gene perturbation benchmark show faster posterior concentration and better recovery of directed effects under tight query budgets. The practical contribution is a way to spend limited expert attention on informative local relationships. Accounting for noisy judgments also lets those answers influence the posterior without treating every expert response as an unquestionable fact.
summary.tldr: Targeted questions about causal edges help a Bayesian discovery system learn more from limited, potentially noisy expert input.

title: Causal Preference Elicitation

abstract: Weight-only quantization has become a standard approach for efficiently serving large language models (LLMs). However, existing methods fail to efficiently compress models to binary (1-bit) levels, as they either require large amounts of data and compute or incur additional storage. In this work, we propose NanoQuant, a post-training quantization (PTQ) method to compress LLMs to both binary and sub-1-bit levels. NanoQuant formulates quantization as a low-rank binary factorization problem, and compresses full-precision weights to low-rank binary matrices and scales. Specifically, it utilizes an efficient alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) solver to precisely initialize latent binary matrices and scales, and then tunes the initialized parameters through a block and model reconstruction process. Consequently, NanoQuant establishes a new Pareto frontier in low-memory post-training quantization, and enables sub-1-bit compression. NanoQuant makes large-scale deployment feasible on consumer hardware. For example, it compresses Llama-2-70B by 24$\times$ in just 13 hours on a single H100, enabling a 70B model to operate on a consumer 8 GB GPU.

paragraphs: Weight quantization reduces the storage needed to serve language models, but reaching binary or smaller effective representations can demand substantial computation, data, or extra storage. NanoQuant targets this extreme compression regime with a post-training method. It represents full-precision weight matrices through low-rank binary matrices and associated scales, allowing binary and sub-one-bit compression.

The method frames compression as a low-rank binary factorization problem. An alternating direction method of multipliers solver initializes the binary factors and scales, after which block-level and model-level reconstruction tune those parameters. The training hardware and deployment hardware serve different roles: the compression computation produces a representation small enough for the latter.
summary.tldr: NanoQuant uses low-rank binary factorization and reconstruction to compress language-model weights to binary and sub-one-bit representations.

title: NanoQuant: Efficient Sub-1-Bit Quantization of Large Language Models

abstract: Despite their theoretical advantages, spectral methods based on the graph Fourier transform (GFT) are seldom used in graph neural networks (GNNs) due to the cost of computing the eigenbasis and the lack of vertex-domain locality in the resulting representations. As a result, most GNNs rely on local approximations such as polynomial Laplacian filters or message passing, which limit their ability to model long-range dependencies. In this paper, we introduce an exact factorization of the GFT into operators acting on subgraphs, which are then combined via a sequence of Cauchy matrices. Building on this factorization, we propose a new class of spectral GNNs, termed L2G-Net (Local to Global Net). Unlike existing spectral methods, which are either fully global (when using the GFT) or local (when using polynomial filters), L2G-Net operates by processing the spectral representations of subgraphs and then combining them via structured matrices. Our algorithm avoids full eigendecompositions, exploiting graph topology to construct the factorization with quadratic complexity in the number of nodes, scaled by the maximum cut size between subgraphs. Experiments stressing long-range dependencies on large graphs show that L2G-Net scales to regimes out of reach for the standard GFT, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods with orders of magnitude fewer learnable parameters.

paragraphs: Spectral graph methods describe signals using the graph Fourier transform, but computing its eigenbasis is expensive and its representations lack vertex-level locality. Common alternatives rely on local message passing or polynomial filters, which limit their ability to capture distant relationships. L2G-Net introduces a construction that connects subgraph processing to a global spectral representation.

The mathematical core is an exact factorization of the graph Fourier transform into operators on subgraphs, combined through a sequence of Cauchy matrices. The resulting network processes spectral information locally and then joins it using these structured matrices. Construction avoids a full eigendecomposition, with complexity quadratic in the number of nodes and scaled by the largest cut between subgraphs.

They show operation at scales beyond the standard graph Fourier transform and performance competitive with state-of-the-art methods using orders of magnitude fewer learnable parameters. The contribution is therefore an exact local-to-global spectral construction with demonstrated scaling benefits, rather than solely another local approximation.
summary.tldr: L2G-Net factors the graph Fourier transform through subgraphs to model long-range structure with fewer parameters and improved practical scalability.

title: L2G-NET: Local to Global Spectral Graph Neural Networks via Cauchy Factorizations

abstract: Modern visual generative models acquire rich visual knowledge through large-scale training, yet existing visual representations (such as pixels, latents, or tokens) remain external to the model and cannot directly exploit this knowledge for compact storage or reuse. In this work, we introduce a new visual representation framework that encodes a signal as a function, which is parametrized by low-rank adaptations attached to a frozen visual generative model. Such implicit representations of visual signals, e.g., an 81-frame video, can further be hashed into a single compact vector, achieving strong perceptual video compression at extremely low bitrates. Beyond basic compression, the functional nature of this representation enables inference-time scaling and control, allowing additional refinement on the compression performance. More broadly, as the implicit representations directly act as a function of the generation process, this suggests a unified framework bridging visual compression and generation.

paragraphs: This paper explores storing visual content through adaptations to a pretrained generative model. Its starting observation is that generative models already contain extensive visual knowledge, but conventional representations such as pixels, tokens, and latent arrays remain separate from that knowledge. The authors seek a representation that makes the model's learned generation process part of how the content is encoded.

They represent a visual signal as a function parameterized by low-rank adaptations attached to a frozen generative model. These adaptations provide the signal-specific representation while the underlying model stays fixed. The resulting implicit representation can also be hashed into a compact vector; the abstract gives an 81-frame video as an example of content represented this way.

The authors report strong perceptual video compression at extremely low bitrates. Because decoding involves a function within the generation process, additional inference-time computation and control can further refine compression performance. This connection suggests a broader framework joining compression and generation, with the pretrained model's visual knowledge contributing directly to representation and reconstruction.
summary.tldr: Visual content can be encoded as small adaptations to a frozen generative model, supporting compact storage and inference-time refinement.

title: Compression as Adaptation: Implicit Visual Representation with Diffusion Foundation Models

abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable success in tasks such as image captioning and visual question answering (VQA). However, as their applications become increasingly widespread, recent studies have revealed that VLMs are vulnerable to backdoor attacks. Existing backdoor attacks on VLMs primarily rely on data poisoning by adding visual triggers and modifying text labels, where the induced image–text mismatch makes poisoned samples easy to detect. To address this limitation, we propose the Clean-Label Backdoor Attack on VLMs via Diffusion Models (CBV), which leverages diffusion models to generate natural poisoned examples via score matching. Specifically, CBV modifies the score during the reverse generation process of the diffusion model to guide the generation of poisoned samples that contain triggered image features. To further enhance the effectiveness of the attack, we incorporate the textual information of the triggered images as multimodal guidance during generation. Moreover, to enhance stealthiness, we introduce a GradCAM-guided Mask (GM) that restricts modifications to only the most semantically important regions, rather than the entire image. We evaluate our method on MSCOCO and VQA v2 with four representative VLMs, achieving over 80% ASR while preserving normal functionality.

paragraphs: Backdoor attacks can alter how vision-language models behave when particular image features appear. Existing attacks often poison training data by inserting visual triggers and changing text labels. The resulting disagreement between an image and its text can make the poisoned examples easier to identify. CBV investigates an attack that preserves the labels.

The method uses a diffusion model to produce natural-looking poisoned images. It changes the model's score during reverse generation to introduce the desired triggered features, and uses associated text as additional multimodal guidance. A GradCAM-guided mask confines image changes to semantically important regions, which the authors introduce to improve stealthiness.

The researchers evaluate CBV on MSCOCO and VQA v2 using four representative vision-language models. They report attack success rates above 80% while preserving normal functionality. The findings show that, in these evaluations, strong backdoor behavior can coexist with ordinary model performance and unchanged labels. This makes the image-generation process itself relevant to understanding poisoned data, beyond checking for obvious image–text mismatches.
summary.tldr: CBV uses diffusion-generated images to implant clean-label backdoors in vision-language models while preserving their normal functionality in reported evaluations.

title: CBV: Clean-label Backdoor Attacks on Vision Language Models via Diffusion Models

abstract: Diffusion Policy has dominated action generation due to its strong capabilities for modeling multi-modal action distributions, but its multi-step denoising processes make it impractical for real-time visuomotor control. Existing caching-based acceleration methods typically rely on $\textit{static}$ schedules that fail to adapt to the dynamics of robot-environment interactions, thereby leading to suboptimal performance. In this paper, we propose $\underline{\textbf{S}}$parse $\underline{\textbf{A}}$ction$\underline{\textbf{G}}$en $(\textbf{SAG})$ for extremely sparse action generation. To accommodate the iterative interactions, SAG customizes a rollout-adaptive prune-then-reuse mechanism that first identifies prunable computations globally and then reuses cached activations to substitute them during action diffusion. To capture the rollout dynamics, SAG parameterizes an observation-conditioned diffusion pruner for environment-aware adaptation and instantiates it with a highly parameter- and inference-efficient design for real-time prediction. Furthermore, SAG introduces a one-for-all reusing strategy that reuses activations across both timesteps and blocks in a zig-zag manner, minimizing the global redundancy. Extensive experiments on multiple robotic benchmarks demonstrate that SAG achieves up to 4$\times$ generation speedup without sacrificing performance. Project Page: https://sparse-actiongen.github.io/.

paragraphs: Sparse ActionGen accelerates diffusion policies used to generate robotic actions. These policies can represent multiple possible action patterns, but repeated denoising steps make real-time control difficult. Existing methods reuse cached computations on static schedules, which may not adapt well as the robot and its environment interact.

The proposed prune-then-reuse mechanism first identifies computations that can be removed across the action-generation process, then substitutes cached activations during diffusion. An observation-conditioned pruner adapts these decisions to the current environment and rollout. Its design is efficient in both parameters and inference, keeping the adaptation itself suitable for real-time prediction.

A further reuse strategy shares activations across both denoising timesteps and network blocks in a zig-zag pattern to reduce overall redundancy. Across multiple robotic benchmarks, Sparse ActionGen reports action-generation speedups of up to fourfold without sacrificing performance. The findings support adapting computation reuse to the ongoing interaction, so acceleration decisions can reflect changing observations rather than depending only on a fixed schedule.
summary.tldr: Sparse ActionGen adapts pruning and activation reuse to robot observations, achieving up to fourfold faster action generation without reported performance loss.

title: Sparse ActionGen: Accelerating Diffusion Policy with Real-time Pruning

abstract: The operational cost of serving large language models remains prohibitively high, largely due to extreme workload heterogeneity in production traffic. We observe that combining disaggregated inference with resource autoscaling enables fine-grained resource adjustment, allowing inference phases and operations to scale independently based on their specific bottlenecks. Building on this insight, we propose HexGen-3, a cost-effective LLM serving framework that leverages a fully disaggregated inference architecture and heterogeneous resource autoscaling. HexGen-3 introduces two key components: (i) A hierarchical scheduling framework that jointly optimizes resource allocation and parallelism configuration for any given resource provisioning, and (ii) an autoscaling framework that dynamically adjusts resources and triggers deployment rescheduling in response to workload fluctuations. Experiments comparing HexGen-3 against state-of-the-art LLM serving systems demonstrate up to 60% (on average 46.5%) improvement in per-cost throughput under static resource provisioning, and up to 78.3% (on average 55.1%) improvement with autoscaling enabled under dynamic workloads.

paragraphs: HexGen-3 targets the cost of serving language models under production traffic with widely varying resource demands. Its central idea is to separate inference phases and operations so their resources can scale independently. This makes it possible to respond to the particular bottleneck of each component instead of adjusting the entire deployment as one unit.

A hierarchical scheduler jointly chooses resource allocation and parallelism settings for the resources currently provisioned. An autoscaling component then changes those resources as workloads fluctuate and triggers a new deployment schedule. Together, these mechanisms address both how to use an available resource pool and when that pool should change.

Compared with state-of-the-art serving systems, experiments report per-cost throughput improvements of up to 60%, averaging 46.5%, with static provisioning. Under dynamic workloads with autoscaling, improvements reach 78.3%, averaging 55.1%. These are efficiency gains measured relative to cost, supporting the value of coordinating fine-grained deployment decisions with changing resource availability.
summary.tldr: HexGen-3 independently scales inference components and coordinates scheduling with autoscaling to improve LLM throughput per unit cost.

title: HexGen-3: A Fully Disaggregated LLM Serving Framework with Fine-Grained Heterogeneous Resource Autoscaling

abstract: Distilling long-form reasoning from teacher models into smaller students requires selecting which candidate solutions to train on. Recent work argues that one should select responses the student model assigns highest probability, i.e., favoring solutions “natural” to the student. However, we find that this approach works within a single teacher but fails when scaling to long reasoning traces from multiple diverse teachers. We identify a key cause: this approach scores entire solutions, but students generalize by recombining familiar reasoning steps, not by memorizing complete solutions. Full-trajectory scoring optimizes the wrong target; it rewards global fluency while the transferable signal lies in local step transitions. We propose Local Average Log Probability (LALP), which scores each reasoning step using only a small window of preceding context, measuring whether each step is justified by its immediate premises rather than whether the full response looks natural to the student. LALP enables two practical use cases: selecting the best teacher before fine-tuning and curating training data from diverse teacher pools. Across math, coding, and science reasoning tasks, LALP consistently improves accuracy when selecting the most natural solutions by a large margin.

paragraphs: Training a smaller model on reasoning from larger teachers requires choosing which solutions to include. One strategy favors complete responses that the student already assigns high probability. The paper finds that this strategy works within a single teacher but fails when selecting long reasoning traces from several diverse teachers.

The authors attribute this failure to scoring at the wrong scale. Whole-response probability rewards global fluency, while the transferable information lies in familiar transitions between reasoning steps. Their Local Average Log Probability score evaluates each step using only a short window of preceding context. Across mathematical, coding, and scientific reasoning tasks, the authors report consistent accuracy improvements by a large margin over selecting the most natural complete solutions. The findings suggest that useful reasoning data can be identified through local step compatibility even when whole-trajectory likelihood is an unreliable selection signal.
summary.tldr: LALP selects reasoning data by scoring local step transitions, improving student accuracy when learning from diverse teachers.

title: The Signal is in the Steps: Local Scoring for Reasoning Data Selection

abstract: Computational protein design typically employs a sequential workflow of structure generation followed by sequence (re)design. While structure generators can be explicitly conditioned on functional objectives, inverse folding models are constrained by their function-agnostic nature and sequence-structure degeneracy. More critically, the associated training objectives do not account for the Best-of-N (BoN) inference protocol, resulting in a fundamental training-inference misalignment. Here, we propose FIDIA, a reinforcement learning framework that enables Function-Informed sequence Design via Inference-Aligned policy optimization. Specifically, FIDIA integrates functional constraints into composite rewards and explicitly optimize the induced policy under BoN toward high-fitness sequence regions. We achieve this via a grounded gradient estimator that directly maximizes the expected maximum reward. FIDIA consistently outperforms both standard and RL-optimized baselines in success rate and precision on a general motif scaffolding benchmark. Further experiments on realworld cases including vaccine and affinity-enhancing enzyme design validate FIDIA’s efficacy in complex therapeutic and biocatalytic contexts.

paragraphs: Protein design often starts by generating a structure and then finding an amino-acid sequence for it. A structure can be designed around a functional goal, yet the subsequent sequence model may not account for that goal. Multiple sequences can correspond to a structure, making structural compatibility alone insufficient to resolve the functional design choice.

FIDIA incorporates functional constraints into reinforcement-learning rewards and aligns training with Best-of-N inference, where several candidates are generated and the best is selected. Its gradient estimator directly targets the expected maximum reward among candidates. This makes the learning objective reflect the selection procedure used at inference, while steering sequence generation toward regions with high functional fitness.

On a general motif-scaffolding benchmark, FIDIA consistently improves success rate and precision over standard and reinforcement-learning-optimized baselines. Additional experiments address vaccine design and enzyme designs intended to enhance affinity. These findings support combining functional objectives with selection-aware training for the studied protein-design tasks, including the reported therapeutic and biocatalytic cases.
summary.tldr: FIDIA optimizes protein sequence design for functional goals and the Best-of-N selection procedure used at inference.

title: FIDIA: Function-Informed Sequence Design via Inference-Aligned Policy Optimization

abstract: Planning and acting in 3D environments is a fundamental capability for robotic manipulation in the real world. Although prior work has explored predictive flow planners to guide 3D manipulation, existing approaches often rely on modular pipelines stacking multiple submodels, resulting in high computational overhead and limited real-time performance. To address these challenges, we introduce RoboFlow4D, a lightweight flow world model that unifies perception and planning by estimating temporal motion in physical 3D space. As an end-to-end framework, RoboFlow4D directly predicts multi-frame 3D flows from visual observations and textual instructions, providing explicit flow-based planning to guide action generation. This design allows seamless integration with general action policies, forming an efficient observation–planning–execution closed loop. Through slow–fast collaboration between flow prediction and action control, RoboFlow4D enables real-time and resource-efficient manipulation. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world settings demonstrate that RoboFlow4D consistently improves manipulation success rates and computational efficiency, advancing flow-guided planning for embodied intelligence. Our project page is available at RoboFlow4D.

paragraphs: RoboFlow4D uses predicted motion in three-dimensional space to guide robotic manipulation. Previous predictive-flow planners often combine multiple submodels, creating computational overhead that limits real-time operation. This paper introduces a lightweight world model that connects perception and planning within an end-to-end framework.

Given visual observations and a textual instruction, the model directly predicts 3D flows across multiple future frames. These flows provide an explicit motion plan that can guide action generation by a general action policy. Flow prediction and action control cooperate at slower and faster rates, respectively, supporting a closed loop from observation through planning to execution.

Experiments in simulation and real-world settings show consistent improvements in manipulation success rates and computational efficiency. The authors also report real-time, resource-efficient operation. The design's significance is that an explicit spatial plan can remain part of the control process without requiring a heavy stack of separate prediction modules. Its integration with general action policies makes flow planning a component that can guide execution within the overall robotic loop.
summary.tldr: RoboFlow4D predicts multi-frame 3D motion from images and instructions to guide efficient, real-time robotic manipulation.

title: RoboFlow4D: A Lightweight Flow World Model Toward Real-Time Flow-Guided Robotic Manipulation

abstract: Post-training with reinforcement learning (RL) has recently shown strong promise for advancing multimodal agents beyond supervised imitation. However, RL remains limited by poor data efficiency, particularly in settings where interaction data are scarce and quickly become outdated. To address this challenge, GIPO (Gaussian Importance sampling Policy Optimization) is proposed as a policy optimization objective based on truncated importance sampling, replacing hard clipping with a log-ratio-based Gaussian trust weight to softly damp extreme importance ratios while maintaining non-zero gradients. Theoretical analysis shows that GIPO introduces an implicit, tunable constraint on the update magnitude, while concentration bounds guarantee robustness and stability under finite-sample estimation. Experimental results show that GIPO achieves state-of-the-art performance among clipping-based baselines across a wide range of replay buffer sizes, from near on-policy to highly stale data, while exhibiting superior bias–variance trade-off, high training stability and improved sample efficiency. Code is available at https://github.com/distanceLu/GIPO.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can improve multimodal agents beyond supervised imitation, but interaction data may be scarce and become outdated as the policy changes. Reusing these data requires accounting for differences between the policy that collected them and the current policy. Extreme importance ratios make that correction difficult and can destabilize learning.

GIPO changes how those ratios influence the optimization objective. Instead of hard clipping, it applies a Gaussian weight based on the logarithm of the ratio. This smoothly reduces the effect of extreme values while preserving nonzero gradients. Theoretical analysis identifies an implicit, adjustable constraint on update size, and concentration bounds address robustness and stability when estimates come from finite samples.

Experiments cover replay buffers ranging from nearly current-policy data to highly stale experience. Among the evaluated clipping-based baselines, GIPO achieves state-of-the-art performance while improving sample efficiency, training stability, and the bias–variance balance. The findings support softer control of importance weights as a way to keep learning from older interactions without letting unusually large corrections dominate updates.
summary.tldr: GIPO softly suppresses extreme importance ratios with Gaussian weights, improving the stability and efficiency of learning from reused interaction data.

title: GIPO: Gaussian Importance Sampling Policy Optimization

abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) is compute-intensive and error-prone: model performance depends sensitively on data quality and hyperparameter choices, and naïve runs can even degrade model performance. This raises a practical question:can we predict fine-tuning performance before committing to a full training run? We present TUNEAHEAD, a lightweight framework for pre-hoc prediction of fine-tuning performance. TUNEAHEAD encodes each candidate run as a meta-feature vector that combines static dataset descriptors with dynamic probe features from a short standardized probe. A predictor maps these features to performance estimates, while SHAP-based attributions provide interpretable diagnostics that reveal which specific features drive the prediction. Across 1,300+ fine-tuning runs on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, TUNEAHEAD consistently outperforms strong baselines such as Early-Stop Extrapolation and ProxyLM. On a held-out test set of 370 runs, TUNEAHEAD achieves an RMSE of 1.47 percentage points and places 95.1% of predictions within $\pm$3 percentage points of the true score. These accurate continuous predictions support practical go/no-go screening policies that can reduce unnecessary full fine-tuning while retaining most promising runs.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning can consume substantial computation and sometimes make a model worse, depending on the data and training choices. TuneAhead predicts performance before committing to a complete run. It uses a short standardized training probe, so the prediction is available before full training rather than requiring no training activity at all.

summary.tldr: TuneAhead combines dataset features and a short training probe to predict fine-tuning performance and screen candidate runs before full training.

title: TuneAhead: Predicting Fine-tuning Performance Before Full Training Begins

abstract: Autoregressive large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in many complex tasks, yet they can still fail in very simple logical reasoning such as the "reversal curse" — when trained on forward knowledge data of the form "$A \rightarrow B$" (e.g., Alice’s husband is Bob), the model is unable to deduce the reversal knowledge "$B \leftarrow A$" (e.g., Bob’s wife is Alice) during test. Extensive prior research suggests that this failure is an inherent, fundamental limit of autoregressive causal LLMs, indicating that these models tend to memorize factual-level knowledge rather than capture higher-level rules. In this paper, we challenge this view by showing that this seemingly fundamental limit can be mitigated by slightly tweaking the training data with a simple regularization data recipe called the Identity Bridge of the form "$A \to A$" (e.g., The name of Alice is Alice). Theoretically, we prove that under this recipe, even a one-layer transformer can break the reversal curse by analyzing the implicit bias of gradient descent. Empirically, we show that a 1B pretrained language model finetuned with the proposed data recipe achieves a 50% success rate on reversal tasks, in stark contrast to a near-zero success rate when trained solely on forward-knowledge data. Our work provides a novel theoretical foundation for the reversal curse and offers a principled, low-cost path to encouraging LLMs to learn higher-level rules from data.
